definition: At the beginning.

Bound by contract.
The quality of being produced by people and not occurring naturally.
Characterized by an inability to mask your feelings; not devious.
example: This pendant has artless charm.

definition: (Hinduism) a posture or manner of sitting (as in the practice of yoga).
etymology: Borrowed from Sanskrit आसन (ā́sana, āsaná, “sitting down”), from आस्ते (ā́ste, “to sit down”).

definition: The state that exists when one person or group has power over another.
The state that exists when one person or group has power over another.
Accumulation of serous fluid in peritoneal cavity.

definition: Free of or using methods to keep free of pathological microorganisms.

definition: Having no evident sex or sex organs.

definition: In an asexual manner.

definition: With suspicion or disapproval.

definition: Someone who asks a question.

definition: A crystalline amino acid found in proteins and occurring naturally in sugar beets and sugar cane.

definition: Remove by suction.

definition: Attack someone physically or emotionally.

etymology: From Middle English assailen, from Old French assaillir, assalir, from Late Latin assalīre, from Latin ad (“at, towards”) + salīre (“jump”). See also assault.

definition: A woman who is a member of a legislative assembly.
In an assertive manner.

definition: A person (or property) that is assessed.

etymology: A learned borrowing from Latin assiduus, from assidere (“to sit down to”), from ad- (“to”) + sedere (“to sit”). Compare sedulous. Cognate (via assidere) to assess.

definition: Legally transferable to the ownership of another.

etymology: From Middle English assignacioun, from Old French assignacion, from Latin assīgnātiō.

definition: (law) the party to whom something is assigned (e.g., someone to whom a right or property is legally transferred).

definition: The regulation of weights and measures of articles offered for sale.

definition: The bone in the ankle that articulates with the leg bones to form the ankle joint.
etymology: From Latin astragalus, from Ancient Greek ἀστράγαλος (astrágalos). Doublet of astragal.

definition: The fur of young lambs.
etymology: Named after the city of Astrakhan in Southern Russia.

definition: The branch of biology concerned with the effects of outer space on living organisms and the search for extraterrestrial life.
A transparent dome on top of an airplane where the navigator can make celestial observations.
An early form of sextant.
etymology: From Middle English astrelabie et al., from Middle French astrolabe, Old French astrelabe, from Ancient Greek ἀστρολάβος (astrolábos, “star-taking”), from ἄστρον (ástron, “star”) + λαμβάνω (lambánō, “I take”).

definition: Enormously.
example: The bill was astronomically high.

definition: In a shrewd manner.
example: He invested his fortune astutely.

definition: In an asymmetrical manner.
example: They were asymmetrically arranged.

definition: Characteristic of an atavist.
A literary or scientific association for the promotion of learning.
Of or relating to atherosclerosis.
A crackling or hissing noise caused by electrical interference.
Characterized by avoidance of traditional western tonality.
An abnormal condition in which a normal opening or tube in the body (as the urethra) is closed or absent.
etymology: From Latin atresia, from Ancient Greek ἀ- (a-, “not, without”) and τρῆσις (trêsis, “perforation”).

definition: Cancellation of civil rights.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman ataindre ("to reach"), with infinitives used as nouns being frequent in Law French. Doublet of attain and attinge.

definition: Essential oil or perfume obtained from flowers.
etymology: Borrowed from Persian عطر (atr, “scent”), from Arabic عِطْر (ʕiṭr, “perfume”).

definition: An electrical device for attenuating the strength of an electrical signal.
Of or relating to attitudes.
etymology: From Italian attitudine + -al, from Latin aptitūdin- + -al, from oblique stem of Latin aptitūdō, from aptus + -tūdō. By surface analysis, attitude + -al.

definition: Having no clothes on the body.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French au naturel (“in the natural state; cooked plainly”), from au (“at the; in the;

definition: A farewell remark.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French au revoir, with relatively formal but otherwise identical meaning, possibly due to the cumbersome nature of formal English equivalents.

definition: A hotel providing overnight lodging for travelers.
etymology: Borrowed from French auberge. The term is attested in the fifteenth century as auberge, a loan from a term attested in eleventh century Old Occitan alberga (“camp, hut”), derived from albergar (“to host”).

definition: A tape recording of sound.
Of or relating to or containing or derived from gold.
Of or relating to the atmospheric phenomenon auroras.
example: A prominent green line in the spectrum of the auroras is called the ‘auroral line’.

definition: One who determines authenticity (as of works of art) or who guarantees validity.
Of rocks, deposits, etc.; found where they and their constituents were formed.
etymology: Literally, “native to the soil”; from autochthon + -ous.

definition: Production of antibodies against the tissues of your own body; produces autoimmune disease or hypersensitivity reactions.
A plant hormone that promotes root formation and bud growth.
etymology: From Ancient Greek αὐξάνω (auxánō, “to grow”) + English -in.

definition: Immoderately desirous of acquiring e.g. wealth.

etymology: From Middle English avaricious, from Old French avaricieux, from avarice, from Latin avaritia (“greed”), from avarus (“greedy”), of avere (“crave, long for”).

definition: Report or maintain.
etymology: From Middle English averren, from Old French averer, from Early Medieval Latin advērō, a verb derived from Latin vērus (“true”). Compare Modern French avérer.

definition: Tending to repel or dissuade.
example: Aversive conditioning.

definition: Conditioning to avoid an aversive stimulus.
Any negative stimulus to which an organism will learn to make a response that avoids it.
By open declaration.
example: Their policy has been avowedly Marxist.

definition: A quality of extreme unpleasantness.
example: The awfulness of this sacred place.
etymology: From Middle English aghfulnesse, equivalent to awful + -ness.

definition: Slender bristlelike appendage found on the bracts of grasses.
The hollow under the arm where it is joined to the shoulder.
A chemical compound containing the azido group combined with an element or radical.
A systemic antibacterial medicine (trade name Zithromax) that is prescribed to treat bacterial infections in many different parts of the body.
Relating to or containing the azo radical.
Any dye containing one or more azo groups.
The bivalent group -N=N- united to two hydrocarbon groups.
The bivalent group -N=N- united to two hydrocarbon groups.
Exceedingly short-lived meson.
South African term for ‘boss’.

definition: An indehiscent fruit derived from a single ovary having one or many seeds within a fleshy wall or pericarp: e.g. grape, tomato, cranberry.
Someone who engages in drinking bouts.

Scatter (radiation) by the atoms of the medium through which it passes.
A failure to maintain a higher state.

Preventing infection by inhibiting the growth or action of microorganisms.

A virus that is parasitic (reproduces itself) in bacteria.

definition: Speak unfavorably about.

The agent to whom property involved in a bailment is delivered.
The area over which a bailiff has jurisdiction.

etymology: From bailie (“bailiff”) and wick (“dwelling”), from Old English wīc.

definition: A child: son or daughter.
etymology: Borrowed from Scots bairn, from Middle English bern, barn, from Old English bearn, from Proto-West Germanic *barn, from Proto-Germanic *barną. Doublet of barn. Compare West Frisian bern.

definition: A horny material from the upper jaws of certain whales; used as the ribs of fans or as stays in corsets.
etymology: From Middle English baleyne, from Old French baleine (“whale, whalebone”), from Latin balaena (“whale”), from Ancient Greek φάλαινα (phálaina, “whale”).

Deadly or sinister.
example: The Florida eagles have a fierce baleful look.
etymology: From Middle English baleful, balful, baluful, from Old English bealuful, which was equivalent to bealu + -ful. By surface analysis, bale (“evil, woe”) + -ful. See bale for further etymology.

definition: A machine mainly used for the compaction of waste, cardboard, plastic and other recyclable materials.
Wire used to make bales.
Ancient missile weapon that throws bolts or stones.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin ballista, from Ancient Greek βαλλίστρα (ballístra), from βάλλω (bállō, “to throw”).

Conceal one's true motives from especially by elaborately feigning good intentions so as to gain an end.
example: He bamboozled his professors into thinking that he knew the subject well.

definition: The act of applying a bandage.

example: The merchant refused to travel in the region due to the ongoing banditry.

Roasting a large piece of meat on a revolving spit out of doors over an open fire.
Organic compound having powerful soporific effect; overdose can be fatal.

definition: Being a bard or relating to a bard's poetry.
example: Bardic poetry.

definition: Characterized by disorderly action and disregard for rules.

Of or relating to or located at the base.

definition: Soft light-colored wood of any of various linden trees; used in making crates and boxes and in carving and millwork.
Weedy plant having short dry chafflike leaves.
A cook who bastes roasting meat with melted fat or gravy.
A loose temporary sewing stitch to hold layers of fabric together.

A temporary bridge built over a series of pontoons.
A person who travels through the water by swimming.

definition: A female orderly assigned to serve a British military officer.
The area on a billiard table behind the balkline.
Line across a billiard table behind which the cue balls are placed at the start of a game.
A very large indefinite number (usually hyperbole).
Vigorous showy goldenrod common along eastern coast and Gulf Coast of North America.
A car that has a long body and rear door with space behind rear seat.
Clothing to be worn at a beach.
Ornamentation with beads.
Hazel of western United States with conspicuous beaklike involucres on the nuts.
Smiling with happiness or optimism.
example: Come to my arms, my beamish boy!

Arboreal civet of Asia having a long prehensile tail and shaggy black hair.
Having no beard.
example: Beardless wheat.
etymology: From Middle English bērdlēs, from Old English beardlēas (“beardless”), from Proto-West Germanic *bardalaus (“beardless”), equivalent to beard + -less.

definition: Any of numerous wild or cultivated irises having no hairs on the drooping sepals (the falls).
The pelt of a bear.
Susceptible to being defeated.

definition: Experiencing or bestowing celestial joy.
example: Beatific peace.
etymology: From Latin beātificus (“making happy or blessed”), from beātus (“blessed”) + -ficus (“making”).

A member of the beat generation; a nonconformist in dress and behavior.
etymology: Coined by American columnist Herb Caen in 1958. From beat (generation) + -nik (“person who exemplifies or endorses something”). Compare jazznik.

etymology: Borrowed from French beau geste (literally “beautiful gesture”). */ˌboʊ ˈʒest/

etymology: From Middle English beautevous, bewteose, beautuous, boyteous, beuteus, beuteowse, bewtyvows, equivalent to beauty + -ous and/or beauty + -eous.

definition: Rendered motionless for lack of wind.
Bug of temperate regions that infests especially beds and feeds on human blood.
example: Fiona rapidly discovered that the hotel was infested with bedbugs.

definition: Limp and soiled as if dragged in the mud.
example: The beggar's bedraggled clothes.

definition: Meat is browned before stewing.
A beef steak usually cooked by broiling.
A popular edible fungus with a cap the color of liver or raw meat; abundant in southeastern United States.
Plant grown for its ornamental red or purple foliage.
Any of several large tomatoes with thick flesh.
An electronic device that generates a series of beeps when the person carrying it is being paged.
Smelling of beer.
Sullen or unfriendly in appearance.
example: Calling this beetle-browed disdainful young person, hair hanging in her face, jaws chewing pecan pie with mechanical precision, honey!

example: His conduct was not befitting an officer of his station.

etymology: Borrowed from translingual Begonia (genus of plants), named after Michel Bégon (1638–1710), French governor of Saint-Domingue.

Influence by slyness.
example: I will never touch The Orb, even though its mysterious glow seduces and beguiles.

An approach to psychology that emphasizes observable measurable behavior.

definition: Perception by means of the eyes.

example: It behooves us to reflect on this matter.

Any of various plants of the genus Campanula having blue or white bell-shaped flowers.
Hostile or warlike attitude or nature.
A noisy mock serenade (made by banging pans and kettles) to a newly married couple.
etymology: From Middle English bellynge, equivalent to bell + -ing.

definition: A scar where the umbilical cord was attached.
example: She had a tattoo just above her bellybutton.

definition: Capable of being bent or flexed or twisted without breaking.
A newly married man (especially one who has long been a bachelor).
etymology: From the character in William Shakespeare's Much Ado About Nothing.

definition: Doing good; feeling beneficent.

example: The most beneficent regime in history.
etymology: From Latin *beneficens, *beneficent-, from bene (“well, good”) + -ficens, combining form from faciens, present participle of facere (“to make or do”). Compare English beneficence.

example: This medicine will act beneficially on you.

definition: Wearing, or having the face adorned with, eyeglasses or an eyeglass.

A sweet tasting alkaloid that occurs in sugar beets.

definition: A detested person.

example: A bicolor flower.

example: This festival takes places biennially.

A child's tight-fitting cap; often ties under the chin.
The most important person in a group or undertaking.
example: The company bigwig is gathering his staff together for a meeting today.
etymology: First arose in the 1730s, from big + wig. Formerly, English men of authority (such as judges and Members of Parliament) wore wigs. Bigwig plays on the idea that higher authority is denoted by a larger wig.

definition: Linear with respect to each of two variables or positions.
example: The function f(x,y)#61;xy is bilinear, because f(ax#43;bu,y)#61;af(x,y)#43;bf(u,y) and f(x,ay#43;bv)#61;af(x,y)#43;bf(x,v) for all values.

definition: Relating to or containing bile.
etymology: From French bilieux, from Latin bīliōsus (“full of bile”), from bīlis (“bile”) + -ōsus (“full of”).

definition: Cheat somebody out of what is due, especially money.
etymology: Uncertain; perhaps a variant form of balk.

definition: Rise up as if in waves.
example: Smoke billowed up into the sky.

definition: Of a distribution; having or occurring with two modes.
Produced by living organisms or biological processes.
example: Fermentation is a biogenic process.

definition: Luminescence produced by physiological processes (as in the firefly).
(of living organisms) emitting light.
example: Fireflies are bioluminescent.

definition: Application of biological principles to the study and design of engineering systems (especially electronic systems).

Safety from exposure to infectious agents.

Of or relating to biosynthesis.
Dark brown to black mica found in igneous and metamorphic rock.

definition: Divided into two portions almost to the base.

Any of various liqueurs made from blackcurrants.
Changing to a darker color.

A bleak and desolate atmosphere.
Tired to the point of exhaustion.
etymology: From Middle English blery, equivalent to blear + -y. Compare Old English bleriġ (“bald”).

definition: Tired to the point of exhaustion.
Talk whiningly.
example: The last thing we need is to hear them bleating to us about organizational problems.

definition: Someone who has hemophilia and is subject to uncontrollable bleeding.
Marred by imperfections.
Highly favored or fortunate (as e.g. by divine grace).
A wound that would cause an English soldier to be sent home from service abroad.
Similar to Gentiana andrewsii but with larger flowers.
A stupid person; these words are used to express a low opinion of someone's intelligence.
A stronghold that is reinforced for protection from enemy fire; with apertures for defensive fire.
etymology: From block + house. Calque of German Blockhaus.

definition: Thoroughbred horses (collectively).
Green chalcedony with red spots that resemble blood.
etymology: From blood + stone, from the fact that the red inclusions in the stone resemble blood.

definition: Marked with irregularly shaped spots or blots.
The spiracle of a cetacean located far back on the skull.
A violent release of energy caused by a chemical or nuclear reaction.
A high shoe with laces over the tongue.
etymology: Named from Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher (1742–1819), a Prussian general.

definition: Bluish-grey North American hawk having a darting flight.
Shrub or small tree of western United States having white flowers and blue berries; fruit used in wines and jellies.
A pasture grass of western North America.
Variety inhabiting the Great Lakes.
An American mint that yields a resinous exudate used especially formerly as an antispasmodic.
An American mint that yields a resinous exudate used especially formerly as an antispasmodic.
Bearing blue fruit.
Bluish warm-water marine food and game fish that follow schools of small fishes into shallow waters.
Important edible sunfish of eastern and central United States.
A short musket of wide bore with a flared muzzle.
etymology: From Dutch donderbus (“blunderbuss”, literally “thunder gun”), which was altered under the influence of blunder.

definition: Yellowish edible agaric that usually turns red when touched.
Blowing in violent and abrupt bursts.
example: Blustering (or blusterous) winds of Patagonia.

definition: A stiff hat made of straw with a flat crown.
etymology: From Middle English botere; equivalent to boat + -er. The use of the term for a straw hat stems from the fact that straw hats were the preferred head covering during sunny boat trips on canals and rivers.

definition: A petty officer on a merchant ship who controls the work of other seamen.
etymology: From Middle English botswain, botswein, bote-swayn, from late Old English bātsweġen, from bāt (“boat”) + sweġen (“swain”), the latter element a borrowing from sveinn (“boy”); equivalent to boat + swain (“boy, servant”).

definition: Mostly white web-footed tropical seabird often found far from land.
A place where boats are built or maintained or stored.
Incorrigible.
example: A bodacious gossip.
etymology: Southern American slang, implied by bodaciously, 1837, either from bodyaciously (“bodily, totally, root and branch”, antebellum South Carolina) or a blend of bold and audacious.

definition: A dagger with a slender blade.
etymology: From Middle English boydekin (“dagger”), apparently from *boyde, *boide (of unknown [Celtic?] origin) + -kin. Cognate with Scots botkin, boitkin, boikin (“bodkin”). Compare button, beat, bad, Old Norse váði.

definition: Meat from an adult domestic bovine.
(British slang) a scientist or technician engaged in military research.
etymology: Origin unknown; a number of possible etymologies have been suggested, but no conclusive evidence exists. One strong theory conjectures a connection from the "Mr.

definition: Small creeping European herb having delicate pink flowers.
A strong post (as on a wharf or quay or ship for attaching mooring lines).
example: The road was closed to vehicular traffic with bollards.

definition: Strong sealed vessel for measuring heat of combustion.
A person devoted to refined sensuous enjoyment (especially good food and drink).
etymology: Borrowed from French bon vivant (literally “one who lives well, good ‘liver’ (living person)”), from bon (“good”) + vivant (“person who is living”), agent noun of vivre (“to live”).

definition: A candy that usually has a center of fondant or fruit or nuts coated in chocolate.
example: The terrine was served with black pudding bonbons.
etymology: Borrowed from French bonbon, reduplication of bon (“good”).

definition: (French) happiness and good humor.
Subject to being reserved or booked.
example: All seats bookable in advance.

definition: A worker whose trade is binding books.
etymology: From Middle English bokebynder, bok-bindere, equivalent to book + binder.

definition: The craft of binding books.
A support placed at the end of a row of books to keep them upright (on a shelf or table).
A male learned person; someone who by long study has gained mastery in one or more disciplines.
etymology: From Middle English bocman, from Old English bōcmann (“bookman, a holder of bookland”), equivalent to book + man.

definition: Work of little or no value done merely to look busy.
example: Opponents consider this another billion-dollar government boondoggle.
etymology: Coined by American scout leader Robert H. Link in 1929; alternatively “boon doggle”. Compare woggle of similar sense, which is attested in the same period.

definition: A crude uncouth ill-bred person lacking culture or refinement.
etymology: Borrowed from Dutch boer (“peasant”). Doublet of bauer, Boer, and bower (“peasant, farmer”).

definition: Someone who makes or sells illegal liquor.
The act of making or transporting alcoholic liquor for sale illegally.
example: The Prohibition amendment made bootlegging profitable.

definition: A salt or ester of boric acid.
A building where prostitutes are available.
etymology: From Italian bordello. Distantly related to brothel, through Proto-Indo-European *bʰer- (“to carve, cut, split, rub”). Doublet of bordel. By surface analysis, Latin borda + Italian -ello (“diminutive”).

definition: A salt of boric and silicic acids.
Formerly a British reform school for youths considered too young to send to prison.
example: You have juvenile courts. Do you have borstal institutions for juveniles?
etymology: Inherited from Middle English *borstile, *borghstile, from Old English beorh (“a hill”) + stigel (“a stile”). The institutions are named after Borstal Prison in Borstal, Rochester, Kent, England.

definition: Gentian of eastern North America having tubular blue or white flowers that open little if at all.
A manufacturer that makes and bottles beverages.
etymology: From Middle English boteller, botullere, equivalent to bottle + -er. Piecewise doublet of butler.

definition: A fish that lurks on the bottom of a body of water.
Any of several South American ornamental woody vines of the genus Bougainvillea having brilliant red or purple flower bracts; widely grown in warm regions.
etymology: From taxonomic name Bougainvillea, from French Bougainville + -a. Named after French admiral and explorer Louis Antoine de Bougainville (1729–1811).

definition: An inlaid furniture decoration; tortoiseshell and yellow and white metal form scrolls in cabinetwork.
etymology: From French boule. Doublet of bull (etymologies 2 and 4) and bulla, or of bowl and pulla, depending on the etymology of the French word.

definition: A pipe of the bagpipe that is tuned to produce a single continuous tone.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English burdoun (“pilgrim's staff”), from Old French bordon, from Medieval Latin burdō, burdōnem (“pilgrim's staff”). The modern pronunciation and form is also influenced by modern French bourdon.

definition: Reduced red wine with onions and parsley and thyme and butter.
example: They ordered a nice red to go with their bourguignon.
etymology: An unadapted borrowing from French bourguignon.

definition: Reduced red wine with onions and parsley and thyme and butter.
An archaic term for a boundary.
A flat double pleat made by folding under the fabric on either side of it.
(usually plural) an expression used when two dice are thrown and both come up showing six spots.
etymology: From the resemblance of the number six (“6”) on a die to a boxcar.

definition: A network of nerves formed by cervical and thoracic spinal nerves and supplying the arm and parts of the shoulder.
Abnormally slow heartbeat.
etymology: From Ancient Greek βραδύς (bradús, “slow”) + καρδία (kardía, “heart”), equivalent to brady- + -cardia.

definition: Exhibiting self-importance.
etymology: From Middle French bragard (“bragging, flaunting, vain", also "a showy, arrogant individual”), from braguer (“to boast, brag”). No firm relation to English brag has been established.

definition: Cook in liquid.
example: Braise beef.
etymology: From French braise (“live coals”) and braiser (“to braise”, from the noun), from Old French brese (“embers”), from Old Low Franconian/Old Dutch;

definition: Cooking slowly in fat in a closed pot with little moisture.
A male railroad employee responsible for a train's brakes.
Having the breasts uncovered or featuring such nudity.
example: To be more comfortable, her sister suggested to going to the store braless under her sweatshirt.

definition: Move or swing back and forth.
example: He brandished his sword at the pirates.
etymology: From Middle English braundischen, from Old French brandiss-, stem of brandir (“to flourish a sword”), from Frankish *brandijan, from Frankish *brand (“firebrand; sword”), from Proto-Germanic *brandaz (“fire; flame;

definition: Armor plate that protects the arm.
etymology: Borrowed from French brassard, from bras (“arm”). The form brasset is attested since at least 1676 (Scots brassat is attested since 1590); brassart since at least 1736, brassard since at least 1788.

definition: An undergarment worn by women to support their breasts.
etymology: Borrowed from French brassière. Doublet of brachiaria.

definition: A geographic region serving as the principal source of grain.
A wooden or plastic board on which dough is kneaded or bread is sliced.
Crumb of bread; used especially for coating or thickening.
etymology: From bread + crumb. The computing and figurative senses allude to the German fairy tale Hansel and Gretel, where Hansel leaves a trail of breadcrumbs to find the way back home when venturing into the woods.

definition: A dyspneic condition.
example: Since he'd entered the urgent care center, his breathlessness had only gotten worse, even though he'd been sitting quietly.

definition: A rudaceous rock consisting of sharp fragments embedded in clay or sand.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian breccia, from French brèche, from Middle French breche, from Old French breche, from Vulgar Latin *breca, of Germanic origin, from Frankish *breka.

definition: A diacritical mark (U-shaped) placed over a vowel to indicate a short sound.
etymology: From Middle English breve, variant of bref, from Old French brieve, breve (feminine form of brief, bref), from Latin brevis (“short”).

definition: (Roman Catholic Church) a book of prayers to be recited daily by certain priests and members of religious orders.
etymology: From Latin breviārium (“summary”) (compare abbreviation), ultimately from brevis (“short”). Doublet of brevier and brimborion.

definition: A combination brewery and restaurant; beer is brewed for consumption on the premises and served along with food.
The craft of laying bricks.
An armed thief who is (usually) a member of a band.
etymology: From Middle English brigaunt, bregaund circa 1400, from Old French brigand (“foot soldier”) attested from 1421, from Italian briga (“trouble, bother”), perhaps ultimately of Proto-Germanic or Celtic origin.

definition: Two-masted sailing vessel square-rigged on the foremast and fore-and-aft rigged on the mainmast.
etymology: Attested 1525, for a small rowing vessel, from earlier brigandyns, from Middle French brigandin, probably from Italian brigante (“skirmisher, pirate, brigand”), from Latin brigō (“to fight”).

definition: Slightly salty (especially from containing a mixture of seawater and fresh water).
example: The briny deep.
etymology: The adjective is from brine (noun) + -y (suffix forming adjectives with the sense ‘having the quality of’).

definition: A vine of the genus Bryonia having large leaves and small flowers and yielding acrid juice with emetic and purgative properties.
Very irritable.
example: Bristly exchanges between the White House and the press.
etymology: From Middle English bristli, brustly, equivalent to bristle + -y.

definition: Large shrub or small tree of the eastern United States having bristly stems and large clusters of pink flowers.
A machine tool that uses a toothed tool, called a broach, to remove material.
example: The two ram pull-down machine is the most common type of broaching machine.

definition: In a broad-minded manner.
example: The authorities broad-mindedly permitted the opening of a center for teenagers.

definition: Having relatively broad rather than needlelike or scalelike leaves.
Cooking by direct exposure to radiant heat (as over a fire or under a grill).
Colloquial terms for an umbrella.
example: It's going to rain today – you'd better take your brolly.

definition: Any of various woodland and meadow grasses of the genus Bromus; native to temperate regions.
etymology: From the genus name, New Latin Bromus, from Ancient Greek βρόμος (brómos, “oat, wild oat”).

definition: An unbroken or imperfectly broken mustang.
Huge quadrupedal herbivorous dinosaur common in North America in the late Jurassic.
example: Near-synonym: thunder lizard (can denote a brontosaurus or an apatosaurus).
etymology: From New Latin, from Ancient Greek roots; by surface analysis, bronto- + -saurus (“thunder lizard”), according to the notion that its massive size must have made its footsteps shake the ground.

definition: A cosmetic powder that comes in various shades of brown, meant to create an impression of tanned skin.
example: Sculpting your face with a bronzing powder will make it appear slimmer.

definition: Physiologically ready to incubate eggs.
example: A broody hen.
etymology: From Middle English *brody, *brodi, from Old English brōdiġ (“broody”), equivalent to brood + -y. Cognate with German brütig (“broody”).

definition: A domestic hen ready to brood.
Loud confused noise from many sources.
example: It caused quite a brouhaha when the school suspended one of its top students for refusing to adhere to the dress code.
etymology: Borrowed from French brouhaha, though its earlier origin is disputed. Possibly from Hebrew בָּרוּךְ הַבָּא (barúkh habá, “welcome”, literally “blessed is he who comes”).

definition: Freshwater catfish of eastern United States.
Infectious bacterial disease of human beings transmitted by contact with infected animals or infected meat or milk products; characterized by fever and headache.
An artist's distinctive technique of applying paint with a brush.
example: The fake was easy to spot because of its inferior brushwork.

definition: Covered with or consisting of bushes or thickets.
example: Brushy undergrowth.

definition: Treat brutally.
A public fountain to provide a jet of drinking water.
A shrub or shrubby tree of the genus Rhamnus; fruits are source of yellow dyes or pigments.
Fruit of various buckthorns yielding dyes or pigments.
Trees and shrubs usually thorny bearing drupaceous fruit many having medicinal value.
Repeated heavy blows.
Acting like a clown or buffoon.
An imaginary monster used to frighten children.
An imaginary monster used to frighten children.
example: What has this Bugbear Death to frighten Man, If Souls can die, as well as Bodies can?
etymology: From obsolete meaning of bug (“something terrifying”) + bear. See Middle English bugge, modern bogey.

definition: An inlaid furniture decoration; tortoiseshell and yellow and white metal form scrolls in cabinetwork.
etymology: A pronunciation spelling of Boulle, a French woodcarver.

definition: Parched crushed wheat.
etymology: From Ottoman Turkish بلغور (bulğur) (modern Turkish bulgur), by metathesis from older بورغول (burğul), from Arabic بُرْغُل (burḡul), from Persian برغول (barġul), پرغول (parġul).

definition: Parched crushed wheat.
Suffering from bulimia.
example: My sister was bulimic and consequently had a number of health problems.

definition: (pathology) an elevation of the skin filled with serous fluid.
example: Auditory bulla; ethmoid bulla.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin bulla (“bubble”). Doublet of bill and bull (“papal bull; bubble”).

definition: A Spanish or Portuguese or Latin American spectacle; a matador baits and (usually) kills a bull in an arena before many spectators.
Someone who fights bulls.
Freshwater sculpin with a large flattened bony-plated head with hornlike spines.
Any of several common freshwater catfishes of the United States.
A stadium where bullfights take place.
A person who is not very intelligent or interested in culture.
etymology: From Dutch boomken (“shrub, little tree”), equivalent to boom + -kin. Note that the English word boom is etymologically related to the aforementioned in the sense of "large stem", or "big tree".

definition: Made by polymerizing butadiene.
Made by polymerizing butadiene.
Unacceptable behavior (especially ludicrously false statements).
A painful swelling of the bursa of the first joint of the big toe.
A batter who bunts.
example: Glavine was a renowned bunter of the ball.

definition: Any of several erect biennial herbs of temperate Eurasia having stout taproots and producing burs.
etymology: From Middle English *bury dokke (attested as plural bury dokkis), equivalent to bur(ry) + dock.

definition: A citizen of an English borough.
etymology: From Middle English burger, burgher, burghere, equivalent to burgh + -er (“inhabitant of”). Likely merged with and reinforced by Middle Dutch burgher (Modern Dutch: burger);

definition: Commit a burglary; enter and rob a dwelling.
The property of being smooth and shiny.
example: With a good burnish, the old table should fetch a higher price.
etymology: The verb is derived from Middle English burnishen, burnysshen (“to polish, burnish; (figuratively) to brighten, give lustre to; to clean (something) until shiny;

definition: A hand tool with polished agate tips (or other gemstone) for rubbing the gold leaf in order to obtain a highly polished surface, used in gilding.
The treasurer at a college or university.
etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin bursārius, from bursa (“purse”) (English purse).

definition: Inflammation of a bursa; frequently in the shoulder.
A male restaurant attendant who sets tables and assists waiters and clears away dirty dishes.
European purple-flowered with slender stems; occurs as a weed in hedges.
A capitalist who engages in industrial commercial enterprise.
Play music in a public place and solicit money for it.
example: Three young men were busking in the plaza.
etymology: Apparently from French busquer or Spanish buscar.

definition: A person who entertains people for money in public places (as by singing or dancing), usually while asking for money.
A close-fitting and strapless top without sleeves that is worn by women either as lingerie or for evening dress.
etymology: Borrowed from French bustier, from buste + -ier.

definition: A person who meddles in the affairs of others.
A gaseous hydrocarbon C4H6; used in making synthetic rubbers.
A rotund individual.
example: What if your baby is a butterball? Does Fat-Proofing mean you should put your infant on diet?.

definition: A hole through which buttons are pushed.
etymology: Originally buttonhold (“a loop of string to hold a button down”), but changed by folk etymology by influence of hole. By surface analysis, button + hole.

definition: A sewing machine that sews all types of buttonholes with or without the gimp thread.
A reinforcing looped stitch for edges, as around a buttonhole.
A colorless pungent liquid sometimes used as a stimulant drug by drug abusers.
Unwanted marine creatures that are caught in the nets while fishing for another species.
A side road little traveled (as in the countryside).
etymology: From Middle English bywey, equivalent to by- + way.

definition: A condensed but memorable saying embodying some important fact of experience that is taken as true by many people.
etymology: From Middle English byword, byworde (“proverb”), from Old English bīword, bīwyrd, bīwyrde (“proverb, household word", also "adverb”), from Proto-West Germanic *bīwurdī, equivalent to by- + word.

definition: The craft of making furniture (especially furniture of high quality).
A highly polished gem that is cut convexly but without facets.
etymology: Borrowed from French cabochon, diminutive form of caboche (“head”), from Old French caboce, from Latin caput (“head”).

definition: Small tree of dry open parts of southern Africa having erect angled branches suggesting candelabra.
Of or relating to the records of a cadastre.
etymology: Borrowed from French cadastral (“relating to the cadastre”), from cadastre.

definition: Cadastral value of a property is the value of the land and the buildings there; serves as a basis for the estimation of incurring taxes.
A brilliant solo passage occurring near the end of a piece of music.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian cadenza, from Latin cadentia. Doublet of cadence and chance.

definition: An insignia used by the medical profession; modeled after the staff of Hermes.
example: For quotations using this term, see Citations:caduceus.
etymology: Via Latin cādūceus, cādūceum, adaptation of Doric Ancient Greek καρύκειον (karúkeion, “herald’s wand or staff”). This and Attic Greek κηρύκειον (kērúkeion) are derived from κῆρυξ (kêrux, “herald, public messenger”).

definition: Relating to abdominal delivery.
The delivery of a fetus by surgical incision through the abdominal wall and uterus (from the belief that Julius Caesar was born that way).
The delivery of a fetus by surgical incision through the abdominal wall and uterus (from the belief that Julius Caesar was born that way).
A soft silver-white ductile metallic element (liquid at normal temperatures); the most electropositive and alkaline metal.
etymology: From Latin caesius (“sky-blue”), in reference to the radiation spectra, + -ium.

definition: An atomic clock based on the energy difference between two states of the caesium nucleus in a magnetic field.
A semiaquatic reptile of Central and South America that resembles an alligator but has a more heavily armored belly.
etymology: From Spanish caimán or Portuguese caimão, from Kari'na acayouman.

definition: Crocodile-like lizard of South America having powerful jaws for crushing snails and mussels.
An ornamental sunken panel in a ceiling or dome.
etymology: Borrowed from French caisson. Doublet of cassone and cajón.

definition: Pain resulting from rapid change in pressure.
Influence or urge by gentle urging, caressing, or flattering.
A soft porous rock consisting of calcium carbonate deposited from springs rich in lime.
Any hypochlorite of calcium; used as a bleaching agent.
Any of numerous chiefly annual herbs of the genus Calendula widely cultivated for their yellow or orange flowers; often used for medicinal and culinary purposes.
etymology: From translingual Calendula, New Latin calendula, diminutive of kalendae. See calends.

definition: Fine leather from the skin of a calf.
Someone skilled in penmanship.
Of or relating to or expressed in calligraphy.
Having calluses; having skin made tough and thick through wear.
example: Calloused skin.

definition: In a callous way.
example: He callously exploited their feelings.

definition: Heat-generating.
example: The calorific properties of fuels.
etymology: From French calorifique or Latin calorificus, from calor + -i- + -ficus.

definition: A measuring instrument that determines quantities of heat.
Measurement of quantities of heat.
Any of several plants of the genus Camassia; North and South America.
etymology: Perhaps from Chinook Jargon qamaš, qawaš (“camas”), from Nootka qawaš (“camas”), or perhaps from Nez Perce qém̓es (“camas”).

definition: An optical device consisting of an attachment that enables an observer to view simultaneously the image and a drawing surface for sketching it.
A short sleeveless undergarment for women.
etymology: From Unadapted borrowing from French camisole, from Old Occitan camisola, diminutive of camisa (“shirt”).

definition: Eurasian plant with apple-scented foliage and white-rayed flowers and feathery leaves used medicinally; in some classification systems placed in genus Anthemis.
Tea-like drink made from camomile leaves and flowers.
The shape of a bell.
A bell tower; usually stands alone unattached to a building.
example: The Leaning Tower of Pisa is a campanile.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian campanile (“bell tower, belfry”), from campana (“bell”) + -ile (suffix forming nouns indicating locations that host animals or objects).

definition: The basic unit of luminous intensity adopted under the Systeme International d'Unites; equal to 1/60 of the luminous intensity per square centimeter of a black body radiating at the temperature of 2,046 degrees Kelvin.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin candēla (“candle”). Doublet of candle and chandelle.

definition: An infection caused by fungi of the genus Monilia or Candida (especially Candida albicans).
Eat human flesh.
Departing or being caused to depart from the true vertical or horizontal.
example: A-six canted bolt head.

definition: A hymn derived from the Bible.
etymology: From Latin canticulum, diminutive of cantus (“song”).

definition: With competence; in a competent capable manner.
Large in capacity.
example: She carried a capacious bag.
etymology: From Latin capāx (“wide, spacious, large; capable”) + -ious. Displaced native Old English numol.

definition: Flesh of a castrated male chicken.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English capoun, from Old English capūn, from Old Northern French capon (Old French chapon), from Latin cāpō, cāpōnem (Vulgar Latin *cappō).

definition: A variety of leaf bug.
(nautical) the event of a boat accidentally turning over in the water.
A windlass rotated in a horizontal plane around a vertical axis; used on ships for weighing anchor or raising heavy sails.
example: To pawl the capstan.

definition: Resembling a capsule.
example: The capsular ligament is a sac surrounding the articular cavity of a freely movable joint and attached to the bones.

definition: A headlike protuberance on an organ or structure.
example: The caput humeri is the head of the humerus which fits into a cavity in the scapula.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin caput (“the head”). Doublet of cape, capo, chef, and chief, and distantly of head and Howth.

definition: Pig-sized tailless South American amphibious rodent with partly webbed feet; largest living rodent.
etymology: From Spanish capibara, from Portuguese capivara, from Old Tupi kapi'iûara (literally “grass eater”).

definition: Water buffalo of the Philippines.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish carabao, from Waray-Waray karabaw, from Malay kerbau, from Proto-Malayic *kAr(ə)baw, ultimately from Proto-Mon-Khmer *krpiʔ ~ *krpiiw ~ *krpuʔ ~ *(kr)puh (“buffalo”).

definition: An oblong metal ring with a spring clip; used in mountaineering to attach a rope to a piton or to connect two ropes.
etymology: Shortened from German Karabinerhaken (“carbine hook”), reflecting that such a link was used for gear slinging even before it was used for rock climbing.

definition: A bottle with a stopper; for serving wine or water.
etymology: Borrowed from French carafe. First attested in 1796. Doublet of carboy.

definition: A colorless nonflammable liquid used as a solvent for fats and oils; because of its toxicity its use as a cleaning fluid or fire extinguisher has declined.
Relating to or containing the carboxyl group or carboxyl radical.
The univalent radical -COOH; present in and characteristic of organic acids.
Treat (a chemical compound) with carboxyl or carboxylic acid.
Deep-red cabochon garnet cut without facets.
etymology: From Middle English carbuncle, charbocle, from Old French carbuncle, charbuncle, from Latin carbunculus (“a small coal; a reddish kind of precious stone; a kind of tumor”), diminutive of carbō (“a coal, charcoal”).

definition: Mixes air with gasoline vapor prior to explosion.
A person who holds a credit card or debit card.
Obtained from a number of plants and used to stimulate the heart in cases of heart failure.
Small Dominican tree bearing masses of large crimson flowers before the fine pinnate foliage emerges.
Small voraciously carnivorous freshwater fishes of South America that attack and destroy living animals.
Music composed for dancing the carioca.
A business engaged in the manufacture of automobiles.
A translucent red or orange variety of chalcedony.
etymology: From cornelian, the red form named carneolus under the influence of Latin carneus (“fleshy”) because of its color.

definition: Long pod containing small beans and sweetish edible pulp; used as animal feed and source of a chocolate substitute.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French carobe, from Arabic خَرُّوب (ḵarrūb), from Classical Syriac ܚܪܘܒܐ (ḥarrūḇā).

definition: A bar of candy made with carob powder.
Long pod containing small beans and sweetish edible pulp; used as animal feed and source of a chocolate substitute.
Powder from the ground seeds and pods of the carob tree; used as a chocolate substitute.
Evergreen Mediterranean tree with edible pods; the biblical carob.
Singing joyful religious songs (especially at Christmas).
example: 1958, Brenda Lee, Rockin' Around the Christmas Tree Later we'll have some pumpkin pie / And we'll do some caroling.

definition: Any of a class of highly unsaturated yellow to red pigments occurring in plants and animals.
Used of riotously drunken merrymaking.
example: Carousing bands of drunken soldiers.

definition: Someone who constantly criticizes in a petty way.
Persistent petty and unjustified criticism.
A large galleon sailed in the Mediterranean as a merchantman.
etymology: From French caraque (compare Spanish and Portuguese carraca, Italian caracca), from Latin carraca, from Latin carrus (“wagon”); or perhaps from Arabic قَرَاقِير (qarāqīr).

definition: Small individual study area in a library.
example: He was busy writing his report in a small library carrel.
etymology: A variant of carol (“small closet or enclosure”), from Middle English carole (“round dance with singing; group of people dancing and singing in a circle; circular thing; braid, chain (?); stall for study or writing;

definition: Small individual study area in a library.
An ointment formerly used to treat burns.
A cartridge (usually with paper casing).
etymology: Borrowed from French cartouche, from Italian cartuccia, from carta, from Latin charta, from Ancient Greek χάρτης (khártēs). Doublet of cartridge.

definition: (of ships) built with flush (rather than overlapping) hull planks.
The action of washing a car.
example: We should have a carwash there.

definition: An older or native quarter of many cities in northern Africa; the quarter in which the citadel is located.
A black garment reaching down to the ankles; worn by priests or choristers.
Large black flightless bird of Australia and New Guinea having a horny head crest.

(used in the plural) a percussion instrument consisting of a pair of hollow pieces of wood or bone (usually held between the thumb and fingers) that are made to click together (as by Spanish dancers) in rhythm with the dance.
An event used to justify starting a war.
example: In ancient times, repeatedly failing to pay tribute by a vassal state was often used as a casus belli by the patron.
etymology: From Latin cāsus (“occasion”) + bellī (“for war”, literally “of war”).

definition: Slanted across a polygon on a diagonal line.
Breakdown in living organisms of more complex substances into simpler ones together with release of energy.
etymology: From Ancient Greek καταβολή (katabolḗ, “throwing down”), from κατά (katá, “down”) + βάλλω (bállō, “I throw”).

definition: An underground tunnel with recesses where bodies were buried (as in ancient Rome).
etymology: From Middle English catacombe, from Old English catacumbe, catacumbas pl, from Late Latin catacumbae pl, name of the underground cemetery of St. Sebastian in Rome, of unclear origin.

definition: Enzyme found in most plant and animal cells that functions as an oxidative catalyst; decomposes hydrogen peroxide into oxygen and water.
An enclosure or receptacle for odds and ends.

A chain of connected ideas or passages or objects so arranged that each member is closely related to the preceding and following members (especially a series of patristic comments elucidating Christian dogma).
etymology: From Medieval Latin catena, from Latin catēna (“chain”). Doublet of chain.

definition: A man who raises (or tends) cattle.
Part of the peritoneum attached to the stomach and to the colon and covering the intestines.
etymology: From Middle English calle, kelle, kalle, kolle (“caul, net, basket”), from Old English cāwl, cāul, cēawl, cēaul (“basket, container, net, sieve”), of uncertain origin.

definition: A waterproof filler and sealant that is used in building and repair to make watertight.
example: Oakum was used for the caulking of the hulls of wooden ships.

definition: Burn, sear, or freeze (tissue) using a hot iron or electric current or a caustic agent.
example: The surgeon cauterized the wart.
etymology: From Middle French cauteriser, from Late Latin cauterizō (“to burn with a hot iron”), from Ancient Greek καυτηριάζω (kautēriázō, “to brand”), from καυτήρ (kautḗr, “branding iron”), from καίω (kaíō, “to burn”).

definition: A male soldier in a motorized army unit.
A commercial principle that without a warranty the buyer takes upon themself the risk of quality.
etymology: Latin for “buyer beware”; from Latin caveat (“may he / she / subject-noun beware”), the third-person subjunctive of caveō (“to beware”) + ēmptor (“buyer”).

definition: An evasion of the point of an argument by raising irrelevant distinctions or objections.
etymology: From Old French caviller (“mock, jest, rail”), from Latin cavillor (“jeer, mock, satirise, reason captiously”), from cavilla (“jeering, raillery, scoffing”);

definition: An informal social gathering at which there is Scottish or Irish folk music and singing and folk dancing and story telling.
etymology: The noun is borrowed from Scottish Gaelic cèilidh (“a pilgrimage; a social call, visit; a sojourn; a social gathering with dancing, etc., ceilidh”) and Irish célidhe (archaic), céilí (“a social call, visit;

definition: Grown for its thickened edible aromatic root.
A specialized part of a cell; analogous to an organ.
An inflammation of body tissue (especially that below the skin) characterized by fever and swelling and redness and pain.
etymology: Learned borrowing from New Latin cellulitis. By surface analysis, cellule + -itis. Doublet of cellulite. First attested in the 1840s.

definition: A container for burning incense (especially one that is swung on a chain in a religious ritual).
etymology: Inherited from Middle English censer, from Anglo-Norman censier, from Old French encensier, from encens (“incense”).

definition: Being at least 100 years old.
etymology: From Latin centēnārius + -an, equivalent to centenary (“100 year, 100th anniversary”) + -an (“person”).

definition: The political policy of concentrating power in a central organization.
The process of separating substances of different densities by the use of a centrifuge.
(American football) putting the ball in play by passing it (between the legs) to a back.
Tending to move toward a center.
example: Centripetal force.
etymology: From New Latin centripetālis coined by Sir Isaac Newton, from Latin centrum (“center”) + petō (“to seek, aim”) + -al. Analysable as centri- + -petal.

definition: The inward force on a body moving in a curved path around another body.
A political philosophy of avoiding the extremes of left and right by taking a moderate position or course of action.
The center of mass of an object of uniform density.
etymology: From centre + -oid. From 1844, used as a replacement for the older terms "centre of gravity" and "centre of mass" in situations described in purely geometrical terms, and subsequently used for further generalisations.

definition: Of or relating to the head.
etymology: From Middle French céphalique, from Latin cephalicus (“head”), from Ancient Greek κεφαλικός (kephalikós, “capital”), from κεφαλή (kephalḗ, “head”).

definition: Ratio (in percent) of the maximum breadth to the maximum length of a skull.
A large vein of the arm that empties into the axillary vein.
Relating or belonging to the class Cephalopoda.
etymology: From French céphalopode, from Ancient Greek κεφαλή (kephalḗ, “head”) + ποδός (podós), genitive singular of πούς (poús, “foot, leg”). By surface analysis, cephalo- + -pod.

definition: The fleshy, waxy covering at the base of the upper beak of some birds.
etymology: From Middle English sere, from Old French cire, from Latin cēra (“wax, cere”), or via Latin cērō (“to smear or coat with wax”).

definition: Anterior portion of the brain consisting of two hemispheres; dominant part of the brain in humans.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English cerebrum, from Latin cerebrum (“a brain; a skull”); see there for more.

definition: In a ceremonious manner.
example: My mother advised her children ceremoniously.

definition: In a ceremonious manner.
example: My mother advised her children ceremoniously.

definition: Of a color at the end of the color spectrum (next to orange); resembling the color of blood or cherries or tomatoes or rubies.
etymology: Borrowed from French cerise (mid 19th century), itself from Vulgar Latin ceresia, from Latin cerasium. Doublet of cherry and kirsch.

definition: A ductile grey metallic element of the lanthanide series; used in lighter flints; the most abundant of the rare-earth group.
etymology: From Ceres (a famous asteroid and dwarf planet), + -ium. The element was discovered and named in 1803.

definition: Large edible mackerel of temperate United States coastal Atlantic waters.
Fit to be certified as insane (and treated accordingly).
Total certainty or greater certainty than circumstances warrant.
example: I have absolute certitude about that.
etymology: From Middle French certitude, from Late Latin certitūdō, from Latin certus.

definition: A covered cistern; waste water and sewage flow into it.
example: Politics devolved into a cesspit of lies and deceit.
etymology: Uncertain. The first part, cess-, is undoubtedly the same as for cesspool, whose origin is likewise uncertain. The second part is pit, a hole in the ground.

definition: Of or relating to whales and dolphins etc.
example: The poached blubber was definitely cetacean in origin, but the particular species could not be identified.
etymology: From translingual Cetacea, from Latin cētus (“whale”), + -an.

definition: Large aquatic carnivorous mammal with fin-like forelimbs no hind limbs, including: whales, dolphins, porpoises, narwhals.
Common in quiet waters of eastern United States.
A long chair; for reclining.
etymology: Borrowed from French chaise longue (literally “long chair”).

definition: A milky or greyish translucent to transparent quartz.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin chalcēdōnius, from Ancient Greek χαλκηδόνιος (khalkēdónios), from Ancient Greek χαλκηδών (khalkēdṓn), cognate to Arabic كَرْكَنْد (karkand).

definition: (Judaism) a loaf of white bread containing eggs and leavened with yeast; often formed into braided loaves and glazed with eggs before baking.
etymology: From Hebrew חַלָּה (ḥallá, “loaf”), influenced by Yiddish חלה (khale).

definition: A maid who is employed to clean and care for bedrooms (now primarily in hotels).
A lightweight fabric woven with white threads across a colored warp.
etymology: From French cambrai (“cambric”), and its source, Cambrai, the city in France where it originated; probably with alteration after chamber.

definition: Small tufted perennial herb of mountains of central and southern Europe having very small flowers of usually leafless stems; sometimes placed in genus Lepidium.
Reed pipe with finger holes on which the melody is played.
example: The piper was near being strangled / They squeezed up his pipes, bellows, chanters and all.
etymology: From Middle English chauntour, from Old French chanteor, from Latin cantor; equivalent to chant + -er. Compare French chanteur. Doublet of cantor.

definition: An attractor for which the approach to its final point in phase space is chaotic.
Shrub of coastal ranges of California and Baja California having hairy branches and spikes of numerous mauve flowers; sometimes placed in genus Sphaeralcea.
Headdress that protects the head from bad weather; has shaped crown and usually a brim.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French chappeau. The interjection is after Modern French chapeau in similar use, originally short for chapeau bas.

definition: One who accompanies and supervises a young woman or gatherings of young people.
etymology: From French chaperon (“hood”), from Middle French, "head covering", from Old French chape.

definition: The driver of a chariot.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English charioter, from Old French charioteur (“charioteer”) and charretier (“coachman”). By surface analysis, chariot + -eer.

definition: In a charitable manner.
example: She treated him charitably.

definition: Gruesomely indicative of death or the dead.
example: A charnel smell came from the chest filled with dead men's bones.
etymology: From Middle English charnel, from Old French charnel, carnel, from Late Latin carnāle (“graveyard”), from Latin carnālis, or possibly an alteration of Anglo-Norman charner, from Medieval Latin carnārium (“charnel”).

definition: A vault or building where corpses or bones are deposited.
A stock market analyst who tries to predict market trends from graphs of recent prices of securities.
(ballet) quick gliding steps with one foot always leading.
Verbal punishment.
etymology: From Old French chastiement, from the verb chastier, from Latin castīgō.

definition: Orchid growing along streams or ponds of western North America having leafy stems and 1 greenish-brown and pinkish flower in the axil of each upper leaf.
A wad of something chewable as tobacco.
example: When the doctor told him to quit smoking, Harvey switched to chaw, but then developed cancer of the mouth.
etymology: An unexplained variation of chewen (“to chew”). First attested in the sixteenth century. See chew for more. Cognate with Middle Dutch cauwen ("to chew";

definition: Lower the grade of something; reduce its worth.
A price below the standard price.
example: His cheapness was legendary; he refused to use candles or lamps, not to reduce the risk of fire but rather to save a penny.

definition: In a brash cheeky manner.
In a good-humoured manner.
example: Having already dismissed the story as a heap of piffle, he cheerily advised the reporters to go for a run.

definition: A coarse loosely woven cotton gauze; originally used to wrap cheeses.
Greatly annoyed; out of patience.
example: I'm really cheesed off about the lack of hand dryers in this washroom!

definition: To play a game or sport in a manner that is effective but requires little skill.
(medicine) the process of removing a heavy metal from the bloodstream by means of a chelate as in treating lead or mercury poisoning.
A woman's sleeveless undergarment.
etymology: From French chemise, from Old French chemise, from Late Latin camisa, camisia ("shirt, undergarment, nightgown";

definition: Of or relating to chemotherapy.
A soft tufted cord used in embroidery.
etymology: Borrowed from French chenille. Doublet of canicule.

definition: A soft tufted cord used in embroidery.
Marked by a large or well-developed chest.
example: He was big-chested, big-shouldered and heavy-armed.

definition: Able to be chewed or cut.
A monochrome picture made by using several different shades of the same color.
etymology: First attested in the mid-17th century, borrowed from Italian chiaroscuro, from chiaro (“clear, bright”) + oscuro (“dark, obscure”).

definition: The use of tricks to deceive someone (usually to extract money from them).
etymology: From French chicanerie (“trickery”), from chicaner, from Middle French chicaner, borrowed from Middle Low German schicken, from Old Saxon *skikkian, from Proto-West Germanic *skikkijan (“to order, arrange”).

definition: An oriental tobacco pipe with a long flexible tube connected to a container where the smoke is cooled by passing through water.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish chicha, from Kuna chichab (“corn”).

definition: Any of various small grey-and-black songbirds of North America.
etymology: Apparent onomatopoeia from these birds' calls having a distinctive “chick-a-dee-dee-dee” sound, possibly influenced by chick or chicken.

definition: Censure severely or angrily.
etymology: From Middle English chiden (“to chide, rebuke, disapprove, criticize; complain, grumble, dispute; argue, debate, dispute, quarrel”), from Old English ċīdan (“to chide, reprove, rebuke;

definition: Rebuking a person harshly.
In a childlike manner.
example: He acted very childishly.

definition: Being or relating to or like a chimera.
example: His Utopia is not as chimeric commonwealth but a practical improvement on what already exists.

definition: Bellflower of southeastern Europe.
A brightly printed and glazed cotton fabric.
(birds or insects) characterized by or tending to chirp.
example: He's surprisingly chirpy for someone who just lost his father.

definition: A tough semitransparent horny substance; the principal component of the exoskeletons of arthropods and the cell walls of certain fungi.
etymology: From French chitine, from Latin chitōn (“mollusk”), from Ancient Greek χιτών (khitṓn). See also chiton.

definition: Characteristic of the time of chivalry and knighthood in the Middle Ages.
example: Chivalric rites.

definition: Perennial having hollow cylindrical leaves used for seasoning.
example: Chive herb. (attributive use).
etymology: From Middle English chive~cyve, from Old French chive~cive, from Latin cēpa (“onion”).

definition: An oral antibiotic (trade name Chloromycetin) used to treat serious infections (especially typhoid fever).
Any salt of chloric acid.
example: Chlorates are powerful oxidizing agents.

definition: Any alga of the genus Chlorella.
etymology: A use as a common noun of the genus name taxonomic name Chlorella, from New Latin chlorella, from chlōrus + -ella (“diminutive”), from Ancient Greek χλωρός (khlōrós, “pale green”).

definition: The addition or substitution of chlorine in organic compounds.
An antimalarial drug used to treat malaria and amebic dysentery and systemic lupus erythematosus.
Eclair topped with chocolate.
The musical director of a choir.
etymology: From choir + master, a calque of German Chormeister. Piecewise doublet of chorusmaster.

definition: Releasing or activated by acetylcholine or a related compound.
Arborescent cacti having very spiny cylindrical stem segments; southwestern United States and Mexico.
etymology: From a Mexican Spanish use of Spanish cholla (“head, skull”). Compare keel.

definition: One of a pair of slender sticks used as oriental tableware to eat food with.
etymology: Apparently a compound of chop + stick, but the sense of the first element is not clear.

definition: Of or concerned with choreography.
Of or relating to a chorion.
example: A chorionic villus is a minute vascular projection on the fetal chorion.

definition: A singer in a choir.
example: None of the new choristers can sing in tune but they will learn soon enough.
etymology: Derived from late Middle English queristre, from an Anglo-Norman variant of Old French cueriste, from cuer (see Middle French cuer). Equivalent to choir + -ster.

definition: A soft partly suppressed laugh.
example: He frequently interrupted himself with chortles while he told us his favorite joke.
etymology: Perhaps a blend of chuckle + snort. Coined by Lewis Carroll in his poem Jabberwocky, completed in 1855 but only introduced to the public in his 1871 novel Through the Looking-Glass.

definition: The readily stainable substance of a cell nucleus consisting of DNA and RNA and various proteins; during mitotic division it condenses into chromosomes.
Of or relating to chromatography.
etymology: Borrowed from German chromatographisch; see there for more.

definition: A brownish-black mineral; the major source of chromium.
(polo) one of six divisions into which a polo match is divided.
A shoe that comes up to the ankle and is laced through two or three pairs of eyelets; often made of suede.
etymology: Alteration of chukker; from a similar polo player's boot.

definition: (psychology) the configuration of smaller units of information into large coordinated units.
Rude and boorish.
etymology: From Middle English cherlisch, cherlissh, from late Old English ċeorlisċ, ċierlisċ (“of or pertaining to churls”), equivalent to churl + -ish. Piecewise doublet of ceorlish.

definition: Freshwater fishes of tropical America and Africa and Asia similar to American sunfishes; some are food fishes; many small ones are popular in aquariums.
Freshwater fishes of tropical America and Africa and Asia similar to American sunfishes; some are food fishes; many small ones are popular in aquariums.
Relating to the ciliary body and associated structures of the eye.
example: Ciliary movement.

definition: One of several arteries supplying the choroid coat of the eye.
The part of the tunic of the eye between the choroid coat and the iris.
example: The ciliary body produces aqueous humor.

definition: Small veins coming from the ciliary body.
Wild sheep of mountainous regions of western North America having massive curled horns.
example: For quotations using this term, see Citations:cimarron.

definition: A long curved structure on the medial surface of the cerebral hemispheres; the cortical part of the limbic system.
A heavy reddish mineral consisting of mercuric sulfide; the chief source of mercury.
etymology: First attested in the mid-15th century. From Middle English cynabare, from Old French cinabre, from Latin cinnabaris, from Ancient Greek κιννάβαρι (kinnábari), of unknown origin.

definition: Large red-and-black European moth; larvae feed on leaves of ragwort; introduced into United States to control ragwort.
An oral antibiotic (trade name Cipro) used against serious bacterial infections of the skin or respiratory tract or urinary tract or bones or joints.
A small circle.
etymology: From Middle French cerclet, diminutive of cercle.

definition: In a circular manner.
etymology: From Middle English circulerlich, equivalent to circular + -ly.

definition: Cut the skin over the clitoris.

definition: A diacritical mark (^) placed above a vowel in some languages to indicate a special phonetic quality.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin circumflexus (“bent about”), calqued from Ancient Greek περισπώμενος (perispṓmenos, “drawn around”).

definition: Any of several paired curving arteries.
Any of several curved parallel veins accompanying arteries of the same name.
Traveling around something (by ship or plane).
example: Magellan's circumnavigation of the earth proved that it is a globe.

definition: (of a celestial body) continually visible above the horizon during the entire 360 degrees of daily travel.
example: A circumpolar star.

definition: Cat-like mammal typically secreting musk used in perfumes.
etymology: From French civette, from Italian zibetto, from Medieval Latin zibethum, from Arabic زَبَاد (zabād).

definition: Small flat green bean similar to lima beans.
Raccoon-like omnivorous mammal of Mexico and the southwestern United States having a long bushy tail with black and white rings.
Teach or refine to be discriminative in taste or judgment.
etymology: Borrowed from French civiliser, corresponding to civil + -ize.

definition: An awkward climb.
example: Reaching the crest was a real clamber.
etymology: From Middle English clambren, clameren, clemeren (“to climb, clamber; to crawl, creep”), then either: * possibly from clam, clamb, clemb, past tense of climben (“to climb, get over;

definition: Sudden restriction on an activity.
Having a hard nonresonant metallic sound.
example: Clanking chains.

definition: A long thin board with one edge thicker than the other; used as siding by lapping one board over the board below.
etymology: From Middle English clapholt, partial translation from Middle Low German klappholt or Middle Dutch klapholt (“barrel stave”), from klappen (“to crack”) + holt (“wood”). The part "holt" was later calqued to "board".

definition: (used in the plural) a percussion instrument consisting of a pair of hollow pieces of wood or bone (usually held between the thumb and fingers) that are made to click together (as by Spanish dancers) in rhythm with the dance.
Pompous or pretentious talk or writing.
etymology: Theater slang, c. 1730, from clap + trap, referring to theatrical techniques or gags used to incite applause.

definition: A musician who plays the clarinet.
Hemophilia caused by a congenital deficiency of factor VIII; occurs almost exclusively in men.
An artistic person who adheres to classicism.
The part of a student's work that is done in the classroom.
Having well-proportioned limbs.
etymology: From clean (“shapely, well-proportioned”) + limbed (“having limbs of a specified kind or quality”, adjective).

definition: Free from obscurity and easy to understand; the comprehensibility of clear expression.
example: The clearness of the water meant I could still see the key lying on the river-bed.
etymology: From Middle English clernesse; equivalent to clear + -ness.

definition: Annual having the stem beset with curved prickles; North America and Europe and Asia.
etymology: From Middle English clivers, probably from Old English clife (“burdock”).

definition: Part of an interior wall rising above the adjacent roof with windows admitting light.
etymology: From Middle English clerestory, from clere (“clear: light, lighted”) + story (“storey/story: level of a building”).

definition: Someone who is expert in climatology.
The sound of a horse's hoofs hitting on a hard surface.
etymology: Onomatopoeia for two footsteps in succession.

definition: (zoology) the cavity (in birds, reptiles, amphibians, most fish, and monotremes but not other mammals) at the end of the digestive tract into which the intestinal, genital, and urinary tracts open.
example: […] that tremendous cloaca of Pauperism […].
etymology: Borrowed from Latin cloāca (“sewer”), related to cluō (“cleanse; purge”), but the derivation is uncertain.

definition: A low transparent cover put over young plants to protect them from cold.
etymology: Borrowed from French cloche (“bell”), from Medieval Latin clocca (“bell”). Doublet of cloak and clock.

definition: An antihypertensive (trade name Catapres) that can be administered orally or via transdermal patches.
The sound of a horse's hoofs hitting on a hard surface.
example: Holonym: clip-clop.
etymology: Perhaps from German or Dutch kloppen (“to hit, knock”), from Middle Dutch cloppen (“to make a clopping sound”), of onomatopoeic origin. See also clap.

definition: Similar to Gentiana andrewsii but with larger flowers.
A sale intended to dispose of all remaining stock.
(used of hooves) split, divided.
The mark of Satan.
The mark of Satan.
Of or relating to the cloven feet of ruminants or swine.
etymology: From Middle English clovefote, from cloven + foot + -ed.

definition: An interchange that does not require left-hand turns.
example: The off-ramp will lead you along the cloverleaf to your next on-ramp.

definition: The sound made by a hen (as in calling her chicks).
A heavy dull sound (as made by impact of heavy objects).
Bellflower of Europe to temperate Asia having dense spikes of violet-blue to white flowers.
An assistant to a bishop.
etymology: From Middle English coadjutowre, from Old French coadjuteur, borrowed from Late Latin coadiūtōrem, from co- + adiūtor (“helper”), from adiuvō (“to help”) + -tor (agent suffix). By surface analysis, co- + adjutor.

definition: An agent that produces coagulation.
example: Magnesium sulfate is the coagulant used in making tofu. It causes the liquid soy milk to separate into solid tofu and water.
etymology: From Latin coagulans, present participle of coāgulō (“to thicken”).

definition: Transformed from a liquid into a soft semisolid or solid mass.
example: Coagulated blood.

definition: The union of diverse things into one body or form or group; the growing together of parts.
etymology: From Middle French coalescence and its etymon Latin coalēscentia. Doublet of coalescency. By surface analysis, coalesce + -ence.

definition: Having coarse hair or fur.
Shrubby tree with silky foliage and spikes of cylindrical yellow nectarous flowers.
Greenish-blue pigment consisting essentially of cobalt oxide and alumina.
The end of the vertebral column in humans and tailless apes.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin coccyx, borrowed from Ancient Greek κόκκῡξ (kókkūx), referring to the curved shape of a cuckoo's beak when viewed from the side.

definition: Participation in the sport of matching gamecocks in a cockfight.
etymology: From Middle English cokfytyng, kokkysfythynge; equivalent to cock + fighting.

definition: Offensive boldness and assertiveness.
Any coarse weed of the genus Xanthium having spiny burrs.
Macaroon containing coconut.
Lean white flesh of important North Atlantic food fish; usually baked or poached.
Usually made of flaked salt cod and mashed potatoes.
Usually made of flaked salt cod and mashed potatoes.
A large plexus of sympathetic nerves in the abdomen behind the stomach.
A substance (as a coenzyme) that must join with another to produce a given result.
An ornamental sunken panel in a ceiling or dome.
etymology: From Middle English cofre, coffre, from Old French cofre, coffre, from Latin cophinus (“basket”), from Ancient Greek κόφινος (kóphinos, “basket”). Doublet of coffin. Cognate with German Koffer (“a suitcase”).

definition: The arrangement of the hair (especially a woman's hair).
etymology: From Middle English coifen, from Old French coifier, from the noun (see above).

definition: The arrangement of the hair (especially a woman's hair).
Insurance issued jointly by two or more underwriters.
Stiff coarse fiber from the outer husk of a coconut.
etymology: Borrowed from Tamil கயிறு (kayiṟu), Malayalam കയർ (kayaṟ).

definition: Of or relating to coitus or copulation.
An analgesic drug derived from the saffron plant and used to treat gout.
A grouping of words in a sentence.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin collocātiō (“a putting together”). By surface analysis, col- (“together”) + location. The technical sense in linguistics was established in 1951, although it may actually be earlier.

definition: A mixture with properties between those of a solution and fine suspension.
etymology: From French colloïde, from Ancient Greek κόλλα (kólla, “glue”) + -oid.

definition: A colloquial expression; characteristic of spoken or written communication that seeks to imitate informal speech.
Someone who helps to found a colony.
A publisher's emblem printed in a book (usually on the title page).
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin colophōn, from Ancient Greek κολοφών (kolophṓn, “peak or finishing touch”).

definition: Milky fluid secreted for the first day or two after parturition.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin colostrum, of uncertain origin.

definition: The timbre of a musical sound.
A small column (or structure resembling a column) that is a part of a plant or animal.
A person who separates and straightens the fibers of cotton or wool.
etymology: From Middle English comber, camber, equivalent to comb + -er.

definition: A female actor in a comedy.
etymology: Borrowed from French comédienne, equivalent to comedy + -ienne. Compare doyenne.

definition: Decline to a lower status or level.
Of or relating to or resembling a comet.
A state or atmosphere of harmony or mutual civility and respect.
etymology: From Late Middle English comite (“association”), from Latin cōmitās.

definition: Take arbitrarily or by force.
example: The Cubans commandeered the plane and flew it to Miami.
etymology: First attested in the late 19th century. From Dutch commanderen (“to command”), partially through its descendant, Afrikaans kommandeer (“to command”).

definition: The position or office of commander.
etymology: From French commanderie, from Late Latin commendaria, from Latin commendare. In the Chinese administrative division sense, used as a translation of 府 (fǔ) and 郡 (jùn).

definition: Living in a state of commensalism.
etymology: From Middle English commensal, from Old French commensal, from Medieval Latin commensālis, from com- + mensa (“table”) + -ālis.

definition: Make a commentary on.
example: For the radio audience he will commentate on the match.
etymology: Back-formation from commentator. Equivalent to comment + -ate (verb-forming suffix).

definition: Organized principally for financial gain.
example: Christmas has become a commercialized spectacle.

definition: To feel or express sympathy or compassion.
example: A few individuals who commiserated the unhappy condition of British negro slaves.
etymology: From commiserātus, the perfect passive participle of commiseror.

definition: A man who is a member of committee.
A plant that is ubiquitous in all but very acid soil; found in most of Europe and North Africa.
Plant having a large edible bulb and linear basal leaves and racemes of light to deep violet-blue star-shaped flowers on tall green scapes; western North America.
Dark fawn-colored eland of southern and eastern Africa.
Tall leafy European biennial or perennial having spectacular clusters of large tubular pink-purple flowers; leaves yield drug digitalis and are poisonous to livestock.
North American raccoon.
Annual weed with finely divided foliage and spikes of green flowers; common in North America; introduced elsewhere accidentally.
The practice of communal living and common ownership.
By a group of people rather than an individual.
example: The mills were owned communally.

definition: Relating to or marked by communism.
example: Communist Party.

definition: Switch for reversing the direction of an electric current.
etymology: Back-formation from commutation (in the late 19th century), as is commutate (verb) too.

definition: In a compact manner or state.
example: The children were packed compactly into the car.

definition: Anatomist who compares the anatomy of different animals.
A mild state of dissociation.
Separate into isolated compartments or categories.
