definition: In a sympathetic manner.
British term for someone who introduces television acts or cabarets etc.
example: Every year I am the compere for our Church Quiz Night.
etymology: A borrowing of French compère (“partner, accomplice”), from Old French comper, from Late Latin compater (“godfather”), from Latin com- (“with”) + pater (“father”). Doublet of compeer, compadre, and goombah.

definition: A person given to excessive complaints and crying and whining.
Behave well or properly.
example: To comport with an injury.
etymology: From late Middle English comporten, from Old French comporter, from Latin comportare (“to bring together”), from com- (“together”) + portare (“to carry”).

definition: One who sets written material into type.
example: I work as an image compositor.
etymology: From French compositeur, from Latin compositor.

definition: The property of being able to occupy less space.
In a manner that cannot be evaded.
example: The ministry considers that contributions to such a fund should be met from voluntary donations rather than from rates compulsorily levied.

definition: A feeling of deep regret (usually for some misdeed).
May be computed or estimated.
example: Computable odds.

definition: The control of processes by computer.
The quality of affording easy familiarity and sociability.
A polyhedron some of whose plane sections are concave polygons.
Someone who holds or operates a concession.
In keeping.
example: Expressed views concordant with his background.
etymology: French concordant, from Latin concordans, present participle of concordare. See concord.

definition: A signed written agreement between two or more parties (nations) to perform some action.
etymology: From French concordat, from Latin concordatum.

definition: With condescension; in a patronizing manner.
example: He treats his secretary condescendingly.

definition: A confectioner's shop.
etymology: From Late Latin cōnfectiōnārius (“one who prepares things by means of ingredients”), from Latin cōnfectiō (“preparing, producing”). See confection. By surface analysis, confection + -ary.

definition: Someone who makes candies and other sweets.
Flowing together.
etymology: From Latin cōnfluēns, present participle of cōnfluō.

definition: Congealed into jelly; solidified by cooling.
example: In Georgia they serve congealed salads.

definition: A Chinese rice gruel eaten for breakfast.
etymology: From late Middle English congie, from Old French congié, congiet (modern French congé), from Latin commeātus (“passage, permission to leave”), from commeō (“to go and come”), from con- + meō (“to go, to pass”).

definition: The act of congregating.
A morel whose pitted fertile body is attached to the stalk with little free skirt around it; the fertile body is grey when young and black in old age.
Based primarily on surmise rather than adequate evidence.
example: Theories about the extinction of dinosaurs are still highly conjectural.

definition: Someone who performs magic tricks to amuse an audience.
etymology: From Middle English conjurer, from Anglo-Norman conjurour (“conjurer, conspirator”). Equivalent to conjure + -er.

definition: The inedible nutlike seed of the horse chestnut.
etymology: As a term for horse chestnut, derived from the name of the game conkers, which came first.

definition: Agreement on a secret plot.
etymology: From early 18th c., replaced earlier form connivence (late 16th c.), from Latin connīventia, from connīvēns (“winking”).

definition: An adventurer (especially one who led the Spanish conquest of Mexico and Peru in the 16th century).
The repetition of consonants (or consonant patterns) especially at the ends of words.
etymology: From Middle English consonance, from Middle French consonance, from Latin cōnsonantia. Doublet of consonancy. By surface analysis, con- + son- + -ance.

definition: An advocate of constitutional government.
The post of consul.
Tending to consume or use often wastefully.
example: Water suitable for beneficial consumptive uses.
etymology: From con- + Latin sūmptus + -ive, from Middle English consumptive, from Latin cōnsūmptus, past participle of cōnsūmō.

definition: During the same period of time.
example: Contemporaneously, or possibly a little later, there developed a great Sumerian civilisation.
etymology: From contemporaneous + -ly, from Latin contemporāneus, from co- (“together”) + tempus (“time”).

definition: Without respect; in a disdainful manner.
example: She spoke of him contemptuously.

definition: With equanimity.
example: ‘I bought it,’ she said contentedly.

definition: The exercise of self constraint in sexual matters.
example: For quotations using this term, see Citations:continence.
etymology: Dated from the 14th century as Middle English contynence, from Old French continence, from Latin continentia (“a repression”). See also countenance.

definition: Twist and press out of shape.
example: Features contorted with fury.
etymology: Equivalent to con- + -tort; from Middle English, borrowed from Latin contortus, past participle of contorqueō, from com- + torqueō (“twist, turn”).

definition: The act of twisting or deforming the shape of something (e.g., yourself).
etymology: Derived from Middle French contortion, from Latin contortiō.

definition: An acrobat able to twist into unusual positions.
Capable of contracting or being contracted.
example: The contractile wings of an insect.

definition: A bodily organ that contracts.
On or relating to the opposite side (of the body).
A woman singer having a contralto voice.
etymology: Contraction of contratenor alto, from Latin contratenor altus.

definition: Relating to or characteristic of or according to the rules of counterpoint.
example: Contrapuntal base.
etymology: From Latin punctus contra punctum (“note against note”).

definition: Of words so related that one contrasts with the other.
example: ‘rich’ and ‘hard-up’ are contrastive terms.

definition: Make or work out a plan for; devise.
example: They contrived to murder their boss.
etymology: From Middle English contrive (15th c.), an alteration of contreve(n), controve(n) (“to invent”, 14th c.), from Old French controver, derived from trover (“to find”). Cognate with Modern French controuver.

definition: Strabismus in which one or both eyes turn inward toward the nose.
A polyhedron any plane section of which is a convex polygon.
The property possessed by a convex shape.
A person who conveys (carries or transmits).

definition: A moving belt that transports objects (as in a factory).
A jovial nature.
example: He's easy to talk to because of his conviviality.

definition: A sudden uncontrollable attack.
example: Convulsions of laughter.

definition: Affected by involuntary jerky muscular contractions; resembling a spasm.
example: Convulsive motions.

definition: In an abundant manner.
A rockfish of the Pacific coastal waters of North America.
Of something having the color of copper.
example: An especially coppery grade of brass.

definition: A dense growth of bushes.
The dried meat of the coconut from which oil is extracted.
etymology: Borrowed from Portuguese copra, from Malayalam കൊപ്ര (kopra). Cognate with Tamil கொப்பரை (kopparai), Kuvi କବ୍ରି (kobri), Sanskrit कूर्पस (kūrpasa), Hindi खोपा (khopā).

definition: Oil from coconuts.
Engage in sexual intercourse.
etymology: From Latin cōpulātus, perfect passive participle of cōpulō (“to couple, join, connect”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Compare French copuler.

definition: Someone employed to make written copies of documents and manuscripts.
A seductive woman who uses her sex appeal to exploit men.
Like a coquette.
Explosive powder (nitroglycerin and guncotton and petrolatum) dissolved in acetone and dried and extruded in brown cords.
etymology: From cord + -ite, because the material is manufactured into long cordlike cylinders.

definition: (of wine) tainted in flavor by a cork containing excess tannin.
example: A corked port.

definition: Larva of a noctuid moth; highly destructive to especially corn and cotton and tomato crops.
Plant of southern and southeastern United States grown for its yellow flowers that can be dried.
etymology: From corn + flower. Piecewise doublet of cornflour.

definition: Erect perennial of southeastern United States having large heads of usually blue flowers.
A shade of medium-to-light blue containing relatively little green compared to blue.
example: Her suit ties in bows of self-fabric on the shoulder, and a circular skirt buttons on with straw flowers of cornflower blue.

definition: Excessively fat.
example: Corpulent person.
etymology: From Middle English corpulent, from Old French corpulent, from Latin corpulentus.

definition: A broad transverse nerve tract connecting the two cerebral hemispheres.
Mutually related.
Erosion by chemical action.
Capable of being corrupted.
example: Corruptible judges.
etymology: From Middle English corruptible, from Latin corruptibilis.

definition: In a corrupt manner.
An arrangement of flowers that is usually given as a present.
A funeral procession.
Having brief brilliant points or flashes of light.
etymology: From Latin coruscāns (“glittering”), present participle of coruscō.

definition: A piece of metal covered by leather with a flexible handle; used for hitting people.
Sign jointly.
For cosmetic purposes to improve appearance.
example: It is used cosmetically by many women.

definition: Sponsor together with another sponsor.
(in India) a unit of length having different values in different localities.
etymology: Borrowed from Hindustani کوس / कोस (kos). Doublet of krosa.

definition: A ball at which young ladies are presented to society.
etymology: First use appears c. 1750, in the sense of the dance, from French cotillon (“petticoat”), extended to the dance because of the distinctive lift of dress revealing the petticoat, from cotte (“dress”) + -illon (diminutive).

definition: Venomous semiaquatic snake of swamps in southern United States.
Common small rabbit of North America having greyish or brownish fur and a tail with a white underside; a host for Ixodes pacificus and Ixodes scapularis (Lyme disease ticks).
Common small rabbit of North America having greyish or brownish fur and a tail with a white underside; a host for Ixodes pacificus and Ixodes scapularis (Lyme disease ticks).
Brought into equipoise by means of a weight or force that offsets another.
A claim filed in opposition to another claim in a legal action.
Refutation by example.
A large scale offensive (more than a counterattack) undertaken by a defending force to seize the initiative from an attacking force.
A return punch (especially by a boxer).
Relating to or being a counterrevolution.
etymology: From counter- + revolutionary. Originally applied to thinkers who opposed themselves to the 1789 French Revolution.

definition: Make a counterattack.
A duty imposed to offset subsidies by foreign governments.
Occurring or extending throughout a county.
example: A countywide war on drugs.

definition: Marrow squash plant whose fruit are eaten when small.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French courgette, diminutive of courge (“vegetable marrow, marrow squash”). Ultimately related to zucchini through Latin cucurbita.

definition: A huntsman who hunts small animals with fast dogs that use sight rather than scent to follow their prey.
etymology: From Middle English courser, Anglo-Norman cursier, corser, from Medieval Latin cursārius. By surface analysis, course + -er. Doublet of corsair and hussar.

definition: In a polite manner.
etymology: From Middle English curteisly, curteisliche; equivalent to courteous + -ly.

definition: Changing so that interrelations with another variable quantity or set of quantities remain unchanged.
Showing extreme cupidity; painfully desirous of another's advantages.

etymology: From Middle English coveitous, from Anglo-Norman *cuveitus, from Medieval Latin as if *cupiditosus, from Latin cupiditas (“desire”); see covet.

definition: Leather made from the hide of a cow.
The helmsman of a ship's boat or a racing crew.

etymology: From Middle English cokswain, equivalent to cock (“small boat”) + swain (“boy, servant”).

definition: In a coy manner.

definition: A party favor consisting of a paper roll (usually containing candy or a small favor) that pops when pulled at both ends.
Someone excellent of their kind.
A capacity unit used for measuring fresh herring.

definition: Someone who gets in (to a party) without an invitation or without paying.
example: Wedding Crashers (2005 movie).

definition: Low space beneath a floor of a building; gives workers access to wiring or plumbing.
A hospital where foundlings (infant children of unknown parents) are taken in and cared for.
An uneasy sensation as of insects creeping on your skin.
Erect European herb with creeping rootstocks and nodding spikelike racemes of blue to violet flowers.
Low-branching leafy annual with flower heads resembling zinnias; found in southwestern United States and Mexico to Guatemala.
Feelings of dislike and anxiety.
example: The cave gave me the creepy-crawlies.

definition: Reduce to ashes.
example: Cremate a corpse.
etymology: First attested in 1889; borrowed from Latin cremātus, perfect passive participle of cremō (“to burn to ashes; to cremate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

definition: A mortuary where corpses are cremated.
Custard sprinkled with sugar and broiled.
Eurasian grass grown in United States great plains area for forage and erosion control.
Brought low in spirit.
etymology: From crest + fallen, from the appearance of a horse with its crest (head) on its chest after defeat in a battle.

definition: A card game (usually for two players) in which each player is dealt six cards and discards one or two.
example: "No one remembers cribbage now," […].
etymology: From crib + -age. Named from the "crib" consisting of certain cards laid aside by each player.

definition: A board with pegs and regularly spaced holes for holding the pegs; used for keeping the score in a game of cribbage.
Legislation that makes something illegal.
example: The criminalization of marijuana.

definition: Declare illegal; outlaw.
example: Marijuana is criminalized in the U.S.

definition: An electrical appliance for crimping the hair so that it becomes wavy, often in a sawtooth fashion.
A hand tool used for joining two pieces of metal or other ductile material (usually a wire and a metal plate) by deforming one or both of them to hold the other.
Uneven by virtue of having wrinkles or waves.
In a well delineated manner.
A pleasing firmness and freshness.
example: Crispness of new dollar bills.

definition: A bicycle race held on a short course (usually less than 5 km or 3 miles).
etymology: From French critérium (“competition”), from Latin critērium, from Ancient Greek κριτήριον (kritḗrion).

definition: The lean flesh of a saltwater fish caught along Atlantic coast of southern U.S.
A harsh hoarse utterance (as of a frog).
example: The croakings of frogs from the nearby pond.

example: He was crooning a song.
etymology: The verb is borrowed from Scots croon (“to utter a deep, long-drawn-out sound; to utter a lament, mourn; to sing in a wailing voice, whimper, whine;

definition: (genetics) an organism that is the offspring of genetically dissimilar parents or stock; especially offspring produced by breeding plants or animals of different varieties or breeds or species.
example: A mule is a cross between a horse and a donkey.

definition: (genetics) the act of mixing different species or varieties of animals or plants and thus to produce hybrids.
An instance of confirming something by considering information from several sources.
Wind blowing across the path of a ship or aircraft.
Lying or extending across the length of a thing or in a cross direction.
example: A crosswise street.
etymology: From Middle English croswyse, crose wyse, equivalent to cross + -wise.

definition: Having a difficult and contrary disposition.
etymology: From crotchet + -y, using crotchet in the 16th-century sense of a whim or fancy.

definition: A disease of infants and young children; harsh coughing and hoarseness and fever and difficult breathing.
European herb resembling vetch; naturalized in the eastern United States; having umbels of pink-and-white flowers and sharp-angled pods.
Shaped like a cross.
Characterized by obscenity.
example: Because I didn't study for my test, I feel like I'm gonna make a pretty cruddy grade.
etymology: From Middle English cruddi, equivalent to crud + -y.

definition: A thick soft cake with a porous texture; cooked on a griddle.
example: Joan Bakewell was famously described as "the thinking man's crumpet".
etymology: First appears c. the 17th century, either from crompid cake (“wafer, literally, curled-up cake”), from crompid, form of crumpen (“to curl up”); cognate to crumpled. An alternate etymology is from Celtic;

definition: The leg from the knee to foot.
Small jar; holds liquid (oil or water).
example: With a thought I tooke for Maudline & a cruse of cockle pottage. with a thing thus tall, skie blesse you all: I befell into this dotage.
etymology: From Middle English crouse, from Old English crūse (“jar, cruse”), from Proto-West Germanic *krūsā, from Proto-Germanic *krūsǭ, *krūsaz (“jar, pot, collar, jug”).

definition: The branch of physics that studies the phenomena that occur at very low temperatures.
In a cryptic manner.
example: ‘we will meet again,’ he said cryptically.

definition: The science of analyzing and deciphering codes and ciphers and cryptograms.
etymology: From crypto- + -logy, from Ancient Greek κρυπτός (kruptós, “hidden”) + λόγος (lógos, “word”); originally after Latin cryptologia, which is apparently first recorded in an English context.

definition: Shaped like a cube.
An ancient unit of length based on the length of the forearm.

The cube shaped bone on the outer side of the tarsus.
A member of a religious cult.
(of farmland) capable of being farmed productively.

definition: Turn into curds.
example: Curdled milk.
etymology: Metathesis of earlier dialectal cruddle, crudle, equivalent to curd + -le (frequentative suffix).

definition: Transformed from a liquid into a soft semisolid or solid mass.
example: Curdled milk.

definition: Old World sandpiper with a curved bill like a curlew.
Crisp spiky leaves with somewhat bitter taste.
A crusty irascible cantankerous old person full of stubborn ideas.
example: There's a cranky curmudgeon working at the hospital who gives all the patients and other doctors flak.
etymology: Numerous folk etymologies exist for this word. An alternative spelling attested in 1600 is cornmudgin, in Holland's translation of Livy, rendering Latin frūmentārius (“corn-merchant”).

definition: The temporal property of being cut short.
In a curt, abrupt and discourteous manner.
example: He told me curtly to get on with it.

Tannin extract derived from any of several mangrove barks of Pacific areas.
Thin slice of meat (especially veal) usually fried or broiled.
A colorless toxic gas with a pungent almond odor; has been used in chemical warfare.

definition: Sexual arousal involving communication on the internet.

definition: A base found in DNA and RNA and derived from pyrimidine; pairs with guanine.

definition: Of or relating to or characteristic of a czar.
Small European freshwater fish with a slender bluish-green body.

definition: Russian country house.
etymology: Borrowed from Russian да́ча (dáča), originally "gift, portion, land (granted by a prince)", from дать (datʹ, “to give”).

definition: A photograph made by an early photographic process; the image was produced on a silver plate sensitized to iodine and developed in mercury vapor.
etymology: From French daguerréotype. Named after French artist Louis Daguerre (1787–1851) who announced the process in 1839. Daguerre developed the process after some years of collaborations with French chemist Nicéphore Niépce.

definition: Radish of Japan with a long hard durable root eaten raw or cooked.
An evil supernatural being.
etymology: A modern romanization of Ancient Greek δαίμων (daímōn, “the one who divides, dispenser, tutelary deity”), intended to distinguish its ancient Greek sense from later conceptions of demons.

definition: The business of a dairy.
The deliberate act of delaying and playing instead of working.
etymology: From Middle English daliaunce et al., from dalien (“to exchange pleasantries, to chat; to flirt”), from Old French dalier, dailer. By surface analysis, dally + -ance.

definition: Of or relating to or characteristic of Damascus or its people.
example: Damascene city gates.

definition: Deserving to be execrated.

etymology: From Middle English dampnable, from Old French dampnable, from Latin damnābilis. By surface analysis, damn + -able.

definition: Dark purple plum of the damson tree.
etymology: From Middle English damascene, damasyn, damacene, from Latin prūnum damascēnum (“Damascene plum, plum of Damascus”). Doublet of damascene.

Small scales from animal skins or hair or bird feathers that can cause allergic reactions in some people.

Minute freshwater crustacean having a round body enclosed in a transparent shell; moves about like a flea by means of hairy branched antennae.
In an original manner.

definition: Bearing dark fruit.
Uncannily or threateningly dark or obscure.

Material used to daub walls.

definition: Cause to lose courage; to be daunted; to be scared away.
Missionary work for Islam.

In a manner or to a degree that dazzles the beholder.
Required by etiquette or usage or fashion.

definition: Deprive of energy.
The part of a lock that is engaged or withdrawn with a key.
So lacking in interest as to cause mental weariness.
example: The deadening effect of some routine tasks.

definition: A nonenterprising person who is not paying their way.
example: The deadheads on the payroll should be eased out as fast as possible.

definition: Caused to hear poorly or not at all.
The official residence of a dean.

definition: A special loved one.
example: Listen, deary: I'd appreciate your not talking about my son like that.

definition: Any of various plants of the genus Zigadenus having glaucous leaves and terminal racemes of mostly white flowers; all are poisonous.
Never dying.
example: Her novels are filled with unforgettable characters and deathless prose.

definition: Any structure that is very unsafe; where people are likely to be killed.
example: Route 9 is a deathtrap; they should at least put up guard rails.

definition: Corrupt morally or by intemperance or sensuality.
etymology: From de- + base, from Old French bas, from Latin bassus. Cognate with Spanish debajo (“under, beneath, below”). Compare abase.

definition: Being mixed with extraneous material; the product of adulterating.
example: There's something ugly and fascinating about reading such intimate tales of debasement and depression and failure and self-doubt.

definition: Used of conduct; characterized by dishonor.
The ability of a customer to obtain goods or services before payment, based on the trust that payment will be made in the future.
etymology: From earlier debentur, from Latin debentur (“they are owing”), supposedly the first word of such a document in early times. The ending was apparently influenced by words in -(t)ure.

definition: The ability of a customer to obtain goods or services before payment, based on the trust that payment will be made in the future.
Lacking energy or vitality.
example: His debilitated body, the victim of the wasting disease, could no longer support his weight.

definition: Surgical removal of foreign material and dead tissue from a wound in order to prevent infection and promote healing.
Coffee with the caffeine removed.
Leave a camp.
example: The hikers decamped before dawn.

definition: Pour out gradually, so as to separate out sediment.
example: The sommelier decanted the wines.
etymology: From French décanter, from Medieval Latin dēcanthāre, from dē- + canthus (“beak of a cup or jug”).

definition: Any of the enzymes that hydrolize the carboxyl group.
The event of dying or departure from life.
example: Upon your decease the capital will pass to your grandchildren.
etymology: From Old French deces (Modern French décès), from Latin dēcessus (“departure”).

definition: (mechanics) Motion with a continually decreasing velocity.
Make less central.
example: After the revolution, food distribution was decentralized.

definition: (statistics) any of nine points that divided a distribution of ranked scores into equal intervals where each interval contains one-tenth of the scores.
example: Although few people scored high marks, everyone did quite well—the lowest decile was over 50%.
etymology: From Latin decilis, equivalent to dec- + -ile.

definition: The trait of resoluteness as evidenced by firmness of character or purpose.
