definition: A representation (a picture or sculpture) of Jesus wearing a crown of thorns.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from Latin ecce homō̆ (“behold the man!”). See John 19:5 in the Bible.

definition: Of or associated with a church (especially a Christian Church).
example: Ecclesiastic history.
etymology: From Middle English ecclesyastyke, from Late Latin ecclēsiasticus (“of the church”), from Ancient Greek ἐκκλησιαστικός (ekklēsiastikós). By surface analysis, ecclesiast + -ic. Doublet of Ecclesiasticus.

definition: The branch of theology concerned with the nature and the constitution and the functions of a church.
etymology: From ecclesio- + -logy. Coined by a writer of the British Critic in 1837, as ecclesialogy.

definition: A graphical image of the heart produced by an echocardiograph.
Oblong cream puff.
Use cautiously and frugally.
example: I try to economize my spare time.

definition: In an ecstatic manner.
example: He reacted ecstatically to my plan to travel to Africa.

definition: (spiritualism) a substance supposed to emanate from the body of the medium during a trance.
etymology: From ecto- (“outside”) + plasm or -plasm, referring to the fact that ectoplasm is believed to emanate from and materialize outside of the medium's body.

definition: A movement promoting union between religions (especially between Christian churches).
Tropical starchy tuberous root.
With the edge forward or on, by, or toward the edge.
example: He sawed the board edgeways.
etymology: From edge + -wise. Compare English edgeling (“edgeways”) and edgelong.

definition: Feelings of anxiety that make you tense and irritable.
In an effectual manner.
A former Turkish term of respect; especially for government officials.
etymology: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish افندی (efendi), from Greek αφέντη (afénti), vocative of αφέντης (aféntis), from Ancient Greek αὐθέντης (authéntēs, “lord, master”). Doublet of authentic.

definition: Of nerves and nerve impulses; conveying information away from the CNS.
example: Efferent nerves and impulses.
etymology: From Latin efferēns, present active participle of efferō (“bring or carry out”), from ē (“out of”), short form of ex, + ferō (“carry, bear”). By surface analysis, ef- + -fer + -ent.

definition: A nerve fiber that carries impulses toward the muscles or glands.
A nerve that conveys impulses toward or to muscles or glands.
A neuron conducting impulses outwards from the brain or spinal cord.
The process of bubbling as gas escapes.
etymology: Borrowed from French effervescence. By surface analysis, ef- + Latin ferv- + -escence.

definition: Affected, overrefined, and effeminate.
example: The young man spoke in effete, accented English.
etymology: From Latin effētus (“exhausted”, literally “that has given birth”), 1620s.

definition: A light shield that allows only a spot of light about the size of an egg to shine out; used to test eggs.
Moth having nonfunctional mouthparts as adults; larvae feed on tree foliage and spin egg-shaped cocoons.
A conceited and self-centered person.
etymology: From French égoïste, from Latin ego + -iste. By surface analysis, ego + -ist.

definition: Concerned chiefly or only with yourself and your advantage to the exclusion of others.
example: The merely egoistic satisfactions of fame are easily nullified.

definition: An abnormally egotistical person.
example: He's a raving egomaniac: all he ever talks about is himself and how important he is.

definition: Duck of the Northern Hemisphere much valued for the fine soft down of the females.
etymology: From Icelandic æðar, genitive of æðr, probably reaching English via Swedish eider (now ejder), from a North Germanic root.

definition: Duck of the Northern Hemisphere much valued for the fine soft down of the females.
Having eight units or components.
etymology: From Middle English [Term?], from Old English eahtafeald. Equivalent to eight + -fold.

definition: Any of several annual Welsh festivals involving artistic competitions (especially in singing).
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from Welsh eisteddfod (“session”), from eistedd (“to sit”) + bod (“to be”), literally “being sitting”.

definition: Either of two large African antelopes of the genus Taurotragus having short spirally twisted horns in both sexes.
etymology: Borrowed from Afrikaans eland, from Dutch eland (“elk”), from Middle Dutch elant, from obsolete early modern German elend, from Middle High German elen, see German Elen for more. Doublet of elk.

definition: For time to move forward.
example: Three years elapsed.
etymology: From Middle French elapser, from Latin elapsus.

definition: A fibrous scleroprotein found in elastic tissues such as the walls of arteries.
Any of various elastic materials that resemble rubber (resumes its original shape when a deforming force is removed).
Jostling with the elbows.
example: Elbowing is a foul in basketball.

definition: A common shrub with black fruit or a small tree of Europe and Asia; fruit used for wines and jellies.
Any of numerous shrubs or small trees of temperate and subtropical Northern Hemisphere having white flowers and berrylike fruit.
A graphical recording of the cardiac cycle produced by an electrocardiograph.
etymology: From electro- + cardio- + -gram, Modelled on German Electrocardiogramm(modern German Elektrokardiogramm)

definition: Branch of chemistry that deals with the chemical action of electricity and the production of electricity by chemical reactions.
A temporary magnet made by coiling wire around an iron core; when current flows in the coil the iron becomes a magnet.
A voltmeter whose sensitivity is increased by amplification.
Of or relating to electrophoresis.
Having the nature or shape of an ellipsoid.

The process of extracting one material from another by washing with a solvent to remove adsorbed material from an adsorbent (as in washing of loaded ion-exchange resins to remove captured ions); used to obtain uranium ions.
Something that is emitted or radiated (as a gas or an odor or a light, etc.).
example: Perfume is an emanation from a flower.

definition: Give equal rights to; of women and minorities.
example: To emancipate a colony.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin ēmancipātus (“liberated, emancipated”) + English -ate (suffix forming verbs, and adjectives with the sense ‘characterized by the specified thing’).

definition: Appropriate (as property entrusted to one's care) fraudulently to one's own use.
example: The accountant embezzled thousands of dollars while working for the wealthy family.
etymology: From Middle English embesilen, from Anglo-Norman embesiler, embesillier, embeseillier (“to steal, cause to disappear”), from em- + Old French besillier (“to torment, destroy, gouge”), of unknown origin.

definition: Decorate with needlework.
etymology: From Middle English embrouderen, frequentative of embrouden (“to decorate, embroider”), equivalent to embroid + -er.

definition: A medicine that induces nausea and vomiting.
etymology: From French émétique, from Vulgar Latin *emeticus, from Ancient Greek ἐμετικός (emetikós), from ἔμετος (émetos, “vomit”); by surface analysis, em(esis) + -etic.

definition: Someone who leaves one country to settle in another.
example: Between the wars, Paris was the center for all the world's emigres.

definition: Hard red wheat grown especially in Russia and Germany; in United States as stock feed.
etymology: First used in 1908; borrowed from German Emmer (compare the obsolescent related German synonym Amelkorn, whence English amelcorn).

definition: Having a softening or soothing effect especially to the skin.
etymology: From French émollient, from Latin emolliēns, present active participle of ēmolliō (“make soft”), from ex- + molliō, from mollis (“soft”). By surface analysis, e- + Latin moll- + -i- + -ent.

definition: Emotional nature or quality.
A person who buys.
A parent whose children have grown up and left home.
A surface-active agent that promotes the formation of an emulsion.
(chess) a chess pawn that is moved two squares can be captured by an opponent's pawn commanding the square that was passed.
etymology: An unadapted borrowing from French en passant.

definition: Enclose in, or as if in, a case.
example: My feet were encased in mud.

definition: A sorcerer or magician.
etymology: From Middle English enchantour, from Old French enchanteor (Modern French enchanteur), from Latin incantātor (“enchanter; spellcaster; conjurer”), from incantāre (“to sing, to consecrate with spells”).

definition: In an encouraging manner.
example: ‘Go on,’ he said encouragingly to his student.

definition: An onerous or difficult concern.
etymology: From Middle English encombraunce, from Old French encombrance, from encombrer.

definition: Comprehensive in scope or content (as an encyclopedia).
example: Encyclopedic knowledge.

definition: Widely cultivated herb with leaves valued as salad green; either curly serrated leaves or broad flat ones that are usually blanched.
etymology: From Middle French endive, from Medieval Latin endivia or Italian indivia~endivia, from Medieval Greek ἐντύβιον (entúbion), from Latin intibus (which see). The ultimate source is likely Semitic.

definition: (pregnancy) the mucous membrane that lines the uterus; thickens under hormonal control and (if pregnancy does not occur) is shed in menstruation; if pregnancy occurs it is shed along with the placenta at parturition.
etymology: From endo- (“inner”) + Late Latin metrium (“womb”), from Ancient Greek μήτριον (mḗtrion, “of a mother”). Compare μήτρᾱ (mḗtrā, “womb”).

definition: A long slender medical instrument for examining the interior of a bodily organ or performing minor surgery.
(of a chemical reaction or compound) occurring or formed with absorption of heat.
etymology: Borrowed from French endothermique, from endo- (“inside”) + thermique (“of heat”), both ultimately from Ancient Greek. By surface analysis, endo- + -thermic.

definition: A chemical reaction accompanied by the absorption of heat.
The philosophical theory that energy is the substrate of all phenomena and that all observable changes can be interpreted as transformations of one kind of energy into another.
Raise to a higher energy level.
Supplying motive force.
Endowed with the rights of citizenship especially the right to vote.
Freedom from political subjugation or servitude.
etymology: Enfranchise is derived from Late Middle English enfraunchisen, enfrauncheisen (“to grant (someone) citizenship; to grant (someone) membership of a guild, etc.;

definition: A postulated biochemical change (presumably in neural tissue) that represents a memory.
etymology: Borrowed from German Engramm which was coined by German evolutionary biologist Richard Semon in 1904. First attested in English in 1921 (see quotation below).

definition: Issue an injunction.
etymology: From Middle English enjoinen, from Old French enjoindre (“to join with”), from Latin iniungo (“to attach”), a compound of in- (“into” “upon”) and iungo.

definition: Enclose in a shrine.
example: The saint's bones were enshrined in the cathedral.

definition: Entrap.
example: The dolphins became entangled in a fishing net.
etymology: From Middle English entanglen (“to involve [someone] in difficulty”, “to embarrass”). Equivalent to en- + tangle.

definition: Of or relating to the enteron.
In an entertaining manner.
example: Byron's consumed memoirs possessed the merit of being well and entertainingly written.

definition: The ceremony of installing a new monarch.
Something that seduces or has the quality to seduce.
Something that provides access (to get in or get out).
example: They waited at the entrance to the garden.

definition: Capturing interest as if by a spell.
example: Antique papers of entrancing design.

definition: A hand shovel carried by infantrymen for digging trenches.
An entrenched fortification; a position protected by trenches.
Speak, pronounce, or utter in a certain way.
example: The terms in which he enunciates the great doctrines of the gospel.
etymology: From Latin ēnuntiātus, past participle of ēnuntiō (“to report, declare”), from ē- + nūntiō (“to report”). Doublet of enounce.

definition: The articulation of speech regarded from the point of view of its intelligibility to the audience.
example: It was time for the enunciation of an important truth.
etymology: From Latin ēnuntiātiō. By surface analysis, enunciate + -ion.

definition: Extend on all sides of simultaneously; encircle.
etymology: From Middle English enviroun (“round about in a circle or ring;

definition: The branch of biochemistry dealing with the chemical nature and biological activity of enzymes.
An older other woman, especially a sister, used by a female.
etymology: Borrowed from Korean 언니 (eonni, “older sister of a woman”).

definition: Of or relating to eosinophil.
An annual publication containing astronomical tables that give the positions of the celestial bodies throughout the year.
example: Today computers calculate the ephemerides.
etymology: From New Latin ephēmeris, from Ancient Greek ἐφημερίς (ephēmerís, “diary, calendar”), from ἐφήμερος (ephḗmeros, “daily”).

definition: (astronomy) a measure of time defined by Earth's orbital motion; terrestrial time is mean solar time corrected for the irregularities of the Earth's motions.
Of or relating to epidemiology.
example: Epidemiological studies.

definition: A witty saying.
etymology: From Middle French epigramme, from Latin epigramma, from Ancient Greek ἐπίγραμμα (epígramma, “inscription”).

definition: A quotation at the beginning of some piece of writing.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἐπιγραφή (epigraphḗ, “inscription”), from ἐπιγράφω (epigráphō, “write upon”), from ἐπῐ- (epĭ-, “on, upon, over, etc.”) + γρᾰ́φω (grắphō, “to draw, paint, write, etc.”).

definition: Embody the essential characteristics of or be a typical example of.
The site on the surface of an antigen molecule to which an antibody attaches itself.
Highly significant or important especially bringing about or marking the beginning of a new development or era.
example: Epochal decisions made by Roosevelt and Churchill.

definition: A body of poetry that conveys the traditions of a society by treating some epic theme.
etymology: From Latin epos, from Ancient Greek ἔπος (épos, “word, song, epic”).

definition: The act of making equal or uniform.
A plant disease caused by the ergot fungus.
Bulky greyish-brown eagle with a short wedge-shaped white tail; of Europe and Greenland.
example: The bald erne.

definition: Sensitive to sexual stimulation.
example: Give him an erogenous massage.

definition: Any area of the body especially sensitive to sexual stimulation.
Wearing away by friction.
example: The erosive effects of waves on the shoreline.

definition: In an erotic manner.
A mature blood cell that contains hemoglobin to carry oxygen to the bodily tissues; a biconcave disc that has no nucleus.
etymology: From erythro- (“red”) + -cyte (“cell”), referring to the red color of hemoglobin when oxygen is bound to it.

definition: An antibiotic (trade name Erythrocin or E-Mycin or Ethril or Ilosone or Pediamycin) obtained from the actinomycete Streptomyces erythreus; effective against many Gram-positive bacteria and some Gram-negative.
etymology: From (Streptomyces) erythr(eus) + -o- + -mycin (“antibiotic from a Streptomyces strain”).

definition: A glycoprotein secreted by the kidneys that stimulates the production of red blood cells.
etymology: From Ancient Greek ἐρυθρός (eruthrós, “red”) and ποιητής (poiētḗs, “creator, maker”) and -in.

definition: Mechanical device that regulates movement.
example: The escapement is the reason why clocks tick.
etymology: From escape + -ment. The watch component is so called because it allows a tooth to escape from a pallet at each vibration.

definition: Edible terrestrial snail usually served in the shell with a sauce of melted butter and garlic.
A flat protective covering (on a door or wall etc.) to prevent soiling by dirty fingers.
etymology: From Middle English scochon, from Anglo-Norman escuchon, Old French escusson (French écusson), ultimately from Latin scutum (“shield”). Related to scutum, scute, scudo, escudo, and écu.

definition: (art) the branch of philosophy dealing with beauty and taste (emphasizing the evaluative criteria that are applied to art).
example: Traditional aesthetics assumed the existence of universal and timeless criteria of artistic value.

definition: Deserving of respect or high regard.
etymology: From Middle English estimable, estymable, from Old French estimable, from Latin aestimābilis. Equivalent to esteem + -able and estimate + -able.

definition: Remove from customary environment or associations.
example: Years of boarding school estranged the child from her home.
etymology: From Old French estranger (“to treat as a stranger”), from Latin extraneus (“foreigner, stranger”) (from which also strange, stranger). Also see Spanish extraño.

definition: Relating to or caused by estrogen.
Applies to nonhuman mammals: a state or period of heightened sexual arousal and activity.
And others (‘et al.’ is used as an abbreviation of ‘et alii’ (masculine plural) or ‘et aliae’ (feminine plural) or ‘et alia’ (neuter plural) when referring to a number of people).
example: The data reported by Smith et al.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin et alii (“and others”).

definition: A philosopher who specializes in ethics.
etymology: From ethics + -ist and dropping the -s in the end of the word ethics.

definition: Centered on a specific ethnic group, usually one's own.
Belief in the superiority of one's own ethnic group.
An anthropologist who does ethnography.
Of or relating to ethnology.
example: Ethnological field work.

definition: The branch of zoology that studies the behavior of animals in their natural habitats.
Pertaining to or causing improvement in the offspring produced.
Of or the nature of euphemism.
example: ‘peepee’ is a common euphemistic term.

definition: In a euphemistic manner.
example: His violent death was euphemistically referred to as a passing away.

definition: A bass horn (brass wind instrument) that is the tenor of the tuba family.
The interpretation in harmonious bodily movements of the rhythm of musical compositions; used to teach musical understanding.
Intentionally cause the painless death of a person or animal.
example: John decided to euthanize his dying dog.

definition: Tending to vanish like vapor.
example: Evanescent beauty.
etymology: Borrowed from French évanescent (“evanescent”), from Latin ēvānēscēns (“disappearing, vanishing”), present participle of ēvānēscō (“to disappear, vanish; to die out, fade away;

definition: (of a leaf shape) pinnate with a pair of leaflets at the apex.
The sixth of the seven canonical hours of the divine office; early evening; now often made a public service on Sundays.
etymology: From Old English ǣfensang, equivalent to even + song. The use of even to mean evening is now obsolete except in poetry.

definition: The latter part of the day (the period of decreasing daylight from late afternoon until nightfall).
example: The mist rises from the lake at eventide.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English eventide, from Old English ǣfentīd, from ǣfen (“evening”) + tīd (“time”). By surface analysis, even + -tide.

definition: Come out in the end.
etymology: American English, from Latin ēventu(s) (“an event, happening”) + -ate (verb-forming suffix), perhaps modeled after actuate.

definition: In a wicked evil manner.
example: Grin evilly.

definition: The quality of being morally wrong in principle or practice.
etymology: From Middle English yvelnesse, from Old English yfelnyss; equivalent to evil + -ness.

definition: Surgically remove a part of a structure or an organ.
etymology: From Latin ēviscerātus, past participle of ēviscerāre (“to disembowel”), from e- (“out”) + viscera (“bowels”), equivalent to e- (“out”) + viscera + -ate.

definition: Surgical removal of an organ (or the contents of an organ) from a patient.
example: The evisceration of the animal was accomplished with a single blow of the knife.

definition: A label identifying the owner of a book in which it is pasted.
etymology: From Latin ex librīs (“from the books [of]”).

definition: Tending to exalt.
example: An exalting eulogy.

definition: Exclude from a church or a religious community.
example: The gay priest was excommunicated when he married his partner.
etymology: From Ecclesiastical Latin excommunicātus, perfect passive participle of excommunicō (“excommunicate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). By surface analysis, ex- + communicate.

definition: Waste matter (as urine or sweat but especially feces) discharged from the body.
etymology: From Latin excrēta, neuter plural of excrētus, past participle of excernere.

definition: Spur on or encourage especially by cheers and shouts.
etymology: From Middle English exorten, from Old French exhorter, from Latin exhortārī (“to encourage”), from ex- (“out of, from”) + hortārī (“to incite, spur”).

definition: Dig up for reburial or for medical investigation; of dead bodies.
example: The archeologist exhumed artifacts from the ground with a shovel.
etymology: From Medieval Latin exhumō, from Latin ex- + humō (“to bury”).

definition: Demanding attention.
example: Regarded literary questions as exigent and momentous.
etymology: From Latin exigēns, present active participle of exigō (“demand, require”). Doublet of exigeant.

definition: A logical quantifier of a proposition that asserts the existence of at least one thing for which the proposition is true.
The quality of being exotic.
example: He loved the exoticism of Egypt.

definition: In an expectant manner.
example: She looked at him expectantly.

definition: Compensation for a wrong.
etymology: From Middle French expiation, from Latin expiātiō(n) (“satisfaction”).

definition: The act of making clear or removing obscurity from the meaning of a word or symbol or expression etc.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French explication and its etymon Latin explicātiō, explicātiōnem. By surface analysis, explicate + -ion.

definition: A systematic interpretation or explanation (usually written) of a specific topic.
Deprive of possessions.
example: The Communist government expropriated the landowners.

definition: With little or no preparation or forethought.
example: An extemporaneous piano recital.
etymology: From Late Latin extemporāneus, from Latin ex tempore (“impromptu”).

definition: Defining a word by listing the class of entities to which the word correctly applies.
A skeletal muscle whose contraction extends or stretches a body part.
A skeletal muscle whose contraction extends or stretches a body part.
The quality or state of being outside or directed toward or relating to the outside or exterior.
example: Waste is a negative externality arising from consumption.
etymology: From external + -ity. In the economic sense coined by British economist Alfred Marshall in 1890.

definition: Outside territorial limits or jurisdiction.
example: Fishing in extraterritorial waters.

definition: (psychology) an extroverted disposition; concern with what is outside the self.
etymology: From New Latin extrāversio, from Classical Latin extrā- (“outside”) + versio (“a turning”). Equivalent to extravert + -sion. Popularized as a psychological term by the German works of Carl Jung.

definition: A Catholic sacrament; a priest anoints a dying person with oil and prays for salvation.
In an exuberant manner.
example: The exuberantly baroque decoration of the church.

definition: Joyful and proud especially because of triumph or success.
etymology: From Latin exsultāns, present participle of exsultō (“rejoice; boast”). See also exult.

definition: Lacking eyes or eyelike features.
example: Eyeless fish that evolved in dark caves.
etymology: From Middle English eyles, eieles, equivalent to eye + -less. Compare West Frisian eachleas (“eyeless”), Dutch oogloos (“eyeless”), German augenlos (“eyeless”), Swedish ögalös (“eyeless”), Icelandic augnalaus (“eyeless”).

definition: A small hole (usually round and finished around the edges) in cloth or leather for the passage of a cord or hook or bar.
example: Push the aglet of the shoelace through each of the eyelets, one at a time.
etymology: From Middle English oylet, from Old French oillet, equivalent to Old French oil (“eye”) + -et (diminutive suffix).

definition: A protective cloth covering for an injured eye.
A protective covering for the front of a machine or device (as a door lock or computer component).
With respect to the face.
example: If a judicial authorization is facially valid, the party challenging it will have the burden of proving that it was invalid.

definition: Something resembling a fact; unverified (often invented) information that is given credibility because it appeared in print.
etymology: From fact + -oid (“similar, but not the same”);

definition: Of or relating to the mental faculties.
example: Facultative feeder.
etymology: From French facultatif. By surface analysis, faculty + -ative.

definition: A sad Portuguese folksong.
etymology: From Portuguese fado (“fate”), from Latin fātum. Doublet of fate.

definition: A small being, human in form, playful and having magical powers.
Glazed earthenware decorated with opaque colors.
etymology: Borrowed from French faïence, named after the city of Faenza, Italy, where it was made in the 16th century.

definition: An irreversible accomplishment.
example: Thanks to a bureaucratic fait accompli, the demolition was already approved and has already started.
etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French fait accompli.

definition: The act of faking (or the product of faking).
A Muslim or Hindu mendicant monk who is regarded as a holy man.
A short broad slightly convex medieval sword with a sharp point.
etymology: From Middle English fauchoun, from Old French fauchon (cognate with Italian falcione), from Vulgar Latin *falciōnem, from Latin falx.

definition: A person who fells trees.
The likelihood of making errors.
Deciduous tree of southeastern United States and Mexico.
Sparsely branched North American perennial with terminal racemes of bright yellow flowers resembling those of the foxglove; sometimes placed in genus Gerardia.
etymology: Named for the resemblance of the type species, Agalinis purpurea, to the common foxglove (Digitalis purpurea).

definition: Western United States bushy herb having yellow pea-like flowers.
Weedy plant having short dry chafflike leaves.
Tall annual marsh elder common in moist rich soil in central North America that can cause contact dermatitis; produces much pollen that is a major cause of hay fever.
Common perennial herb having aromatic roots used as a substitute for sarsaparilla; central and eastern North America.
Make familiar or conversant with.
example: We familiarized ourselves with the new surroundings.

definition: The experience of becoming familiar with something.
Having achieved a comfortable relation with your environment.
Serving to make familiar.
In an intimately familiar manner.
example: Sid, as he was familiarly known by his friends, was one of the most respected and devoted members of the socialist minority group.
etymology: From Middle English familierly, equivalent to familiar + -ly.

definition: In a passionately fanatic manner.
example: He followed the teachings of his guru fanatically.

definition: Having fangs.
A creator of fantasies.
A hired hand on a farm.
Able to see distant objects clearly.
Relating to or characteristic of fascism.
example: Fascist propaganda.

definition: A rate (usually rapid) at which something happens.
etymology: From Middle English fastnes, fastnesse (“immovableness, stability; firmness, solidness; secure attachment; constancy; obstinacy; something giving firmness or strength; of sleep: soundness; of a wound: healing;

definition: Extremely silly or stupid.
A New Orleans district lying outside the original city limits; used in combination with the names of various quarters of the city.
example: In Faubourg Sainte-Marie.

definition: In a practicable manner; so as to be feasible.
In a faint and feeble manner.
example: The lighthouse, flashing feebly against the sleet-blurred, rocky backdrop of the coast of north west Norway.
etymology: From Middle English febly; equivalent to feeble + -ly, euphonically blending -le and -ly. Compare nimbly, nobly, and Latinate -ably and -ibly.

definition: A building where livestock are fattened for market.
One of a pair of mobile appendages on the head of e.g. insects and crustaceans; typically sensitive to touch and taste.
example: Are you more of a feeler or more of a thinker?
etymology: From Middle English feler, feeler, felar, equivalent to feel + -er. Animal organ definition from 1660s. Transferred sense of "proposal put forth to observe the reaction it gets" is from 1830.

definition: A nervous belligerent little mongrel dog.
etymology: Earliest sense is “fart”, and later “stink” as abbreviation for fysting cur “stinking dog” (1520s). From Middle English fysten (mid-15th century), from Old English. Cognate with Middle Dutch veest and Dutch vijst.

definition: Involving or being or having the nature of a crime.
example: Felonious intent.
etymology: From Middle English *felonious (implied in feloniously; compare felonous); equivalent to felony + -ous.

definition: Made by combining fibers with a binder using heat and pressure.
example: Felt is a felted cloth.

definition: One quadrillionth (10^-15) of a second; one thousandth of a picosecond.
example: Sheldon Cooper: My hair is growing at the rate of 4.6 yoctometers per femtosecond.

definition: Annual herb or southern Europe and eastern Asia having off-white flowers and aromatic seeds used medicinally and in curry.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English fenygreke, borrowed from Old French fenigrec, from Latin foenum-graecum (literally “Greek hay”), from foenum (“hay”, variant of faenum) + graecus (“Greek”).

definition: Aromatic seeds used as seasoning especially in curry.
A weekday on which no festival or holiday is celebrated.
Any particle that obeys Fermi-Dirac statistics and is subject to the Pauli exclusion principle.
example: The fermions treated by the Standard Model are the (composite) baryons and the (elementary) leptons and quarks.
etymology: From Fermi + -on. Named after Italian-American physicist Enrico Fermi. Coined by English physicist Paul Dirac in 1945 in a lecture titled "Developments in Atomic Theory".

definition: A protein containing 20% iron that is found in the intestines and liver and spleen; it is one of the chief forms in which iron is stored in the body.
etymology: From Latin ferrātus (“iron-bearing”) and -in; compare also ferri- and ferro-.

definition: A material possessing a property of spontaneous electric polarization that can be reversed by the application of an external electric field.
A boat that transports people or vehicles across a body of water and operates on a regular schedule.
A male man who operates a ferry.
Grass with wide flat leaves cultivated in Europe and America for permanent pasture and hay and for lawns.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English festu, from Old French festu (modern fétu), from Late Latin *festūcum, from Latin festūca (“stalk, stem, straw”).

definition: Grass with wide flat leaves cultivated in Europe and America for permanent pasture and hay and for lawns.
A collection of writings published in honor of a scholar.
etymology: Borrowed from German Festschrift, from Fest (“celebration; festival”) + Schrift (“writing (work of an author)”).

definition: One who engages in fetishism (especially of a sexual nature).
A shackle for the ankles or feet.
etymology: From Middle English feter, from Old English feter, Proto-West Germanic *fetur, from Proto-Germanic *feturaz (“fetter”), from Proto-Indo-European *ped- (“to step, walk; to fall, stumble”). Related to foot.

definition: The part between the fetlock and the hoof.
Showy evergreen shrub of southeastern United States with shiny leaves and angled branches and clusters of pink to reddish flowers that resemble an umbel.
Pasta in flat strips wider than linguine.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian fettuccine, plural of fettuccina (literally “little ribbon”), diminutive of fettuccia, from fetta + -uccia.

definition: Wallboard composed of wood chips or shavings bonded together with resin and compressed into rigid sheets.
A white insoluble fibrous protein formed by the action of thrombin on fibrinogen when blood clots; it forms a network that traps red cells and platelets.
etymology: From fibre + -in (used to form chemical names of proteins, etc).

definition: A protein present in blood plasma; converts to fibrin when blood clots.
Benign tumor containing fibrous tissue (especially in the uterus).
Benign tumor containing fibrous tissue (especially in the uterus).
Adopted in order to deceive.
example: A fictitious address.

definition: Annual grass of Europe and temperate Asia.
White-flowered Eurasian herb widely cultivated for forage and erosion control.
Stone that occurs naturally in fields; often used as building material.
As a devil; in an evil manner.
The property of being wild or turbulent.
etymology: From Middle English fersnesse; equivalent to fierce + -ness.

definition: Consisting of or forming human or animal figures.
example: A figural design.
etymology: From Old French figural, from late Latin figūrālis, from figūra (“figure”).

definition: Inability to see shapes and contours.
Representing figuratively as by emblem or allegory.
etymology: Late Middle English figuracion, from Middle French figuration, from Latin figūrō (“to form”). Equivalent to figurate + -ion.

definition: Small nut-bearing tree much grown in Europe.
etymology: Earlier filbert-nut, Philibert-nut, from Middle English filbert-note, from Anglo-Norman noix de filbert, so named because they are ripe near Saint Philibert’s Day.

definition: So thin as to transmit light.
example: Filmy wings of a moth.
etymology: From film + -y. Cognate with Middle Dutch velmich, vilmich (“filmy, membranous”). Piecewise doublet of filmic.

definition: Any fern of the genus Trichomanes having large pinnatifid often translucent fronds; most are epiphytic on tree branches and twigs or terrestrial on mossy banks.
The act of finalizing.
Not having or having lost fingers.
example: Born with a fingerless hand.

definition: An ornament at the top of a spire or gable; usually a foliated fleur-de-lis.
etymology: From Late Middle English finial (“(adjective) final;

definition: A bomb that is designed to start fires; is most effective against flammable targets (such as fuel).
example: A Molotov cocktail is a simple firebomb.

definition: A criminal who illegally sets fire to property.
The light of a fire (especially in a fireplace).
etymology: From Middle English fire liȝt, fyre lyghte, from Old English fȳrlēoht, equivalent to fire + light.

definition: A state treasury or exchequer or a royal treasury; originally the public treasury of Rome or the emperor's private purse.
etymology: Partly from Middle French fisc and partly from its etymon, Latin fiscus (“basket, money-bag, public treasury”); see fiscal.

definition: A bone of a fish.
example: He choked on a fishbone.

definition: Slow down by moving the tail sideways.
example: The airplane fishtailed on the runway.
etymology: From Middle English fisch tayle, equivalent to fish + tail.

definition: A drilling bit with cutting edges usually hardened against wear.
Attractive East Indian palm having distinctive bipinnate foliage.
Occurring in spells and often abruptly.
example: Fitful bursts of energy.
etymology: From fit (“convulsion, seizure; sudden burst of activity”) + -ful (suffix forming adjectives from nouns, with the sense of being full of, tending to, or thoroughly possessing the quality expressed by the noun).

definition: Any of the items furnishing or equipping a room (especially built-in furniture).
example: She liked the kitchen fitments.

definition: Hissing and bubbling.
example: A fizzing mass of froth.

definition: A whip used to inflict punishment.
etymology: From Latin flagellum (“whip”), diminutive of flagrum.

definition: A large metal or pottery vessel with a handle and spout; used to hold alcoholic beverages (usually wine).
Stratified stone that splits into pieces suitable as paving stones.
Made of or resembling flakes.
A flaming torch (such as are used in processions at night).
Extravagant elaborateness.
example: He wrote with great flamboyance.

definition: The quality of being easily ignited and burning rapidly.
A flat cake of thin batter fried on both sides on a griddle.
example: Sven ordered a stack of flapjacks with maple syrup, two strips of bacon, and an egg, sunny side up.
etymology: From flap (“to toss sharply”) + jack (“generic object”). So called from the process of baking it by flipping and catching it in the griddle when done on one side.

definition: A card with words or numbers or pictures that is flashed to a class by the teacher.
example: Many people use flashcards to learn languages.

definition: Tableware that is relatively flat and fashioned as a single piece.
A ketone that forms the nucleus of certain natural yellow pigments like riboflavin.
Any of a large class of plant pigments having a chemical structure based on or similar to flavone.
etymology: From flavone + -oid, from Latin flāvus (“yellow”). Not related to flavor.

definition: Lacking taste or flavor or tang.
example: Flavorless supermarket tomatoes.

definition: A muzzle loader that had a flintlock type of gunlock.
Containing flint.
example: Flinty slate.

definition: In a flippant manner.
example: He answered the reporters' questions flippantly.

definition: The phenomenon of floating (remaining on the surface of a liquid without sinking).
A flat mass of ice (smaller than an ice field) floating at sea.
etymology: Early 19th century. Probably from Norwegian Nynorsk flo (“layer, slab”), from Old Norse fló (“layer”).

definition: Something that restrains a flood or outpouring.
example: Suspension of surveillance opened the floodgates to illegal immigrants.
etymology: From Middle English flodegate, flodgate, flodeyate, floodȝate, flodȝete, equivalent to flood + gate.

definition: Light that is a source of artificial illumination having a broad beam; used in photography.
Illuminated by means of floodlights.
example: The floodlit courtyard.

definition: A board in the floor.
An embarrassing mistake.
etymology: Possibly suggested by fluff and flop. First appeared in the US as a verb c. 1924, and as a noun c. 1953.

definition: Failure to reach a minimum required performance.
example: He got two flunks on his report.
etymology: Alteration of funk, or perhaps a blend of flinch + funk.

definition: A soft mineral (calcium fluoride) that is fluorescent in ultraviolet light; chief source of fluorine.
A selective-serotonin reuptake inhibitor commonly prescribed as an antidepressant (trade names Prozac or Sarafem); it is thought to work by increasing the activity of serotonin in the brain.
Laid edge to edge (not overlapping).
Someone who plays the flute.
etymology: Probably from Middle French flutiste, equivalent to flute + -ist. Replaced Middle English flouter (“flute player”) from Old French flauteur.

definition: A simple type of jet engine; must be launched at high speed.
A trap for catching flies.
To force onto another.
example: He foisted his work on me.
etymology: Probably from archaic Dutch vuisten (“to take into one’s hand”), from Middle Dutch vuysten, from vuyst (“fist”); akin to Old English fyst (“fist”).

definition: Sell as genuine, sell with the intention to deceive.
(psychiatry) a psychological disorder of thought or emotion; a more neutral term than mental illness.
A tale circulated by word of mouth among the common folk.
Theater light at the front of a stage that illuminate the set and actors.
A trunk for storing personal possessions; usually kept at the foot of a bed (as in a barracks).
Someone who hunts for food and provisions.
example: In Japan a fungus forager can earn a good living.

definition: Refrain from doing.
etymology: From Middle English forberen, from Old English forberan (“to forbear, abstain from, refrain; suffer, endure, tolerate, humor; restrain; do without”), from Proto-Germanic *fraberaną (“to hold back, endure”);

definition: The topsail on a foremast.
The anterior portion of the brain; the part of the brain that develops from the anterior part of the neural tube.
The founder of a family.
example: Keep the faith of our forefathers.
etymology: From Middle English forefader, forfader, vorvader, from Old English forefæder (“forefather”), but possibly also merged with Old Norse forfaðir. Equivalent to fore- + father.

definition: A front foot of a quadruped.
etymology: From Middle English forefot, forfote, equivalent to fore- + foot.

definition: A natural elevation (especially a rocky one that juts out into the sea).
etymology: From Middle English foreland, equivalent to fore- + land.

definition: An early limited awareness of something yet to occur.
etymology: From Middle English fortaste, equivalent to fore- + taste (noun).

definition: A statement made about the future.
example: Foretellings of doom.

definition: An early warning about a future event.
etymology: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

definition: Either of the anterior pair of wings on an insect that has four wings.
A 10% solution of formaldehyde in water; used as a disinfectant or to preserve biological specimens.
The act of making formal (as by stating formal rules governing classes of expressions).
Of or relating to or derived from ants.
etymology: Formed from the root of Latin formīca (“ant”) + -ic.

definition: A colorless pungent fuming vesicatory liquid acid HCOOH found naturally in ants and many plants or made catalytically from carbon monoxide and steam; used in finishing textiles and paper and in the manufacture of insecticides and fumigants.
By good fortune.
example: Fortunately the weather was good.

definition: (of a ship) sinking.
In the fourth place.
example: Fourthly, you must pay the rent on the first of the month.

definition: Area consisting of a small depression in the retina containing cones and where vision is most acute.
etymology: From Latin fovea (“ditch, pit”). Doublet of foiba.

definition: Any of several plants of the genus Digitalis.
etymology: From Middle English fox-glove, foxes glove, from Old English foxes glōfa (“foxglove”). By surface analysis, fox + glove.

definition: A small dugout with a pit for individual shelter against enemy fire.
etymology: From Middle English foxhol, from Old English foxhol, equivalent to fox + hole.

definition: Someone who makes frames (as for pictures).
example: The Framers of the Constitution.

definition: Device or marking such as postage stamp, printed or stamped impressions, codings, labels, manuscript writings, or any other authorized form of markings affixed or applied to mails to qualify them to be postally serviced.
A machine that automatically stamps letters or packages passing through it and computes the total charge.
Make secure by lashing.
example: Frap a sail.
etymology: From Middle English frapen, from Old French fraper.

definition: Born free of free parents.
The owner of a freehold.
etymology: From Middle English free holder, freholdere, equivalent to freehold + -er. Compare Old Northern French fraunc tenaunt.

definition: Someone who takes advantage of the generosity of others.
Fruit (especially peach) whose flesh does not adhere to the pit.
Done of your own accord.
example: A freewill offering.

definition: Minute conical gastropod superficially resembling a limpet but living and feeding on freshwater plants.
Easily broken into small fragments or reduced to powder.
example: Friable sandstone.
etymology: Borrowed from French friable, from Latin friābilis (“friable”), from friō (“to crumble”).

definition: Of speech sounds produced by forcing air through a constricted passage (as ‘f’, ‘s’, ‘z’, or ‘th’ in both ‘thin’ and ‘then’).
etymology: From New Latin fricatīvus, from Latin fricāre (“to rub”). By surface analysis, fricate + -ive.

definition: A continuant consonant produced by breath moving against a narrowing of the vocal tract.
Having decorative ruffles or frills.
Large arboreal insectivorous Australian lizard with a ruff of skin around the neck.
Any of various herbs of the genus Gentianopsis having the margins of the corolla lobes fringed; sometimes included in genus Gentiana.
An almost pleasurable sensation of fright.
example: A frisson of surprise shot through him.

definition: Italian omelet with diced vegetables and meats; cooked until bottom is set then inverted into another pan to cook the top.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian frittata, from fritto (“fried”).

definition: Batter for making fritters.
Compound leaf of a fern or palm or cycad.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin frons, frond- (“leafy branch”).

definition: A man who lives on the frontier.
In a frugal manner.
example: In villages, the new pipeline marks the end of water as a precious liquid, to be dispensed frugally, weighed out drop by drop.

definition: The quality of something that causes or assists healthy growth.
In an unproductive manner.
(British informal) an airless smoky smelly atmosphere.
etymology: The origin of the noun is unknown;

definition: Unpleasantly and excessively suave or ingratiating in manner or speech.
example: Gave him a fulsome introduction.
etymology: From Middle English fulsom, equivalent to full + -some. The meaning has evolved from an original positive connotation "abundant" to a neutral "plump" to a negative "overfed".

definition: A psychology based on the assumption that all mental process are useful to an organism in adapting to the environment.
An adherent of functionalism.
(anatomy) the base of a hollow organ or that part of the organ farthest from its opening.
example: The uterine fundus.
etymology: PIE word *bʰudʰmḗn From Latin fundus (“bottom”). Doublet of fond and fund.

definition: Suited to or suggestive of a grave or burial.
example: Funereal gloom.
etymology: From Middle French funerail, from Latin funereus + -al.

definition: A commercially operated park with stalls and shows for amusement.
Of goods or commodities; freely exchangeable for or replaceable by another of like nature or kind in the satisfaction of an obligation.
etymology: 1765 as noun, 1818 as adjective, from Medieval Latin fungibilis, from Latin fungor (“to perform, discharge a duty”) + -ible (“able to”).

definition: Relating to or operated by a cable.
example: Funicular railway.
etymology: From Latin fūniculus (“thinner cord”), diminutive from fūnis (“rope, cord”) + -culus. By surface analysis, funicul(us) + -ar.

definition: A railway up the side of a mountain pulled by a moving cable and having counterbalancing ascending and descending cars.
Commonly used diuretic (trade name Lasix) used to treat hypertension and edema.
A full body animal suit.
In a furtive manner.
example: The soldiers were furtively crawling through the night.
etymology: From Middle English furtyvely; equivalent to furtive + -ly.

definition: Very spiny and dense evergreen shrub with fragrant golden-yellow flowers; common throughout western Europe.
etymology: From Middle English firse, furs, from Old English fyrs (“furze, gorse, bramble”), from Old English fyres (“furze”), related to Old English fȳr (“fire”); otherwise of unknown origin.

definition: Tapering at each end.
example: Fusobacteria are fusiform bacilli (spindled rods).

definition: (formerly) a British infantryman armed with a light flintlock musket.
etymology: Borrowed from French fusilier, from fusil.

definition: The quality of being indistinct and without sharp outlines.
(of a roof) constructed with a single slope on each side of the ridge supported at the end by a gable or vertical triangular portion of an end wall.
example: A gabled roof.

definition: A persistently annoying person.
example: He’s a regular gadfly and takes advantage of his friend’s generosity.
etymology: From gad (“sharp point, spike; (dialectal) sharp-pointed rod for driving cattle, horses, etc., goad”) + fly, in the sense of a fly which irritates cattle, etc., by biting them, similar to the prodding of a goad.

definition: Appliances collectively.
example: Laborsaving gadgetry.

definition: A ductile silvery-white ductile ferromagnetic trivalent metallic element of the rare earth group.
etymology: Named after chemist Johan Gadolin, a Swedish-speaking Finn, + -ium.

definition: A triangular fore-and-aft sail with its foot along the gaff and its luff on the topmast.
In a gay manner.
example: The scandals were gaily diverting.

definition: In a gainful way.
example: Are you gainfully employed now?

definition: An organ shaped like a helmet; usually a vaulted and enlarged petal as in Aconitum.
Someone who develops a game.
A traditional Indonesian ensemble typically including many tuned percussion instruments including bamboo xylophones and wooden or bronze chimes and gongs.
etymology: Borrowed from Javanese gamelan, from Old Javanese gamĕlan.

definition: In an intrepid manner.
example: He was seen by a shepherd, gamely negotiating a particularly tricky section of the mountain road to San Doloroso.
etymology: From game + -ly; compare Old English gamenlīċ (“belonging to games, sportive, theatrical, ridiculous”) and Middle High German gāmelich, gemelich (“joyful”).

definition: The use of dubious (although not technically illegal) methods to win a game.
example: They kept the other team waiting on the field until the last possible moment – that was a clear case of gamesmanship.

definition: Suggestive of sexual impropriety.
A plasma protein containing the immunoglobulins that are responsible for immune responses.
(British informal) sore or lame.
example: A gammy foot.
etymology: Origin obscure and uncertain. Possibly from the English dialectal (North Midlands) adjective game (“lame”), Welsh cam (“crooked”), or from Irish cam (“bent”), by way of Shelta.

definition: Tall and thin and having long slender limbs.
example: A gangling teenager.
etymology: An American English alteration of gangling.

definition: A temporary bridge for getting on and off a vessel at dockside.
etymology: From gang (“way, path, course of travel”) + plank (“board”).

definition: Large heavily built seabird with a long stout bill noted for its plunging dives for fish.
etymology: From Middle English ganet, gante, from Old English ganot, from Proto-West Germanic *ganat, *ganatō, from Proto-Germanic *ganatuz, *ganutô (“gander”), ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *ganzô.

definition: A musical scale with fewer than seven notes.
Cassava with long tuberous edible roots and soft brittle stems; used especially to make cassiri (an intoxicating drink) and tapioca.
A plant of eastern Asia; larger than Allium schoenoprasum.
Relating to or tasting or smelling of garlic.
example: Garlicky sauce.

definition: A court order to an employer to withhold all or part of an employee's wages and to send the money to the court or to the person who won a lawsuit against the employee.
Full of trivial conversation.
etymology: Adapted borrowing of Latin garrulus (“talkative”) + -ous, from the verb garriō (“to chatter”).

definition: A car with relatively low fuel efficiency.
A maser in which microwave radiation interacts with gas molecules.
Lower part of a horse's thigh between the hock and the stifle.
etymology: Uncertain; possibly a form of Gascoigne (“Gascon”).

definition: Surgical removal of all or part of the stomach.
etymology: From international scientific vocabulary, reflecting New Latin combining forms: gastr- + -ectomy, from Ancient Greek γαστήρ (gastḗr).

definition: An agent that counteracts or neutralizes acidity (especially in the stomach).
Washing out the stomach with sterile water or a saltwater solution; removes blood or poisons.
example: When the doctor ordered a gastric lavage the hospital pumped out my stomach.

definition: A physician who specializes in diseases of the gastrointestinal tract.
Of or relating to or involving the stomach and esophagus.
The workplace where coal gas is manufactured.
An oversize page that is folded in to a book or magazine.
Wild ox of mountainous areas of eastern India.
etymology: Borrowed from Hindi गौर (gaur), from Sanskrit गौर (gaura). Attested in English since the early 19th century. Doublet of gayal.

definition: So thin as to transmit light.
example: Gauzy clouds of dandelion down.

definition: A soup made with chopped tomatoes and onions and cucumbers and peppers and herbs; served cold.
etymology: From Spanish gazpacho, perhaps via Mozarabic *gazpelağo from Latin gazophylacium (“treasure-chest in a church”), alluding to the diversity of its contents. Alternatively, related to Spanish caspicias (“remnants”).

definition: A mechanical device for engaging and disengaging gears.
example: In Britain they call a gearshift a ‘gear lever’.

definition: Cut off the testicles (of male animals such as horses).
example: The vet gelded the young horse.
etymology: From Middle English gelden, from Old Norse gelda (“to geld, castrate”), from Proto-Germanic *galdijaną (“to castrate”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰel- (“to cut”).

definition: Speak or write in generalities.
Of or related to the genital and urinary organs or their functions.
example: Genitourinary infections.

definition: The system that includes all organs involved in reproduction and in the formation and voidance of urine.
An antibiotic (trade name Garamycin) that is derived from an actinomycete; used in treating infections of the urinary tract.
etymology: Alteration of gentamycin, as a blend of gentian violet + kanamycin, from the color of the actinomycete.

definition: Any of various plants of the family Gentianaceae especially the genera Gentiana and Gentianella and Gentianopsis.
etymology: Via Middle English from Latin gentiāna, which, according to Pliny the Elder, was named after Gentius (Ancient Greek Γένθιος (Génthios)), the last king of Illyria, who supposedly discovered the plant's medicinal benefits.

definition: Chiefly herbaceous plants with showy flowers; some are cultivated as ornamentals.
A green crystal (violet in water) used as a dye or stain or bactericide or fungicide or anthelmintic or burn treatment.
Elegance by virtue of fineness of manner and expression.
A woman of refinement.
etymology: From Middle English gentilwoman, modelled after gentilman (“gentleman”), equivalent to gentle + -woman.

definition: The parallax of a celestial body using two points on the surface of the earth as the earth rotates.
(mineralogy) a hollow rock or nodule with the cavity usually lined with crystals.
etymology: From French géode, from Latin geōdēs, from Ancient Greek γεώδης (geṓdēs, “earthlike”), equivalent to γῆ (gê, “earth”) + -ώδης (-ṓdēs).

definition: The branch of geology that studies the shape of the earth and the determination of the exact position of geographical points.
etymology: From French géodésie, from Medieval Latin geōdaesia, from Ancient Greek γεωδαισία (geōdaisía), from γῆ (gê, “earth”) + δαίω (daíō, “to divide”). By surface analysis, geode + -esy.

definition: A geologist who uses physical principles to study the properties of the earth.
Of or having an orbit with a fixed period of 24 hours (although the position in the orbit may not be fixed with respect to the earth).
A circular orbit around the Earth having a period of 24 hours.
A noun formed from a verb (such as the ‘-ing’ form of an English verb when used as a noun).
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin gerundium, from gerendus (“which is to be carried out”), future passive participle (gerundive) of gerō (“carry, bear”).

definition: Making gestures while speaking.
example: Her gesticulating hands and arms made words almost unnecessary.

definition: Used of the language of the deaf.
Footwear usually with wooden soles.
Any of various small cucumbers pickled whole.

A gastrointestinal hormone produced by epithelial cells lining the fundus of the stomach; appears to be a stimulant for appetite and feeding, but is also a strong stimulant of growth hormone secretion from the anterior pituitary.
etymology: From g(rowth) h(ormone)-rel(easing peptide) + -in (suffix forming names of chemical compounds), influenced by Proto-Indo-European *gʰreh₁- (“to grow”): see the December 1999 quotation.

definition: Large dark striped eland of western equatorial Africa.
Large brownish petrel chiefly of Antarctic seas.
A female giant.
etymology: From Middle English geauntesse, geaunesse, from Old French; equivalent to giant + -ess.

definition: A suspected cause of diarrhea in humans.
Hang on an execution instrument.
etymology: From Middle English gibet, from Old French gibet (French gibet), either from Frankish *gibb (“forked stick”) or from Latin gibbus (“hunchbacked”).

definition: Edible viscera of a fowl.
etymology: From Middle English giblets, from Old French gibelet (“game bird stew”), probably from gibier (“birds hunted for sport”).

definition: An impulsive scatterbrained manner.
Someone whose occupation is to apply an overlay of gold or gilt.
etymology: From Middle English gilder (“gilder; goldsmith”) [and other forms], from gilden (“to cover with gilding, gild;

definition: A young male attendant on a Scottish Highlander chief.
etymology: From Scottish Gaelic gille (“helper”), from Middle Irish gilla (“youth, young man; boy, male child; messenger, page, servant”), possibly borrowed from Old Norse gildr (“brawny, stout; of full worth”).

definition: A cocktail made of gin or vodka and lime juice.
example: Yeah, a piece of advice — once you’re back in circulation, don’t keep topping off a lady’s vodka gimlet when she’s not looking.
etymology: From Middle English gimlet etc., from Old French guinbelet, guimbelet, guibelet, probably a diminutive of the Anglo-Norman wimble, a variation of guimble (“drill”), from the Middle Low German wiemel;

definition: Prepare oneself for a military confrontation.
example: The U.S. is girding for a conflict in the Middle East.
etymology: From Middle English girden, gerden, gürden, from Old English gyrdan (“to put a belt around, to put a girdle around”), from Proto-Germanic *gurdijaną (“to gird”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰerdʰ-.

definition: The childhood of a girl.
Covered with ice (as by a glacier) or affected by glacial action.
Make glad or happy.
Tall coarse American herb having palmate leaves and numerous small white dioecious flowers; found wild in most alluvial soils of eastern and central United States.
Any of numerous plants of the genus Gladiolus native chiefly to tropical and South Africa having sword-shaped leaves and one-sided spikes of brightly colored funnel-shaped flowers; widely cultivated.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin gladiolus (“little sword, sword lily”), diminutive of gladius (“sword”). Compare Middle English gladiol, whence gladiole.

definition: Having an air of allure, romance and excitement.
example: Glamorous movie stars.

definition: A policy of the Soviet government allowing freer discussion of social problems.
Fitted or covered with glass.
Having a frosted look from a powdery coating, as on plants.
example: Glaucous stems.
etymology: From Latin glaucus, from Ancient Greek γλαυκός (glaukós, “blue-green, blue-grey”), 1670s. See Irish glas.

definition: Someone who picks up grain left in the field by the harvesters.
etymology: From Middle English glenar, glenere, equivalent to glean + -er.

definition: Sustentacular tissue that surrounds and supports neurons in the central nervous system; glial and neural cells together compose the tissue of the central nervous system.
etymology: From Ancient Greek γλία (glía), γλοία (gloía, “glue”), γλοιός (gloiós, “a glutinous substance, gum”)

definition: Having brief brilliant points or flashes of light.
example: Glinting eyes.

definition: Someone who travels widely and often.
Having the shape of a sphere or ball.
etymology: From Latin globosus (“round as a ball, spherical, globular”).

definition: Of or relating to glomeruli.
etymology: From glomerulus + -ar. By surface analysis, glomerul- + -ar.

definition: Thin double membrane surrounding the glomerulus of a nephron.
Having glossy hair.
example: A glossy-coated foxhound.

definition: Of or relating to or produced by the glottis.
example: Glottal stops.

definition: A stop consonant articulated by releasing pressure at the glottis; as in the sudden onset of a vowel.
A stop consonant articulated by releasing pressure at the glottis; as in the sudden onset of a vowel.
Showing a brooding ill humor.
Appearing to be glowing.
A glycoside derived from glucose.
Make a gurgling sound as of liquid issuing from a bottle.
example: The wine bottles glugged.
etymology: Onomatopoeic, imitating the sound of pouring or swallowing liquid.

definition: A gauge boson that mediates strong interaction among quarks.
etymology: From glue + -on. From being a particle (suffix "-on") that "glues" (attracts) together particles that feel the force carried by the gluon. Coined by American physicist Murray Gell-Mann in 1962.

definition: An amino acid occurring in proteins; important in the nitrogen metabolism of plants; used in monosodium glutamate to enhance the flavor of meats.
An enzyme in the body that is a powerful scavenger of free radicals.
Any one of three large skeletal muscles that form the buttock and move the thigh.
Of or relating to or near the gluteus muscles.
Branches of the internal iliac artery that supply the hip joint and gluteal region.
Any one of three large skeletal muscles that form the buttock and move the thigh.
Veins draining the gluteal muscles on either side of the body.
Any one of three large skeletal muscles that form the buttock and move the thigh.
example: I'm going to kick your gluteus.
etymology: From New Latin glūtæus, from Ancient Greek γλουτός (gloutós, “rump, buttock”).

definition: The outermost of the three gluteal muscles.
example: Look at the gluteus maximus on that woman!

definition: Any one of three large skeletal muscles that form the buttock and move the thigh.
Given to excess in consumption of especially food or drink.
example: Over-fed women and their gluttonous husbands.
etymology: From Middle English glotenose, glotenouse, glotonos, glotonous, glotounius, glotynous, from Middle French glotonos; equivalent to glutton + -ous.

definition: A sweet syrupy trihydroxy alcohol obtained by saponification of fats and oils.
etymology: From glyco- + -ine, from French glycérine, from Ancient Greek γλυκερός (glukerós, “sweet”) (compare γλυκύς (glukús, “sweet”)).

definition: A translucent crystalline compound found in sugar cane and sugar beets and unripe grapes.
Grind together, of teeth.
example: Gnashing your teeth.
etymology: From Middle English gnasten. Origin unknown; the word is probably either Germanic or ultimately onomatopoeic.

definition: A hasty eater who swallows large mouthfuls.
example: My dog is such a gobbler: she can empty her food dish in less than a minute.

definition: Small spiny-finned fish of coastal or brackish waters having a large head and elongated tapering body having the ventral fins modified as a sucker.
etymology: From Latin gobius (“gudgeon”), from Ancient Greek κωβιός (kōbiós), a type of small fish, of unknown ultimate origin. See also gudgeon.

definition: A female godchild.
etymology: From Middle English goddoghter, goddoȝter, from Old English goddohtor (“goddaughter”), equivalent to god- + daughter.

definition: Abnormally enlarged thyroid gland; can result from underproduction or overproduction of hormone or from a deficiency of iodine in the diet.
Any of numerous chiefly summer-blooming and fall-blooming North American plants especially of the genus Solidago.
A district where gold is mined.
Of or relating to the gonads.
example: Gonadal hormones.

definition: Hormone secreted by the anterior pituitary gland and placenta; stimulates the gonads and controls reproductive activity.
A common venereal disease caused by the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae; symptoms are painful urination and pain around the urethra.
Someone who spells words.
Disposed to please.
Disposed to please.
Low-growing perennial having leaves silvery beneath; northern United States, Europe, Asia.
Italian blue cheese.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian Gorgonzola, a town in northern Italy where the cheese originated.

definition: Large hawk of Eurasia and North America used in falconry.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English goshauk, from Old English gōshafoc (“goose hawk”), from gōs (“goose”) and hafoc (“hawk”). Compare also Old Norse gáshaukr and Late Middle English gosling.

definition: A rich meat stew highly seasoned with paprika.
etymology: From French goulasch, itself from Hungarian gulyás (“herdsman”), an ellipsis of gulyáshús (“herdsman meat”), gulyásétel (“herdsman food”), and/or gulyástokány (“herdsman stew”). First attested in English in 1866.

definition: A person who is devoted to eating and drinking to excess.
etymology: From Middle English gourmaunt, gormond, gromonde, from Old French gormant (“a glutton”, noun), from gormant (“gluttonous”, adjective), of uncertain origin.

definition: Small sometimes shrubby tree native to California; often used as an ornamental; in some classification systems includes the pygmy cypress and the Santa Cruz cypress.
Immoderately desirous of acquiring e.g. wealth.
Lacking graciousness.
example: A totally graceless hostess.
etymology: From Middle English graceles; equivalent to grace + -less.

definition: Excellence of manners or social conduct.
Pasture grass of plains of South America and western North America.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish grama (“grass”), from Latin grāmina, plural of grāmen (“grass”).

definition: Pasture grass of plains of South America and western North America.
A linguist who specializes in the study of grammar and syntax.
example: Huddleston and Pullum are well-known grammarians of the 21st century.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English gramarien, from Middle French gramarien, gramairien. Displaced native Old English stæfcræftiga.

definition: A nobleman of highest rank in Spain or Portugal.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish grande (adjective), from Latin grandis (“large, great”). Doublet of grand and grande.

definition: High-flown style; excessive use of verbal ornamentation.
example: The grandiosity of his prose.

definition: Showing unfeeling resistance to tender feelings.
A person who makes a grant in legal form.
example: Conveyed from grantor to grantee.

definition: A trust established to shift the income to someone who is taxed at a lower rate than the grantor for a period of 10 years or more.
New connective tissue and tiny blood vessels that form on the surfaces of a wound during the healing process.
etymology: From Late Latin grānulum (“granule”) + -ation. Attested earlier than granule and granulate. By surface analysis, granulate + -ion.

definition: New connective tissue and tiny blood vessels that form on the surfaces of a wound during the healing process.
A tumor composed of granulation tissue resulting from injury or inflammation or infection.
etymology: From granule + -oma. Among the many words derived from -oma that are in current common use, this word is one of only a few that do not denote a neoplasm; another is hematoma.

definition: An arbor where grapes are grown.
A silver-white mineral consisting of silver gold telluride; a source of gold in Australia and America.
Italian brandy made from residue of grapes after pressing.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian grappa. Doublet of grape.

definition: Combatant who tries to throw opponent to the ground.
Annual European vetch with red flowers.
Submerged marine plant with very long narrow leaves found in abundance along North Atlantic coasts.
Having leaves that resemble grass.
Warm friendly feelings of gratitude.
Cut into a desired shape.
example: Graven images.
etymology: From Middle English graven, igraven, from Old English grafen, ġegrafen, from Proto-Germanic *grabanaz, past participle of Proto-Germanic *grabaną (“to dig, trench”).

definition: A material effigy that is worshipped.
example: Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image.

definition: Of or relating to hydrometry.
Quantitative analysis by weight.
With respect to gravitation.
example: Gravitationally strong forces.

definition: A gauge boson that mediates the (extremely weak) gravitational interactions between particles.
etymology: From gravity + -on. Coined by Russian physicists Dmitrii Blokhintsev and F. M. Gal'perin in 1934, and reintroduced by English physicist Paul Dirac in 1959 in a lecture to the American Physical Society.

definition: A printing process that uses an etched or engraved plate; the plate is smeared with ink and wiped clean, then the ink left in the recesses makes the print.
A dyer's weed of Canada and the eastern United States having yellow flowers sometimes used in dyeing.
(ethnic slur) offensive term for a person of Mexican descent.
etymology: From grease + -er. Applied to mechanics because they frequently become greasy during the course of their work.

definition: Burdock having heart-shaped leaves found in open woodland, hedgerows and rough grassland of Europe (except extreme N) and Asia Minor; sometimes cultivated for medicinal and culinary use.

Burdock having heart-shaped leaves found in open woodland, hedgerows and rough grassland of Europe (except extreme N) and Asia Minor; sometimes cultivated for medicinal and culinary use.
A variety of kudu.
Small compact-bodied almost completely aquatic bird that builds floating nests; similar to loons but smaller and with lobate rather than webbed feet.
Tall herb with panicles of white flowers flushed with green; northwestern United States; sometimes placed in genus Swertia.
A grocer who sells fresh fruits and vegetables.
An awkward and inexperienced youth.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English grene horn, which is attested for “horn of a recently killed animal” and as the name of a horse. It may also have been used of young horned animals.

definition: The lush appearance of flourishing vegetation.
etymology: From Middle English grennesse, from Old English grennes; equivalent to green + -ness.

definition: Thin syrup made from pomegranate juice; used in mixed drinks.
etymology: Borrowed from French grenadine, from Middle French grenade (“pomegranate”).

definition: A dyer's weed of Canada and the eastern United States having yellow flowers sometimes used in dyeing.
Tropical American feather palm having a swollen spiny trunk and edible nuts.
A former English silver coin worth four pennies.
etymology: From Middle English grot, from Old English grot, from Proto-West Germanic *grot, from Proto-Germanic *grutą, related to *greutą. More at grit, grout.

definition: The hulled and crushed grain of various cereals.
Fastener consisting of a metal ring for lining a small hole to permit the attachment of cords or lines.
etymology: From obsolete French gromette (“curb chain”) (modern spelling gourmette).

definition: The quality of lacking taste and refinement.
100 groszy equal 1 zloty in Poland.

definition: Someone who maintains the grounds (of an estate or park or athletic field).

The basic unit of money in Paraguay; equal to 100 centimos.

definition: A burst of deep loud hearty laughter.

definition: The basic unit of money in Suriname; equal to 100 cents.
Free from evil or guilt.

etymology: From Middle English giltles, gultles, gyltles, from Old English *gyltlēas, equivalent to guilt + -less. Compare Old English sċyldlēas (“guiltless”).

definition: The basic unit of money in Suriname; equal to 100 cents.
etymology: From Middle English, from Middle Dutch gulden (florijn) (“golden (florin)”).

definition: Tendency to believe too readily and therefore to be easily deceived.
Covered with adhesive gum.
An adhesive label.
Someone who is a detective.

definition: Drink greedily or as if with great thirst.
example: The boys guzzled the cheap vodka.
etymology: Probably imitative of the sound of drinking eagerly; or from Old French gouziller, gosillier (“to pass through the throat”), from gosier (“throat”), and akin to Italian gozzo (“throat; a bird's crop”).

definition: Someone who drinks heavily (especially alcoholic beverages).
example: He's a beer guzzler every night.

definition: A meet at which riders and horses display a range of skills and aptitudes.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin gȳrus (“circle; circular motion”), from Ancient Greek γῦρος (gûros, “circle; ring”), from Proto-Indo-European *gew- (“to bend; to curve”). The English word is a doublet of gyro and gyrus.

A store where men's clothes are sold.
Suitability for living in or on.

definition: A feeling of anger and animosity.

definition: Of or relating to a hemorrhage.
A group of illnesses caused by a viral infection (usually restricted to a specific geographic area); fever and gastrointestinal symptoms are followed by capillary hemorrhage.
Stroke caused by the rupture of a blood vessel in the brain.
The handle of a weapon or tool.

Offensive breath.

Tranquilizer (trade name Haldol) used to treat some psychotic disorders and Tourette's syndrome.
etymology: From halo- + (pi)perid(ine) + -ol. By surface analysis, halo- + -peridol.

definition: Stable gear consisting of either of two curved supports that are attached to the collar of a draft horse and that hold the traces.
etymology: From Middle English hame, home, from Old English hama, homa (“a cover, skin”), from Proto-Germanic *hamô (“clothes, skirt”).

definition: A work produced by hand labor.
etymology: From Middle English handcrafte, handecraft, hond-craft, from Old English handcræft, equivalent to hand + -craft. Cognate with Dutch handkracht, German Handkraft.

definition: Someone who sets the betting odds based on calculations of the outcome of a contest (especially a horse race).
In a subordinate position.
example: Theology should be the handmaiden of ethics.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English handemayde, hand-maide, handmaide, handmayd, hand mayde, hand-mayde, haundmaid, hondemayde, hondmaide, hond-mayde.

definition: A work produced by hand labor.
etymology: From Middle English hondwerk, from Old English handweorc (“work done by hand; handiwork”), from Proto-Germanic *handuwerką; equivalent to hand + work. Cognate with Dutch handwerk, German Handwerk, Swedish hantverk.

example: Harmonically interesting piece.

Any recently hatched animal (especially birds).

A personal version of the fantasy world from popular media.

etymology: From head + canon. First attested in c. 2007.

definition: The position of headmaster or headmistress.
etymology: From head + -ship. Piecewise doublet of chiefship.

definition: The source of a river.

definition: Someone who listens attentively.

definition: The older inactive central wood of a tree or woody plant; usually darker and denser than the surrounding sapwood.

etymology: From heath + land. Compare Saterland Frisian Heedelound (“heathland”).

definition: A chronic emphysema of the horse that causes difficult expiration and heaving of the flanks.

A fence formed by a row of closely planted shrubs or bushes.

definition: Devoted to pleasure.
example: A hedonic thrill.

definition: Someone motivated by desires for sensual pleasures.
Marked by or paying little heed or attention.
example: We have always known that heedless self-interest was bad morals; we know now that it is bad economics.

definition: Having the sun as the center.

An airport for helicopters.

definition: A rowdy or mischievous person (usually a young man).
example: He chased the young hellions out of his yard.
etymology: An alteration, under the influence of hell, of northern English/Scottish dialectal hallion (“scamp, worthless fellow”), of unknown origin.

definition: Equipped with or wearing a helmet.
The property of providing useful assistance.
Lacking a visible order or organization.
etymology: In form a reduplication (similar to hurry-scurry and harum-scarum, both with initial /h-/ and /sk-/); perhaps based on Middle English skelten ("to hasten;

Of or relating to or involved in hematology.

Lysis of erythrocytes with the release of hemoglobin.

definition: Surgical procedure of stopping the flow of blood (as with a hemostat).
etymology: From hemo- + stasis. From Ancient Greek αἱμόστασις (haimóstasis, “styptic drug”).

definition: A farm building for housing poultry.
A man who drives a herd.
In this general vicinity.
example: The people are friendly hereabouts.

definition: Interpretive or explanatory.
etymology: Derived from Ancient Greek ἑρμηνευτικός (hermēneutikós, “of or for interpreting”), from Ancient Greek ἑρμηνεύς (hermēneús, “interpreter”).

Someone who worships heroes.
Eruptions along a nerve path often accompanied by severe neuralgia.
Containing a closed ring of atoms of which at least one is not a carbon atom.
A compound containing a heterocyclic ring.
A ring of atoms of more than one kind; especially a ring of carbon atoms containing at least one atom that is not carbon.
A colorless flammable liquid alkane derived from petroleum and used as a solvent.
A portable brazier that burns charcoal and has a grill for cooking.

definition: In a hierarchical manner.
example: Hierarchically organized.

In a high-minded manner.
example: He talks high-mindedly, but we don't know whether he acts according to his principles.

definition: A mixed drink made of alcoholic liquor mixed with water or a carbonated beverage and served in a tall glass.
etymology: From high + ball, of the same railroad origins as lowball.

The activity of excessive spending.
Noisy and mischievous merrymaking.
The fleshy part of the human body that you sit on.
The gatepost on which the gate is hung.
Having hips; or having hips as specified (usually in combination).

A tile shaped so as to cover the hip of a hip roof.
Having or covered with hair.
Of or relating to histology.
Involving the use of histology or histological techniques.
example: Histologically identifiable structures.

A performance of a play.

definition: (of a batter) without a hit.

North American annual or biennial with long soft hairs on the leaves.
A message that seems to convey no meaning.

definition: Restraint that attaches to something or holds something in place.
Allowing passage in and out.
example: Fred loved holey Dutch cheese.

definition: The branch of optics that deals with the use of coherent light from a laser in order to make a hologram that can then be used to create a three-dimensional image.

definition: Of or related to or being homonyms.

Dwarf aromatic shrub of Crete.

definition: East Indian tree cultivated for its immense edible fruit and seeds.
A hard green mineral consisting of sodium aluminum silicate in monoclinic crystalline form; a source of jade; found principally in Burma.
Unrefined brown sugar made from palm sap.

A Basque or Spanish game played in a court with a ball and a wickerwork racket.

definition: Affected by jaundice which causes yellowing of skin etc.

definition: Bourbon and sugar and mint over crushed ice.

definition: Place side by side.

definition: An unstable meson produced as the result of a high-energy particle collision.
A woman's dress style that imitates the caftan cloaks worn by men in the Near East.

Sores resulting from a tropical infection by protozoa of the genus Leishmania which are spread by sandflies.

Being three more than fifty.
