example: The legislation ran into a logjam.

definition: A garment that provides covering for the loins.
etymology: From loin + cloth. Compare Dutch lendenkleed (“loincloth”), German Lendenkleid (“loincloth”), Danish lændeklæde (“loincloth”), Norwegian lendeklede (“loincloth”), Icelandic lendarklæði (“loincloth”).

definition: Having long legs.
The largest boat carried by a merchant sailing vessel.
Having words written out in full by hand.
example: Longhand writing.
etymology: From long + hand, by analogy with shorthand.

definition: The dried fibrous part of the fruit of a plant of the genus Luffa; used as a washing sponge or strainer.
The basic unit of money in Canada.
example: The loonie continued to rise against the greenback today.
etymology: From loon + -ie from the depiction of a loon on the reverse (tail-side) of the Canadian one-dollar coin.

definition: Frequent and watery bowel movements; can be a symptom of infection or food poisoning or colitis or a gastrointestinal tumor.
example: See if that nut has too much looseness and tighten it if it does.

definition: Someone who takes spoils or plunder (as in war).
example: After the hurricane, before law was restored, looters stole everything that wasn't nailed down.

definition: Full of trivial conversation.
etymology: From Latin loquāx, loquācis (“talkative”) + -ous or from loquacity + -ous, ultimately from Latin loquor + -acious.

definition: Of or befitting a lord.
example: Heir to a lordly fortune.
etymology: From Middle English lordly, lordlich, from Old English hlāfordlīċ (“lordly; heroic; noble”), equivalent to lord + -ly (forming adjectives).

definition: Small brightly colored Australasian parrots having a brush-tipped tongue for feeding on nectar and soft fruits.
etymology: From Malay luri, name of kind of parrot, said to be a dialectal variant of Malay nuri. Doublet of lourie. Unrelated to Spanish loro.

definition: A globular water bottle used in Asia.
etymology: From Hindi लोटा (loṭā) / Urdu لوٹا (loṭā). (person who switches loyalties): From the fact that the lota pot has a tendency to fall over and roll around, as it is not stable sitting on its base.

definition: Unwillingness to do something contrary to your custom.
example: I was loth to return to the office without the Henderson file.
etymology: From German Loth (obsolete), Lot, later also from Dutch lood, both specific usages of the word for ‘lead’. Doublet of lead.

definition: Become louder.
example: The room loudened considerably.

definition: Someone who wastes time.
Pajamas worn while lounging.
Small magnifying glass (usually set in an eyepiece) used by jewelers and horologists.
An awkward stupid person.
etymology: From Middle English louten, from Old English lūtan, from Proto-West Germanic *lūtan, from Proto-Germanic *lūtaną. Cognate with Old Norse lúta, Danish lude (“to bend”), Norwegian lute (“stoop”), Swedish luta.

definition: Unhappy in love; suffering from unrequited love.
example: [Bhuvan, English captions, O Rey Chhori]: Even if Krishna were to meet a lovelorn Gopi in the grove...

definition: Make a deliberately low estimate.
example: The construction company wanted the contract badly and lowballed.
etymology: American railroad term that described one of two positions of the ball of a ball signal. Compare highball.

definition: Characteristic of a person who is not cultivated or does not have intellectual tastes.
example: Lowbrow tastes.
etymology: A bahuvrihi compound of low + brow. An Americanism whose first use appears c. 1902.

definition: Having or bringing misfortune.
example: The search party returned dejected from the luckless search.

definition: Informal terms for money.
etymology: From Middle English lūcre, lucor, lucour, lucur (“gain in money, profit; money; wages; illicit gain; advantage, benefit”), from Old French lucre or Latin lucrum (“advantage, profit;

definition: Excessively mournful.
example: His client’s lugubrious expression tipped off the detective that something lurked beneath her optimistic words.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin lūgubris (“mournful; gloomy”), with the suffix -ious.

definition: A workplace where lumber is stocked for sale.
example: I'll just go to the lumberyard and buy some more two by fours so we can finish building this.

definition: Of or relating to or characteristic of wolves.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin lupīnus, from lupus (“wolf”) + -īnus (“pertaining to”). Doublet of lupin and piecewise doublet of wolven, Latin lupus being a cognate of wolf and -ine being a doublet of -en.

definition: A chronic inflammatory collagen disease affecting connective tissue (skin or joints).
Someone waiting in concealment.
A craftsman who makes stringed instruments (as lutes or guitars or violins).
etymology: Borrowed from French luthier, from luth (“lute”).

definition: Become extravagant; indulge (oneself) luxuriously.
example: Luxuriate in the wonderful service of our five-star hotel.
etymology: First attested in 1621; borrowed from Latin lūxuriātus, perfect passive participle of lūxuriō, see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

definition: Being one more than sixty.
Being ten more than sixty.
Carotenoid that makes tomatoes red; may lower the risk of prostate cancer.
Swelling (usually in the legs) caused by lymph accumulating in the tissues in the affected areas.
A form of lymphocytic leukemia in which the abnormal cells in the circulating blood are almost totally lymphoblasts.
A central cohesive source of support and stability.
A sweet meringue-based confection made with egg white, icing sugar, granulated sugar, almond powder or ground almond, and food colouring.
Chewy cookie usually containing almond paste.
example: Like a big wife, at sight of lothed meat, Ready to travail; so I sigh and sweat, To hear this macaroon talk on in vain.
etymology: From French macaron. Doublet of macaron.

definition: Small silvery fish; Nova Scotia to Brazil.
A short plaid coat made of made of thick woolen material.
etymology: Respelling of Mackinac, a strait between Lake Huron and Lake Michigan, an island in the strait, and an important trading-post on the island;

definition: A relatively coarse lace; made by weaving and knotting cords.
A cooler darker spot appearing periodically on the sun's photosphere; associated with a strong magnetic field.
etymology: From Middle English macula (“spot on the skin or in the eye”), borrowed from Latin macula (“spot, stain”). Doublet of macchia and macule.

definition: Muslim schools in Bangladesh and Pakistan.
example: The Pakistan government decided to close down madrasas that provided military training for their students.
etymology: Borrowed from Arabic مَدْرَسَة f (madrasa, “school”), a noun of place from the verb دَرَسَ (darasa, “to learn, to study”).

definition: A woman lunatic.
The position of magistrate.
Liberality in bestowing gifts; extremely liberal and generous of spirit.
etymology: From Middle French magnanimité, from Old French [Term?], from Latin magnanimitās.

definition: A hypothetical particle with a single magnetic pole instead of the usual two.
The branch of science that studies magnetism.
A diode vacuum tube in which the flow of electrons from a central cathode to a cylindrical anode is controlled by crossed magnetic and electric fields; used mainly in microwave oscillators.
A female domestic.
etymology: From Middle English maide servant; equivalent to maid + servant.

definition: Pouch used in the shipment of mail.
example: In our mailbag this month, we've got no less than 12 letters from those of you who think that Jones should not have been benched.

definition: A woman's one-piece bathing suit.
A topsail set on the mainmast.
Capable of being maintained.
Highly decorated earthenware with a glaze of tin oxide.
example: […] the coloured glaze decorated wares which we now call majolica, but which Minton referred to as Palissy wares.
etymology: From Italian maiolica, named after the Island of Mallorca (formerly known as Maiòlica), which was once a commerce center for work produced in Valencia, Spain. Doublet of Mallorca and Majorca.

definition: Celebrate noisily, often indulging in drinking; engage in uproarious festivities.
Abnormal absorption of nutrients from the digestive tract.
A pattern of symptoms including loss of appetite and bloating and weight loss and muscle pain and steatorrhea; associated with celiac disease and sprue and cystic fibrosis.
Poorly adjusted to demands and stresses of daily living.
example: A maladjusted child.
etymology: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

definition: The arch of bone beneath the eye that forms the prominence of the cheek.
etymology: From modern Latin malaris, from Latin mala (“jaw, cheek-bone”).

definition: The arch of bone beneath the eye that forms the prominence of the cheek.
Discontented as toward authority.
etymology: From Middle French malcontent, from mal- + content; compare Late Latin malecontentus.

definition: The properties characteristic of the male sex.

An organic compound with the formula HO2CCH2CHOHCO2H; it is a dicarboxylic acid that is made by all living organisms, contributes to the pleasantly sour taste of fruits, and is used as a food additive.
A tumor that is malignant and tends to spread to other parts of the body.
The property of being physically malleable; the property of something that can be worked or hammered or shaped without breaking.
Any of several low-growing Australian eucalypts.
etymology: Probably borrowed from Wemba-Wemba mali; compare Woiwurrung mali.

definition: Australian mound bird; incubates eggs naturally in sandy mounds.
Adult female mallee fowl.
Not having enough food to develop or function normally.
A white crystalline sugar formed during the digestion of starches.
Black honeycreepers with yellow feathers around the tail; now extinct.
An unspecified time in the future.

An extraordinary writ commanding an official to perform a ministerial act that the law recognizes as an absolute duty and not a matter for the official's discretion; used only when all other judicial remedies fail.
A deep concavity in the temporal bone at the root of the zygomatic arch that receives the condyle of the mandible.
Any of various rotating shafts that serve as axes for larger rotating parts.
In a manful manner; with qualities thought to befit a man.
example: Having said her say, Peggy manfully shouldered her burden and prepared to break up yet another home.
etymology: From Middle English manfully; equivalent to manful + -ly.

definition: Having many worn or threadbare spots in the nap.
example: A mangy carpet.

definition: Handle roughly.
example: I was manhandled by the police.

definition: A starch made by leaching and drying the root of the cassava plant; the source of tapioca; a staple food in the tropics.
etymology: From French manioc, through Portuguese mandioca, ultimately from Old Tupi mani'oka. Doublet of manihot.

definition: An adverbial that describes how the action of a verb is carried out.
example: Manner adverbials (‘peacefully’) come before place adverbials (‘in our beds’).

definition: Resembling or imitative of or suggestive of a man rather than a woman.
example: A mannish stride.
etymology: From Middle English mannish, mannisshe, mannysh, from earlier mennish (“human”), from Old English mennisċ (“human, natural, humane”), from Proto-West Germanic *mannisk, from Proto-Germanic *manniskaz (“human”).

definition: A diuretic (trade name Osmitrol) used to promote the excretion of urine.
etymology: From earlier mannite (from manna + -ite) + -ol. By surface analysis, mann(ose) + -itol.

definition: The quality of being maneuverable.
example: Articulated buses were invented to improve the manoeuvrability of long buses capable of carrying a large number of passengers.

definition: Of or relating to or based on the manor.
example: Manorial accounts.

definition: A man servant.
example: I asked my manservant to attend to the washing and cleaning.
etymology: From Middle English man servant, man servaunt; equivalent to man + servant.

definition: Chiefly evergreen shrubs of warm dry areas of western North America.
etymology: Borrowed from Spanish manzanita, so named because the fruits look like little apples.

definition: Distilled from fermented juice of bitter wild marasca cherries.
etymology: From Italian maraschino, from marasca (“morello cherry”) + -ino (“diminutive suffix”), from amarasca, from amaro (“bitter”).

definition: Dalmatian bitter wild cherry tree bearing fruit whose juice is made into maraschino liqueur.
etymology: Derived from the historical use of the technique of preserving cherries in maraschino liqueur, an alcoholic beverage produced by the fermentation of marasca cherries;

definition: Distilled from fermented juice of bitter wild marasca cherries.
Someone who participates in long-distance races (especially in marathons).
The intermixture of fat and lean in a cut of meat.
Notes written in the margin.
example: We know what the composer was thinking as he wrote the piece because we can read his handwritten marginalia on the manuscript.
etymology: From New Latin marginālia (cf. margināle (neuter singular (adjective / noun)), from Medieval Latin neuter plural of marginālis (“on the periphery”), from Latin margō (“border, edge”). By surface analysis, marginal + -ia.

definition: The social process of becoming or being made marginal (especially as a group within the larger society).
example: The marginalization of the underclass.

definition: The military governor of a frontier province in medieval Germany.
etymology: From Middle Dutch marcgrāve (modern Dutch markgraaf), cognate with Old High German marcgrāvo (modern German Markgraf), from Proto-Germanic *markō (“boundary;

definition: A strong-smelling plant whose dried leaves can be smoked for a pleasant effect or pain reduction.
Aromatic Eurasian perennial.
etymology: From Old French majorane, from Medieval Latin maiōrana.

definition: Small soft-furred South American and Central American monkey with claws instead of nails.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French marmouset (“a gargoyle; a small child”), probably from marmouser (“to mumble”), of imitative origin.

definition: Inlaid veneers are fitted together to form a design or picture that is then used to ornament furniture.
example: Strawen marquetry.

definition: Very large red gum tree.
Of girls or women who are eligible to marry.
Bellflower common in marshes of eastern North America having lanceolate linear leaves and small whitish flowers.
Perennial Eurasian gentian with sky-blue funnel-shaped flowers of damp open heaths.
Perennial plant of Europe and America having racemes of white or purplish flowers and intensely bitter trifoliate leaves; often rooting at water margin and spreading across the surface.
Someone who demands exact conformity to rules and forms.
etymology: After the example of 17th-century French army officer Jean Martinet.

definition: A harness strap that connects the nose piece to the girth; prevents the horse from throwing back its head.
example: If a gambler plays a fair game repeatedly, his payoff over time is a martingale.
etymology: From Middle French martingale, from Occitan martegalo, feminine form of martegal, an inhabitant of Martigues, which is from Latin maritima. Possibly merged with Spanish almártaga.

definition: (used as an intensifier) excellently.
example: The plan worked marvellously, even better than we had expected.
etymology: From Middle English merveilously; equivalent to marvellous + -ly.

definition: An acronym for microwave amplification by stimulated emission of radiation; an amplifier that works on the same principle as a laser and emits coherent microwave radiation.
etymology: From MASER, acronym of microwave amplification by stimulated emission of radiation.

definition: A man who is aggressive in making amorous advances to women.
Having or furnished with a mast; often used in combination.
example: Probably was so masted when she set forth.

definition: An achievement demonstrating great skill or mastery.
An aromatic exudate from the mastic tree; used chiefly in varnishes.
etymology: From Middle English mastik, from Old French mastic, from Latin mastiche, from Ancient Greek μαστίχη (mastíkhē), from μαστιχάω (mastikháō, “to chew”) (note the chewing gum sense). Related to masticate.

definition: An evergreen shrub of the Mediterranean region that is cultivated for its resin.
Conifer of Australia and New Zealand.
A small folder of paper safety matches.
example: My company had matchbooks printed with the corporate logo as giveaway promotional items.
etymology: From match + book, since the 1890s. Paper matches were developed in the 1880s; folded books containing them, and the strike-on-cover concept, were developed in the 1890s; more in Wikipedia at matchbook.

definition: A short thin stick of wood used in making matches.
example: A piece of wood or cardboard becomes a matchstick once the end has been dipped in a sulfurous compound to turn it into a complete match.

definition: The first canonical hour; at daybreak.
etymology: From Middle English matyns, matynes, from Old French matines.

definition: A form of social organization in which a female is the family head and title is traced through the female line.
etymology: Coined after patriarchy, from Latin māter (“mother”) and Ancient Greek ἄρχω (árkhō, “to rule”). By surface analysis, matri- + -archy.

definition: Based on or tracing descent through the female line.
example: Matrilineal inheritance.
etymology: From matri- + lineal. Coined by British government anthropologist Northcote Whitridge Thomas in 1904 along with patrilineal.

definition: One related on the mother's side.
In a mature manner.
example: She acts very maturely for her age.

definition: Brittle flat bread eaten at Passover.
example: Matzo is eaten by Jews on Passover.
etymology: When stressed on the first syllable, from Yiddish מצה (matse), from Hebrew מַצָּה (matsá); pronunciations stressed on the second syllable are borrowed directly from Hebrew.

definition: A Jewish dumpling made of matzo meal; usually served in soup.
Meal made from ground matzos.
Slender insect with delicate membranous wings having an aquatic larval stage and terrestrial adult stage usually lasting less than two days.
A vertical pole or post decorated with streamers that can be held by dancers celebrating May Day.
example: How would you like the maypole decorated?
etymology: Compound of May + pole, so called in reference to its use on May Day.

definition: Grass with wide flat leaves cultivated in Europe and America for permanent pasture and hay and for lawns.
Large North American goldenrod having showy clusters of yellow flowers on arching branches; often a weed.
North American songbirds having a yellow breast.
The quality of having great value or significance.
A message that seems to convey no meaning.
example: All the little meaninglessnesses of human existence.

definition: The condition of having a highly technical implementation.
Intrusive in a meddling or offensive manner.
example: If those meddlesome kids hadn't turned me in, I'd have gotten away with my nefarious scheme!

definition: The evacuation of persons (usually by air transportation) to a place where they can receive medical care.
etymology: Syllabic abbreviation of medical evacuation, equivalent to med + evac.

definition: The ocular muscle whose contraction turns the eyeball medially.
In a medial position.
example: This consonant always occurs medially.

definition: In a medicinal manner.
Containing or consisting of or resembling bone marrow.
etymology: From Classical Latin medullāris. By surface analysis, medulla + -ary.

definition: A sheet of vascular tissue separating the vascular bundles.
A layer of myelin encasing (and insulating) the axons of medullated nerve fibers.
The feeling of patient, submissive humbleness.
etymology: From Middle English mekenesse, meknes, meocnesse; equivalent to meek + -ness.

definition: One million periods per second.
Of or relating to megaliths or the people who erected megaliths.
example: Megalithic monuments like Stonehenge.
etymology: PIE word *méǵh₂s From mega- (prefix meaning ‘very large, great’) + -lith (suffix meaning ‘stone’) + -ic (suffix meaning ‘of or pertaining to’, forming adjectives from nouns), probably modelled after monolithic;

definition: Memorial consisting of a very large stone forming part of a prehistoric structure (especially in western Europe).
A psychological state characterized by delusions of grandeur.
etymology: Borrowed from French mégalomanie; equivalent to megalo- + -mania.

definition: A very large urban complex (usually involving several cities and towns).
example: The Eastern Seaboard megalopolis extends from New Hampshire to Alexandria, VA.

definition: Of or relating to meiosis.
With respect to melody.
example: Melodically interesting themes.

definition: Melted snow or ice.
Relating to or made of or similar to a membrane.
example: Membranous lining.
etymology: From Middle French membraneux; equivalent to membrane + -ous.

definition: The sensory structures of the inner ear including the labyrinthine receptors and the cochlea; contained within the bony labyrinth.
Given to lying.
example: A mendacious child.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French mendacieux, from Latin mendācium (“lie, untruth”), from mendāx (“lying”), + -ious.

definition: The tendency to be untruthful.
etymology: From Late Latin mendacitas, from Latin mendāx (“deceitful, deceptive, lying”) + -itās (suffix forming nouns indicating a state of being). Mendāx is derived from mentior (“to deceive, lie”) (from mēns, mentis (“mind;

definition: A male member of a religious order that originally relied solely on alms.
etymology: From Middle English mendicant, from Latin mendīcāns, present participle of mendīcō (“beg”). Compare French mendiant.

definition: The monthly discharge of blood from the uterus of nonpregnant women from puberty to menopause.
example: A woman does not take the gout unless her menses be stopped.
etymology: From Latin mēnsis (“month”), the plural being mēnsēs (“months”), corresponding to the approximately month-long span of the menstrual cycle. Compare month.

definition: One who is being mentored.
example: A student mentor may support up to seven mentees.

definition: An economic system (Europe in 18th century) to increase a nation's wealth by government regulation of all of the nation's commercial interests.
A businessperson engaged in retail trade.
Relating to or characteristic of a meritocracy.
example: Meritocratic society.

definition: Of or relating to or located in a mesentery.
One of two branches of the aorta that pass between the two layers of the mesentery to the intestines.
A plexus of autonomic nerves.
A tributary of the portal vein passing from the intestine between the two layers of mesentery.
Attracting and holding interest as if by a spell.
example: She had a warm mesmeric charm.

definition: The middle germ layer that develops into muscle and bone and cartilage and blood and connective tissue.
Of or relating to a middle period of the Stone Age (following the paleolithic).
An elementary particle responsible for the forces in the atomic nucleus; a hadron with a baryon number of 0.
etymology: From Ancient Greek μέσον (méson, “middle”). Doublet of medium.

definition: Involving metabolism.
example: Metabolically important substances.

definition: Of or relating to the metacarpus.
example: Metacarpal bones.

definition: Dorsal and palmar arteries of the hand.
Any bone of the hand between the wrist and fingers.
Dorsal and palmar veins of the hand.
An engineer trained in the extraction and refining and alloying and fabrication of metals.
Change in the structure of rock by natural agencies such as pressure or heat or introduction of new chemical substances.
Expressing one thing in terms normally denoting another.
example: A metaphorical expression.

definition: In a metaphysical manner.
example: He thinks metaphysically.

definition: (of physical systems) continuing in its present state of equilibrium unless sufficiently disturbed to pass to a more stable state of equilibrium.
Spread throughout the body.
example: The cancer had metastasized and the patient could not be saved.
etymology: From metastasis + -ize (suffix forming verbs meaning to do things denoted by the adjectives or nouns the suffix is attached to).

definition: Antibiotic drug of the penicillin family used in the treatment of certain staphylococcal infections.
In a methodological manner.
example: Let us proceed methodologically.

definition: A liquid ester with a strong odor of wintergreen; applied externally for minor muscle and joint pain.
Central nervous system stimulant (trade name Ritalin) used in the treatment of narcolepsy in adults and attention deficit disorder in children.
Antiprotozoal medication (trade name Flagyl) used to treat trichomoniasis and giardiasis.
A heterosexual man that is particularly interested in his appearance, being well-groomed and fashion.
etymology: Blend of metropolitan + heterosexual, equivalent to metro- + -sexual. Coined by British writer Mark Simpson in 1994, it enjoyed a brief popularity in the early 2000s.

definition: A small spineless globe-shaped cactus; source of mescal buttons.
(often followed by ‘of’) a large number or amount or extent.
example: Many a little makes a mickle.
etymology: From Middle English mickle, michel, mikel, mochel, muchel, mukel (“much; many; large, tall; great”), from Old English miċel, myċel (“big, large; great; much”), from Proto-Germanic *mikilaz (“great, large;

definition: A small brewery; consumption of the product is mainly elsewhere.
An abnormally small head and underdeveloped brain.
Of or relating to microeconomics.
An economist who specializes in microeconomics.
Of or relating to or consisting of miniature electronic components.
Small sheet of microfilm on which many pages of material have been photographed; a magnification system is used to read the material.
Neuroglial tissue of mesodermal origin that can become phagocytic.
Caliper for measuring small distances.
A substance needed only in small amounts for normal body function (e.g., vitamins or minerals).
By using a microscope; so as to be visible only with a microscope; as seen with a microscope.
example: The blood was examined microscopically.

definition: One millionth (10^-6) of a second; one thousandth of a millisecond.
Surgery using operating microscopes and miniaturized precision instruments to perform intricate procedures on very small structures.
example: Reattaching his severed finger required microsurgery to suture together the tiny blood vessels.

definition: The middle portion of the brain.
(archeology) a mound of domestic refuse containing shells and animal bones marking the site of a prehistoric settlement.
The vein in the center of a leaf.
Giving milk; bred or suitable primarily for milk production.
example: Milch goats, milch camels.

definition: Cattle that are reared for their milk.
etymology: From Middle English melche cow, mylche cowe, equivalent to milch (“yielding milk”) + cow.

definition: Stone post at side of a road to show distances.
A person who advocates war or warlike policies.
example: It is widely agreed that rule by intransigent militarists led the Empire of Japan to ruin.

definition: Any of various plants of the genus Astragalus.
Any of various plants of the genus Astragalus.
A woman who works in a dairy.
A metric unit of volume equal to one thousandth of a liter.
Woodwork that has been machined at a mill.
A workman who designs or erects mills and milling machinery.
etymology: From Middle English mylle wryte; equivalent to mill + wright.

definition: A term of address for an English lord.
etymology: From French milord, from English my Lord. Compare milady.

definition: The imitative representation of nature and human behavior in art and literature.
etymology: From Ancient Greek μῑ́μησις (mī́mēsis), from μιμεῖσθαι (mimeîsthai, “to imitate”), from μῖμος (mîmos, “a mime”). By surface analysis, mime + -esis.

definition: Characterized by or of the nature of or using mimesis.
example: A mimetic dance.
etymology: From Latin mīmēticus or its etymon Ancient Greek μῑμητικός (mīmētikós, “imitative”). By surface analysis, mime + -etic.

definition: In a careful deliberate manner.
etymology: From Middle English myndefully, myndfolly, equivalent to mindful + -ly.

definition: A scientist trained in mineralogy.
etymology: From mineral + -logist. Compare later mineralogy and French minéralogiste.

definition: Excavation consisting of a vertical or sloping passageway for finding or mining ore or for ventilating a mine.
A minicar used as a taxicab.
The act of reducing something to the least possible amount or degree or position.
The fifth digit; the little finger or little toe.
example: Jones Minimus wants to join the rowing team.

definition: Bourbon and sugar and mint over crushed ice.
Coins collectively.
A small or minor detail.
example: He had memorized the many minutiae of the legal code.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin minutia, from minūtus (“small, little”), from minuō (“make smaller”). By surface analysis, minute + -ia.

definition: Someone who dislikes people in general.
etymology: From Ancient Greek from μισέω (miséō, “I hate”) and ἄνθρωπος (ánthrōpos, “man; human”); compare miser.

definition: Believing the worst of human nature and motives; having a sneering disbelief in e.g. selflessness of others.
Hatred of mankind.
etymology: From Ancient Greek μισανθρωπία (misanthrōpía), from μισάνθρωπος (misánthrōpos), from μῖσος (mîsos, “hatred”) + ἄνθρωπος (ánthrōpos, “human”). The word is analysable as miso- + -anthropy.

definition: An understanding of something that is not correct.
Improper or wicked or immoral behavior.
Be unsuccessful.
etymology: From Middle English miscarien. By surface analysis, mis- + carry.

definition: Cast an actor, singer, or dancer in an unsuitable role.
example: To miscast a glance.
etymology: From Middle English miscasten, equivalent to mis- + cast.

definition: In a disobedient or naughty way.
example: He mischievously looked for a chance to embarrass his sister.
etymology: From Middle English mischevously, myschevously, equivalent to mischievous + -ly.

definition: Interpret in the wrong way.
example: She misconstrued my remarks.
etymology: From Middle English misconstruen, equivalent to mis- + construe.

definition: A person without moral scruples.
example: The teacher sent the miscreants to see the school principal.
etymology: From Middle English myscreaunt, miscreaunt, from Old French mescreant (1080) "mis-believer", present participle of mescreire "to misbelieve" (modern mécroire). Cognate with French mécréant.

definition: A crime less serious than a felony.
Corrupt morally or by intemperance or sensuality.
Judge incorrectly.
example: I misjudged you. I don't like your politics but I appreciate your loyalty to your friends.

definition: Branded or labeled falsely and in violation of statutory requirements.

etymology: From picaro (“adventurer, rogue”) + -esque (suffix meaning ‘in the style or manner of’ forming adjectives), modelled after Spanish picaresco (“in the style or manner of a picaro;

definition: Flesh of young or small pike.
etymology: From Middle English pikerel; equivalent to pike + -rel.

definition: A meadow frog of eastern North America.
American plant having spikes of blue flowers and growing in shallow water of streams and ponds.
A representation of the Virgin Mary mourning over the dead body of Jesus.
Electricity produced by mechanical pressure on certain crystals (notably quartz or Rochelle salt); alternatively, electrostatic stress produces a change in the linear dimensions of the crystal.
A specific (often simplistic) category.
example: Fred was disappointed to find his pigeonhole empty except for bills and a flyer offering 20% off on manicures.
etymology: The noun is derived from pigeon + hole. The verb is derived from the noun.

definition: A plait of braided hair.
Rice cooked in well-seasoned broth with onions or celery and usually poultry or game or shellfish and sometimes tomatoes.
Make off with belongings of others.
example: Pilfer goods.
etymology: From earlier pilfre, from Middle English pilfre (“booty”), from Old French pelfre (“plunder, booty, spoils”), of unknown origin. Compare pelf.

definition: Having pillars.
example: The pillared portico.

definition: A small round woman's hat.
A seat behind the rider of a horse or motorbike etc.
etymology: From Scottish Gaelic pillean (“little rug”), from Latin pellis (“animal skin, pelt”).

definition: Expose to ridicule or public scorn.
etymology: From Middle English pilory, pillorie, from Old French pilori, pellori, which is either from Old Occitan espilori or Latin pīla (“pillar”).

definition: Plant bearing large mild thick-walled usually bell-shaped fruits; the principal salad peppers.
etymology: Borrowed from Portuguese pimento (“bell pepper; later any pepper”), similar to Spanish pimiento, from Latin pigmentum (“coloring;

definition: Butter blended with mashed pimento.
Aromatic West Indian tree that produces allspice berries.
European garden herb with purple-tinged flowers and leaves that are sometimes used for salads.
example: Lined up solidly with the Pimpernels and with the persecuted.

definition: A sleeveless dress resembling an apron; worn over other clothing.
etymology: Univerbation of pin + afore. The pinafore was originally pinned to the front of a dress, as it had no buttons.

definition: South American tamarin with a tufted head.
A small stiff cushion into which pins are stuck ready for use.
example: Insulin-dependent diabetics are human pincushions.
etymology: The noun is derived from pin + cushion. The verb is derived from the noun.

definition: Old World annual having fragrant purple to deep crimson flower heads; naturalized in United States.
The seed-producing cone of a pine tree.
(of a leaf shape) featherlike; having leaflets on each side of a common axis.
example: Mimosa is a tree with pinnate leaves.

definition: A leaf resembling a feather; having the leaflets on each side of a common axis.
Having pinnate leaves.
A woman's cap with two long flaps pinned on.
etymology: Variant of pinder, from Middle English pindere, pyndere, pundere, pendere, equivalent to pend (“to pen”) + -er.

definition: A meson involved in holding the nucleus together; produced as the result of high-energy particle collision.
etymology: From pi + -on, as alteration of pi-meson.

definition: Insincere talk about religion or morals.
The flues and stops on a pipe organ.
Having an agreeably pungent taste.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French piquant (“pricking, stimulating, irritating”), present participle of piquer, possibly from Old French pikier (“to prick, sting, nettle”). Doublet of picong. Related to pike.

definition: A card game for two players using a reduced pack of 32 cards.
(ballet) a rapid spin of the body (especially on the toes as in ballet).
etymology: Borrowed from French pirouette, see there for more; attested since 1706.

definition: An expedient adopted only in desperation.
example: ‘pis aller’ is French for ‘worst going’.

definition: Inspiring mixed contempt and pity.
example: Pitiable lack of character.
etymology: From Middle French [Term?], from Old French piteable. By surface analysis, pity + -able.

definition: As of footsteps.
(of instruments in the violin family) to be plucked with the finger.
etymology: Borrowed from Italian pizzicato, past participle of pizzicare (“to pluck”).

definition: Intended to pacify by acceding to demands or granting concessions.
example: Placating (or placative) gestures.

definition: The beach at a seaside resort.
etymology: From French plage, from Late Latin plagia, from Latin plaga (“region”) (cognate with English flake). Doublet of playa.

definition: Copied and passed off as your own.
example: Used plagiarized data in his thesis.

definition: Take without referencing from someone else's writing or speech; of intellectual property.
example: She was caught trying to plagiarize an article for her thesis.
etymology: From plagiary + -ize, ultimately from Latin plagiare (“to kidnap, to abduct”).

definition: Any of a series of triclinic feldspars that form rocks.
Flesh of large European flatfish.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English playce, plays, from Old French plaiz, from Late Latin platessa, from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús, “broad”). See platy-, plat and flat.

definition: Of or relating to plankton.
Unicellular algae, one of four families of Charophyte green algae.
An inactive form of plasmin that occurs in plasma and is converted to plasmin by organic solvents.
Wallboard with a gypsum plaster core bonded to layers of paper or fiberboard; used instead of plaster or wallboard to make interior walls.
A worker skilled in applying plaster.
A trowel used to spread and smooth plaster.
An explosive material that is easily molded around the object it is intended to destroy.
etymology: From French plastique. Doublet of plastic.

definition: Work table of a machine tool.
etymology: From French platine, from plat (“flat”). See plate, and compare platin.

definition: A skilled worker who coats articles with a film of metal (usually silver or gold).
A trite or obvious remark.
etymology: Borrowed from French platitude, from plat (“flat”).

definition: Play truant from work or school.
example: The boy often plays hooky.
etymology: See hooky for its origin; the construction of the phrase is in the same vein as play truant.

definition: A theatrical program.
example: He couldn't find her name on the playbill.

definition: A pleasant and secluded part of a garden; usually attached to a mansion.
etymology: From Middle English plaisaunce, plesaunce, from Old French plaisance. By surface analysis, please + -ance.

definition: In a pleasing manner.
example: The room was pleasingly large.
etymology: From Middle English plesingliche; equivalent to pleasing + -ly.

definition: Pleat or gather into a ruffle.
example: Pleat my hair.
etymology: From Middle English, from a variant of plait, from Old French pleit. Doublet of plait.

definition: Inflammation of the pleura of the lungs (especially the parietal layer).
etymology: From Middle English pleuresi, pleresye, that borrowed from Old French pleuresie (French pleurésie), from Late Latin pleurisis, alteration of Latin pleuritis. By surface analysis, pleur- + -isy.

definition: Erect perennial of eastern and southern United States having showy orange flowers.
Capable of being influenced or formed.
example: A pliant nature.
etymology: From Middle English pliaunt, from Old French ploiant, present participle of ploiier (“to fold”).

definition: Drop heavily.
A male man who plows.
etymology: From Middle English plowman, ploghmon, plouȝman, equivalent to plow + man. Compare Middle Dutch ploechman.

definition: Having or covered with or abounding in plumes.
example: The plumed serpent.

definition: Any of numerous biennial to perennial herbs with handsome purple or yellow or occasionally white flower heads.
Very large; of exceptional size for its kind.
example: Won by a plumping majority.

definition: Make or move along with a sound as of a horse's hooves striking the ground.
example: Enrique plunked his money down on the counter with a sigh and bellied up to the bar.
etymology: Onomatopoeic; the noun is attested earlier than the verb. Noun etymology 1, noun sense 3 (“dollar; large sum of money”) may refer to the sound of a coin hitting a surface. Compare plonk, plink.

definition: Set (something or oneself) down with or as if with a noise.
Be behind; approve of.
A cleric who holds more than one benefice at a time.
A political system governed by the wealthy people.
Large mass of intrusive igneous rock believed to have solidified deep within the earth.
Of igneous rock that has solidified beneath the earth's surface; granite or diorite or gabbro.
Large mass of intrusive igneous rock believed to have solidified deep within the earth.
Large watertight chamber used for construction under water.
The branch of mechanics that deals with the mechanical properties of gases.
Of or derived from or caused by bacteria of the genus pneumococcus.
Pneumonia caused by bacteria of the genus pneumococcus.
Vaccine (trade name Pneumovax) effective against the 23 most common strains of pneumococcus.
Pertaining to or characterized by or affected by pneumonia.
example: Pneumonic plague.
etymology: From the post-Classical Latin pneumonicus and its etymon, the Ancient Greek πνευμονικός (pneumonikós).

definition: A rapidly progressive and frequently fatal form of the plague that can spread through the air from person to person; characterized by lung involvement with chill, bloody expectoration and high fever.
A pustule in an eruptive disease.
etymology: From Middle English pok, from Old English poc, pocc (“pock; pustule; ulcer”), from Proto-West Germanic *pokk, from Proto-Germanic *pukkaz, *pukkǭ (“pock; swelling”), from Proto-Indo-European *bew-, *bʰew- (“to grow;

definition: The quantity a pocket will hold.
The branch of medicine concerned with the feet.
A woman poet.
etymology: From poet + -ess. Compare Middle English poetresse (“poetess”).

definition: Tropical American plant having poisonous milk and showy tapering usually scarlet petallike leaves surrounding small yellow flowers.
A strain of pest accidentally imported into Florida from the Middle East then spread to California where it is a very serious pest feeding on almost all vegetable crops and poinsettias.
In a pointless manner.
example: He spent his life in pointlessly tiresome drudgery.

definition: A common perennial death camas; Tennessee to Kansas to Texas.
An athlete who jumps over a high crossbar with the aid of a long pole.
American musteline mammal typically ejecting an intensely malodorous fluid when startled; in some classifications put in a separate subfamily Mephitinae.
etymology: From Middle English polcat, pulkat, of uncertain origin. Perhaps from Middle English *pole, *poule (“hen”), from Old French poule (“hen”) + Middle English cat. Compare English foulmart.

definition: Deciduous perennial low-growing fetid swamp plant of eastern North America having minute flowers enclosed in a mottled greenish or purple cowl-shaped spathe.
The brightest star in Ursa Minor; at the end of the handle of the Little Dipper; the northern axis of the earth points toward it.
An acute viral disease marked by inflammation of nerve cells of the brain stem and spinal cord.
etymology: Borrowed from German Poliomyelitis, from the Ancient Greek πολιός (poliós, “grey”) + μυελός (muelós, “marrow”) + -ῖτις (-îtis, “-itis”). Compare French poliomyélite.

definition: The virus causing poliomyelitis.
etymology: From polio + virus, the first element shortened from poliomyelitis.

definition: Vaccine prepared from poliovirus to provide immunity to poliomyelitis.
A power tool used to buff surfaces.
example: Where do you keep the floor-polisher?

definition: Give a political character to.
example: Politicize the discussion.

definition: A person or organization that causes pollution of the environment.
A polymer containing repeated amide groups.
Someone who is married to two or more people at the same time.
Of or relating to or resembling a polyhedron.
The space enclosed by three or more planes that intersect in a vertex.
A solid figure bounded by plane polygons or faces.
etymology: From New Latin polyedron, from Ancient Greek πολύεδρος (polúedros, “having many seats”), from πολυ- (polu-, “many”) + ἕδρα (hédra, “seat”); compare French polyèdre. By surface analysis, poly- + -hedron.

definition: A person of great and varied learning.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Ancient Greek πολυμαθής (polumathḗs, “having learnt much”), first attested in 1624. From πολύς (polús, “much”) (for more, see poly-) + μανθάνω (manthánō, “to learn”).

definition: A polymer containing repeated amide groups.
Very large yellowish-brown American silkworm moth with large eyespots on hind wings; larvae feed on fruit and shade trees.
etymology: Partial calque of translingual Antheraea polyphemus, named after Polyphemus due to the false eye patterns on their wings.

definition: Worshipping or believing in more than one god.
A lightweight thermoplastic; used especially in packaging and insulation.
Lack of elegance as a consequence of being pompous and puffed up with vanity.
example: With their super-formal tone and heavy use of jargon, legal documents are renowned for their pomposity.
etymology: From Middle English pomposite (“solemnity”), from Latin pompōsitās. By surface analysis, pomp + -osity.

definition: Cornbread often made without milk or eggs and baked or fried (southern).
etymology: Inherited from Middle English pone, from Anglo-Norman pone, from Late Latin pone, from Latin pōne, imperative of pōnere (“to place”).

definition: A member of the highest council of priests in ancient Rome.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin pontifex. Doublet of pontiff.

definition: Someone who spells words.
An establishment maintained at public expense in order to provide housing for the poor and homeless.
Cater to popular taste to make popular and present to the general public; bring into general or common use.
example: They popularized coffee in Washington State.

definition: An interpretation that easily understandable and acceptable.
Meat patties rolled in rice and simmered in a tomato sauce.
Someone who presents shows or sells writing or pictures that are sexually explicit in violation of the community mores.
A genetic abnormality of metabolism causing abdominal pains and mental confusion.
Gate consisting of an iron or wooden grating that hangs in the entry to a castle or fortified town; can be lowered to prevent passage.
etymology: From Middle English portcolyse, from Old French porte colëice, from porte (“door”) + feminine of colëiz (“sliding”), ultimately from Latin colāre.

definition: Indicate, as with a sign or an omen.
example: Let it be known that the Rapture portends the End of Days.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin portendere (“to foretell”), from por- (“forward”) + tendere (“to stretch”).

definition: Of momentous or ominous significance.
example: Such a portentous … monster raised all my curiosity.
etymology: From Late Middle English portentuous, from Middle French portentueux (“extraordinary, prodigious;

definition: Large steak from the thick end of the short loin containing a T-shaped bone and large piece of tenderloin.
Large steak from the thick end of the short loin containing a T-shaped bone and large piece of tenderloin.
A tagging program whose labels indicate a word's part of speech.
Of or relating to positivism.
example: Positivist thinkers.
etymology: Perhaps borrowed from French positiviste. Equivalent to positive + -ist, after positivism.

definition: A temporary police force.
etymology: From Late Latin posse comitātūs (“force of the county”, literally “power of the county”).

definition: Excessive desire to possess or dominate.

Postage stamps, or any other markings recognized and accepted by the postal system or systems providing service, which indicate the payment of sufficient fees for the class of service which the item of mail is to be or had been afforded.
Of or relating to postmodernism.
example: Postmodernist architecture.

definition: Low blood pressure occurring in some people when they stand up.
An arrangement of flowers that is usually given as a present.
Aromatic Eurasian perennial.
A white salt (KClO3) used in matches, fireworks, and explosives; also used as a disinfectant and bleaching agent.
Slang for a paunch.
The inherent capacity for coming into being.
example: Filled with potentiality.

definition: (medicine) the synergistic effect of two drugs given simultaneously.
A measuring instrument for measuring direct current electromotive forces.
A medical dressing consisting of a soft heated mass of meal or clay that is spread on a cloth and applied to the skin to treat inflamed areas or improve circulation etc.
etymology: From Middle English pultes, from Latin pultes, plural of puls. The phonological development from Middle English is regular; compare poultry.

definition: A boat propelled by an internal-combustion engine.
One of the most handsome prairie wildflowers having large erect bell-shaped bluish flowers; of moist places in prairies and fields from eastern Colorado and Nebraska south to New Mexico and Texas.
North American annual with red or rose-colored flowers.
Cookie-sized candy made of brown sugar and butter and pecans.
A crash involving a car or plane.
etymology: Originally World War II Royal Air Force slang; probably imitative.

definition: Make pregnant.
Idle or foolish and irrelevant talk.
etymology: From prate + -le (early modern English frequentative suffix). Compare Dutch pruttelen and Dutch preutelen (“to mutter”).

definition: The judicial principle asserting the supremacy of federal over state legislation on the same subject.
Someone who acquires land by preemption.
The stipend assigned by a cathedral to a canon.
example: C. 1593, Francis Bacon, letter to Sir Thomas Coneysby a lease of the prebend of Withington.
etymology: From Middle French prebende, from Medieval Latin prebenda, from Late Latin praebenda, from Latin praebendus, verbal adjective of praebere. Doublet of provender.

definition: A canon who receives a prebend for serving the church.
etymology: From Medieval Latin praebendārius, from Late Latin praebenda (“literally ‘things to be supplied’; prebend”), neuter plural of gerundive of praebeō (“supply”), from prae- (“pre-”) + habeō (“have, hold”).

definition: Of or relating to a growth that is not malignant but is likely to become so if not treated.
A sketchy summary of the main points of an argument or theory.
Knowledge of an event before it occurs.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French precognition or its source, Latin praecognitio, from praecognōscō (“to know beforehand”). Doublet of Germanic-based foreknowledge and Greek-based prognosis. Equivalent to pre- + cognition.

definition: An opinion formed beforehand without adequate evidence.
example: He did not even try to confirm his preconceptions.

definition: A glucocorticoid (trade names Pediapred or Prelone) used to treat inflammatory conditions.
An infant that is born prior to 37 weeks of gestation.
High status importance owing to marked superiority.
Clean with one's bill.
example: The birds preened.
etymology: Variant of prune (by influence of preen above). Attested in Chaucer (c. 1395) in the variants preyneth, prayneth, proyneth, prunyht, pruneth, from Old French proignier (“to trim the feathers with the beak”).

definition: Oil-secreting gland situated at the base of the tail in most birds.
The act of preferring.
example: The preferment went to the younger candidate.
etymology: From Middle English preferment, preferrement, prefferment; equivalent to prefer + -ment.

definition: Adapted for grasping especially by wrapping around an object.
example: A monkey's prehensile tail.
etymology: Borrowed from French préhensile, from Latin perfect passive participle prehēnsus, from prehendō (“grasp, seize”) + adjective suffix -ile, from Latin -ilis.

definition: Judge beforehand, especially without sufficient evidence.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French préjuger, itself an adaptation of Latin praeudico, praeiudicare. Doublet of prejudicate.

definition: Of or relating to or occurring during the time just before menstruation.
A syndrome that occurs in many women from 2 to 14 days before the onset of menstruation.
etymology: Coined by Katharina Dalton in 1953 to replace the earlier premenstrual tension, which she considered accidentally created the impression of focusing solely on PMS's mental aspects.

definition: Pay for something before receiving it.
example: To prepay postage.

definition: Of or relating to or formed with a preposition.
example: Prepositional phrase.
etymology: From Latin praepositiō (“a setting before, a preposition”), a calque of Ancient Greek πρόθεσις (próthesis, “a setting before, preposition (grammar)”) + -al.

definition: The object governed by a preposition.
A phrase beginning with a preposition.
(especially of human beings) at the age immediately before puberty; often marked by accelerated growth.
A foreboding about what is about to happen.
etymology: From Middle English presage, from Latin praesāgium.

definition: An elder in the Presbyterian Church.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin presbyter, from Ancient Greek πρεσβύτερος (presbúteros), from πρέσβυς (présbus, “elder, older”). Doublet of prester and priest.

definition: A child who attends a preschool or kindergarten.
The power to foresee the future.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English prescience, from Old French prescience, from Latin praescientia.

definition: Of or relating to a presentation (especially in psychology or philosophy).
example: What Whitehead calls ‘perception in the presentational immediacy’.

definition: Increase the pressure on a gas or liquid.
Take for granted or as a given; suppose beforehand.
example: I presuppose that you have done your work.
etymology: From Middle French presupposer, from Latin praesuppōnō.

definition: The act of presupposing; a supposition made prior to having knowledge (as for the purpose of argument).
etymology: From Middle French présupposition, from Latin praesuppositio, from the past participle stem of praesuppōnere (“to presuppose”).

definition: Surpassing the ordinary or normal.
example: Beyond his preternatural affability there is some acid and some steel.
etymology: From preter- + natural, after Latin prēternātūrālis/praeternātūrālis, from praeter nātūram, from praeter (“beyond”) + nātūra (“nature”); compare supernatural.

definition: In a pretty manner.
example: All this is most prettily done.
etymology: From Middle English pratily, prately, pratyly, pratylych; equivalent to pretty + -ly.

definition: The quality of being appealing in a delicate or graceful way (of a girl or young woman).
The act of puncturing with a small point.
example: He gave the balloon a small prick.

definition: Having prickly leaves.
Having a high price.
An extremely unrealistic, archaic form of idealization.
A wild or unrefined state.
Right of inheritance belongs exclusively to the eldest son.
Any of numerous short-stemmed plants of the genus Primula having tufted basal leaves and showy flowers clustered in umbels or heads.
etymology: The genus Primula was named by botanist Carl von Linnaeus (1707-1778) after Latin primus (“first”) because it flowers early.

definition: An artist who designs and makes prints.
The superior of a group of nuns.
etymology: From Middle English prieresse, priorasse, priores, prioresse, priorisse, priouresse, priures, priuresse, prowres, pryoras, pryorys, pryowresse, from Medieval Latin priōrissa and Old French prioresse, prieuresse;

definition: Deciduous much-branched shrub with dense downy panicles of small bell-shaped white flowers.
(of a restaurant meal) complete but with limited choices and at a fixed price.
etymology: Borrowed from French prix fixe, literally "fixed price".

definition: A professional boxer.
etymology: From prize + fighter or prizefight + -er (“person, agent”). See prizefight for sense development.

definition: Tending to prove a particular proposition or to persuade you of the truth of an allegation.
example: Evidence should only be excluded if its probative value was outweighed by its prejudicial effect.

definition: An official in a modern colony who has considerable administrative power.
Someone who postpones work (especially out of laziness or habitual carelessness).
example: Live a procrastinator, likely die a procrastinator.

definition: To a prodigious degree.
example: The prices of farms rose prodigiously.

definition: Treated irreverently or sacrilegiously.
etymology: From the past and past participle of the verb profane.

definition: The social process whereby people come to engage in an activity for pay or as a means of livelihood.
example: The professionalization of American sports.

definition: The trait of spending extravagantly.
etymology: From proflig(ate) + -acy (with -acy a suffixal construction from -ate + -cy), from Latin prōflīgātus, past participle of Latin prōflīgō, from prō- (“forward”) + flīgō (“to strike, dash”) (whence pro-).

definition: Wisdom that is recondite and abstruse and profound.
example: The situation's profundity escaped most observers.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English profundite, from Middle French profondite or its etymon Latin profunditās; by surface analysis, prof(o)und + ity. Compare profoundness.

definition: Any of a group of steroid hormones that have the effect of progesterone.
A reformer who opposes the use of intoxicating beverages.
The person who operates the projector in a movie house.
Antihistamine (trade name Phenergan) used to treat allergies; also an antiemetic used to treat motion sickness.
example: For quotations using this term, see Citations:promethazine.

definition: Someone who assists a performer by providing the next words of a forgotten speech.
Fleet antelope-like ruminant of western North American plains with small branched horns.
Relating to pronouns.
example: Pronominal reference.
etymology: From Late Latin prōnōminālis, from Latin prōnōmen, prōnōminis. By surface analysis, pro- + nominal.

definition: A phrase that functions as a pronoun.
Someone who reads proof in order to find errors and mark corrections.
Of or relating to or characterized by propaganda.
A woman prophet.
etymology: From Middle English prophetesse, from Old French prophetesse, from Late Latin prophetissa. By surface analysis, prophet + -ess.

definition: Presenting favorable circumstances; likely to result in or show signs of success.
example: Propitious omens.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman and Old French propicius, from Latin propitius (“favorable, well-disposed, kind”). Compare French propice, Portuguese propício and Spanish propicio.

definition: Someone who advances a suggestion or proposal.
The first beta blocker (trade name Inderal) used in treating hypertension and angina pectoris and essential tremor.
The part of a modern theater stage between the curtain and the orchestra (i.e., in front of the curtain).
etymology: From Latin proscaenium (“in front of the scenery”), from Ancient Greek προσκήνιον (proskḗnion), from πρό (pró, “before”) + σκηνή (skēnḗ, “scene building”).

definition: The arch over the opening in the proscenium wall.
The wall that separates the stage from the auditorium in a modern theater.
Convert to another faith or religion.
example: It is illegal to proselytize [children] in some countries.

definition: Of or relating to the rhythmic aspect of language or to the suprasegmental phonemes of pitch and stress and juncture and nasalization and voicing.
etymology: From prosody or its etymon Classical Latin prosōdia + -ic, probably after French prosodique, New Latin prosōdicus.

definition: The system of accentuation used in a particular language.
Surgical removal of part or all of the prostate gland.
An abrupt failure of function or complete physical exhaustion.
example: The commander's prostration demoralized his men.
etymology: From Middle English prostracioun, prostracyon, from Middle French prostration and its etymon Latin prōstrātiō, from prōstrātus, past participle of prōsternō. By surface analysis, prostrate + -ion.

definition: Taking on different forms.
example: Eyes … of that baffling protean grey which is never twice the same.
etymology: From Proteus + -an, referring to the Greek warden of sea-beasts, renowned for his ability to change shape.

definition: In a protective manner.
example: He bent protectively over the woman.

definition: The presence of excessive protein (chiefly albumin but also globulin) in the urine; usually a symptom of kidney disorder.
The hydrolysis of proteins into peptides and amino acids by cleavage of their peptide bonds.
The full complement of proteins produced by a particular genome.
etymology: Blend of protein + genome or proteo- + -ome.

definition: Formed in the later of two divisions of the Precambrian era.
example: Proterozoic life forms.

definition: A normal gene that has the potential to become an oncogene.
Of or relating to the Protozoa.
etymology: From translingual Protozoa + -an, equivalent to proto- + -zoan.

definition: Drafting instrument used to draw or measure angles.
example: Plastic protractor.

definition: In an obvious and provable manner.
Of or relating to Provence or its people or their culture.
Peculiarly fortunate or appropriate; as if by divine intervention.
example: A providential recovery.

definition: By the province; through the province.
example: Provincially controlled.

definition: In or of the next month after the present.
example: Scheduled for the 6th prox.

definition: Characterized by lust.
example: Prurient literature.
etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin prūriēns, present participle of prūriō (“itch”).

definition: An intense itching sensation that can have various causes (as by allergies or infection or lymphoma or jaundice etc.).
etymology: Borrowed from Latin prūrītus (“an itch, an itching”), from prūriō (“to itch”).

definition: Chronic itching of the skin around the anus.
A composer of sacred songs.
example: David is called The Psalmist because he is believed to be the author of the Book of Psalms.

definition: Poisonous crystalline alkaloid occurring with ephedrine and isomorphic with it.
Bearing or identified by an assumed (often pen) name.
example: The writings of Mark Twain are pseudonymous.

definition: In a strident manner.
